articles.title: No solo fue en 2026, Apple también subiría los precios de iPhone en 2027
articles.text:
Apple podría verse forzada a encarecer el iPhone por segunda vez en poco más de un año. Según información de la cadena de suministro citada por DigiTimes, la compañía habría aceptado pagarle a Samsung precios significativamente más altos por la memoria que utiliza en sus dispositivos a partir de 2027.
La empresa pagaría cerca de 2,00 dólares por gigabit de memoria RAM LPDDR5X y 0,33 dólares por gigabit de almacenamiento NAND desde el primer trimestre de 2027. En el tercer trimestre de 2026, esos mismos componentes rondaban los 1,50 dólares y los 0,26 dólares por gigabit, respectivamente. Eso equivale a una subida cercana al 33% en RAM y al 27% en almacenamiento.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuánto costaría un iPhone en 2027
El impacto varía según la memoria y la capacidad de cada modelo. Un iPhone con 12 GB de RAM y 256 GB de almacenamiento utiliza aproximadamente 96 gigabits de RAM y 2.048 gigabits de NAND.
Con las nuevas tarifas, solo esos dos componentes pasarían de costar cerca de 676 dólares a unos 868 dólares, un incremento de aproximadamente 192 dólares. Se trata de una estimación teórica basada en precios por gigabit, no del costo final que Apple paga por cada módulo integrado ya ensamblado.
Algunos analistas citados por DigiTimes van más allá: calculan que la memoria representa hoy alrededor del 10% del costo de los componentes de un iPhone, pero podría dispararse hasta el 45% en 2027. En un modelo de 256 GB, el costo de la memoria en el tercer trimestre de 2026 sería casi cuatro veces más alto que un año antes.
PUBLICIDAD
La subida de precios de un iPhone en 2027 dependerá de cuánto suba realmente el costo de la memoria RAM y NAND que Apple compra a Samsung. Si el acuerdo reportado se confirma, el gigabit de RAM pasaría de 1,50 a 2,00 dólares y el de NAND de 0,26 a 0,33 dólares, lo que podría trasladarse al precio final de los dispositivos.
Un aumento que ya empezó en 2026
Apple no llegaría a 2027 sin haber tocado antes los precios. Los iPhone 18 Pro y iPhone 18 Pro Max salieron al mercado con 100 dólares más que sus equivalentes de 2025, un incremento que también alcanzó a modelos más antiguos de las series iPhone 17 e iPhone 16.
PUBLICIDAD
En junio, Apple ya había subido los precios de Mac e iPad en al menos 100 dólares, con aumentos de hasta 1.300 dólares en ciertos modelos. A comienzos de septiembre, los iPhone se encarecieron entre 100 y 500 dólares según la variante.
El expresidente ejecutivo de Apple, Tim Cook, comparó en su momento la escasez de RAM provocada por la inteligencia artificial con una catástrofe centenaria, y advirtió sobre su consecuencia directa: el encarecimiento de los productos tecnológicos.
Hasta ahora, la compañía había logrado contener buena parte de esa presión mediante la optimización de su cadena de suministro y la absorción de costos. El ajuste de junio se consideró el resultado de meses de esfuerzo por limitar el impacto directo sobre los consumidores.
PUBLICIDAD
Por qué se encarece la memoria
El origen del problema está en la demanda de hardware para inteligencia artificial. Samsung, SK Hynix y Micron fabrican tanto la memoria de los dispositivos de consumo como los chips de memoria de alta capacidad para centros de datos, incluida la memoria de alto ancho de banda (HBM).
A medida que empresas como NVIDIA, OpenAI, Microsoft, Google y Anthropic aumentan agresivamente su demanda de HBM para sus centros de datos, la capacidad de fabricación se reorienta hacia ese mercado en detrimento de la memoria LPDDR y NAND que usan los teléfonos. Apple también contribuye a esa demanda a través de su computación en la nube privada, aunque a una escala mucho menor.
PUBLICIDAD
Las líneas de producción están dedicadas a distintos tipos de memoria, por lo que la capacidad destinada a IA no puede reconvertirse de inmediato para abastecer a la industria de los teléfonos inteligentes.
Las proyecciones citadas por DigiTimes anticipan que la demanda global de DRAM y NAND crecerá un 36,2% en 2027, mientras que la oferta apenas subirá un 19,3%. Esa brecha llevaría el déficit del 8,1% registrado en 2026 a un 13,6% en 2027, y podría mantenerse como mínimo hasta la primera mitad de 2028, cuando se espera que entre en funcionamiento nueva capacidad de producción.
Ese desequilibrio explica por qué, según DigiTimes, los precios globales de los teléfonos inteligentes ya habrían subido un 15% de media este año a causa del costo de la memoria.

articles.title: Sumo Logic expands Data Pipelines to cut observability and security data costs - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Sumo Logic expands Data Pipelines to cut observability and security data costs
Data analytics software firm Sumo Logic Inc. today unveiled an expanded Data Pipelines service that lets customers cut and reroute telemetry before any of it is ingested and stored.
The controls sit inside the company’s own platform rather than in a separate tool. Security and operations teams are collecting more telemetry than ever, and Sumo Logic argues that artificial intelligence workloads are steepening that curve. Ingesting everything gets expensive fast. The usual alternative is to collect less, which saves money until the missing data turns out to be what an investigation needs.
Sumo Logic pointed to a recent Gartner Inc. report published Sept. 2 that describes organizations defaulting to ingesting all their operational data and analyzing it later. Ingestion and storage costs have made that unworkable, the research firm said. Gartner also said high volumes of poor-quality telemetry hold back the generative AI and large language models reading that data.
The company said it ingests and analyzes close to seven exabytes of data a day for thousands of security and operations customers. What stays out of that flow is now the customer’s call, made before ingestion.
Two capabilities carry the release. The first is a live preview that shows what a rule will do to a stream before it is switched on, including routing data to a lower-cost tier or out to a destination outside Sumo Logic. The second is an assistant that writes those rules, work the company said used to take hours. Anomalies and format shifts in incoming data are flagged as they appear. Recommendations on what to route, transform or drop still go to a person for approval.
Keith Kuchler, chief product and technology officer at Sumo Logic, said the company has spent 15 years turning “exabytes of noise into actionable insights” for customers. AI has made that job harder and more expensive, he said. Moving data strategy decisions upstream, he added, lets teams set the purpose of their data before they pay to keep it.
More is due later this year. Sumo Logic said a visual, AI-assisted way to shape telemetry before it lands in its platform or a customer’s own cloud storage will follow, with controls over what gets collected from cloud and edge sources. A platform-neutral version, covering data headed to other vendors’ tools, comes after that.
An OpenTelemetry-native management layer is also planned, putting collector configuration, monitoring and deployment in one console. Sumo Logic said that removes the cost of running additional agents.
Sumo Logic is owned by Francisco Partners, which took the company private in 2023 for $1.7 billion. The company is showing the expanded pipelines in London this week, at the Gartner Security & Risk Management Summit.

articles.title: Apple Mac mini (Late 2026) Review: Strong performance, but losing its grip on value
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
Apple’s latest mini machine delivers the generational performance improvements we expect, dampened by the realities of AI price hikes.
Pros
- +Strong single- and multi-threaded performance
- +Storage performance improvements over previous M4 model
- +Small footprint
Cons
- -Recent price hikes erode the Mac mini’s value proposition
- -Memory and storage upgrades are now even pricier
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
It’s been nearly two years since Apple updated the Mac mini. And for better or worse, things have changed a lot during that time. The last Mac mini with an M4 processor went on sale in early November 2024, with a starting price of $599. The latest Mac mini that we’re testing today starts at $899, which we can directly blame on the rising costs of components due to the voracious demand for everything related to artificial intelligence (AI).
A $300 price hike in less than two years is unprecedented, but it’s a sign of the times, and we have to factor those realities when evaluating any product today. So with that context in mind, we’ll take a look at Apple’s newest Mac mini, which looks very familiar on the outside, but has undergone some internal hardware upgrades, to deliver some significant performance improvements over its predecessor.
Design of the Apple Mac mini (M6)
The Mac mini hasn’t changed on the design front, and that’s mostly a good thing. I’m always impressed with not only the minimalist style of this small form-factor computer, but also its tiny size. It has a 5-inch x 5-inch footprint, while standing just 2 inches tall. My only gripe is the power button, which remains stubbornly on the bottom of the system (back left corner). You’ll need to lift the system any time you want to turn it on (or force it to shut down in the event of a crash), and you’ll need to double-tap the power button when setting up Touch ID with an Apple Magic Keyboard for the first time. However, this is just a minor annoyance, as interacting with the power button on a modern Mac is a rarity.
Despite its trim dimensions, you do get a fairly decent number of ports on the exterior of the Mac mini. However, let’s get this out of the way first: Apple doesn’t give you any USB-A ports on the Mac mini, so keep that in mind before purchasing. So, if you have USB-A devices around, you’ll either need to keep some cheap USB-A to USB-C adapters on hand, or invest in a USB-C or Thunderbolt dock for connecting legacy devices.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Instead, our Mac mini review unit features two USB-C ports (10 Gbps) and a 3.5 mm headphone jack up front, along with three Thunderbolt 4 ports on the rear (M5 Pro systems swap the Thunderbolt 4 ports for Thunderbolt 5). You’ll also find a 2.5 GbE port (up from 1 GbE), an HDMI port, and the power port on the back. We should note that while our review unit was specced with the 2.5 GbE LAN, you can individually option a 10 GbE port for $100 extra. A 10 GbE USB-C adapter would set you back around $100, so Apple’s upgrade is surprisingly reasonably priced, and you don’t lose a port in the process.
When it comes to wireless connectivity, the Mac mini uses Apple’s new in-house N1 wireless chip instead of relying on a third-party design. It provides tri-band Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, which is an upgrade from the Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3 on the previous generation.
One thing to keep in mind with the Mac mini is that what you see is what you get when you purchase one. There are no internal upgrades available for the system once you’ve purchased it, so choose wisely before you click the buy button. Base systems come with an M6 chip (12-core CPU, 12-core GPU), 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. Our review unit features the M6 chip, 24GB of RAM, and a 512GB SSD. If you want to add storage post-purchase, we’d suggest taking a look at one of the best external SSDs.

Apple Mac mini (M6) Specifications
| Processor | Apple M6 (2 super cores, 4 performance cores, 6 efficiency cores) | 
| Graphics | 12-core GPU | 
| Memory | 24GB LPDDR5X unified memory | 
| Storage | 512GB SSD | 
| Networking | 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 | 
| Front Ports | 2x USB Type-C (10GB/s), 3.5 mm headphone jack | 
| Rear Ports | 3x Thunderbolt 4 ports (USB-C), HDMI, Ethernet | 
| Power Supply | Internal, 155W | 
| Operating System | macOS 27 Golden Gate | 
| Dimensions | 5 x 5 x 2 inches | 
| Price as Configured | $1,399 | 
Productivity Performance on the Apple Mac mini (M6)
Although the Mac mini is available with a more potent M5 Pro processor, our review unit came with the base M6 processor (12 CPU cores, 12 GPU cores). It also incorporates 24GB of LPDDR5X memory and a 512GB SSD.
This is the first system we’ve tested with the new 2-nanometer M6 processor. So, we were eager to see how it would perform against not only the M4 Pro in the previous Mac mini, but also the M5, which can be found in the current-generation MacBook Air and base MacBook Pro.
The M6 chip in the Mac mini had no trouble dispatching the M4, M4 Pro, and M5-equipped systems in the Geekbench synthetic CPU benchmark. In fact, it was 21 percent faster than the last M4 Pro Mac Mini in the single-core test. It also completely obliterated the M4 (10-core CPU, 10-core GPU) version of the Mac mini. The advantage versus the M5 system was lessened, but it was still a clear victory for the M6. The M6 actually slightly trailed the M4 Pro Mac mini (21,045 versus 22,661) in the multi-core test, which wasn’t too surprising given that the 12-core M6 was going up against a 16-core M4 Pro. But it was still a strong showing for the M6, given the architectural improvements that allowed it to get that close.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
We had some trouble obtaining consistent performance from our usual 25GB file transfer test, so we fell back to the Blackmagic Disk Speed Test for benchmarking the 512GB SSD. Needless to say, it presented a marked improvement over the preceding M4 Mac mini.
Storage performance was comparable to the M5 MacBook Pro on sequential writes, but slightly behind for sequential reads. It also slightly outperformed the M4 Pro Mac mini in writes, but was over 1,000 MBps ahead in reads. However, the M6 Mac Mini nearly doubled the write performance and more than doubled the read performance of the M4 Mac mini.
The similar multi-core performance in Geekbench was mirrored in our HandBrake test, during which we transcoded a 4K video file to 1080p. The M6 Mac mini completed the task in 2 minutes and 46 seconds, while the M4 Pro version was just one second behind. The M6 Mac mini was nearly 2 minutes faster than its M4 counterpart.
We ran Cinebench 2026 through 10 runs with the Mac mini, keeping track of its scores along the way. The Mac mini started off with a score of 5403, which rose to 5557 for the second run. For the remaining eight runs, the Mac mini was highly consistent, hovering between 5530 and 5554.
The M6 used in the Mac mini isn't yet fully supported by TG Pro, so we could only use the average of the available temperature sensors (power management sensors, power supply, and SSD). At idle, the fan spun at just around 1,000 revolutions per minute (RPM), with an average system temperature of 44 degrees Celsius. However, when running Cinebench 2026, the average system temperature rose to 64 degrees C, while the fan settled at around 2615 RPM.
Gaming and Graphics on the Apple Mac mini (M6)
Gaming shouldn’t be the primary goal with the Mac mini, but it can do some light lifting. I played Cyberpunk 2077 for a bit and benchmarked it. Although I was provided an Apple Studio Display (5K resolution) to test with the Mac mini, I ran benchmarks at 2560 x 1440 and 1920 x 1080, because the native 5K is a bridge too far for this game, given the hardware.
Using the "For this Mac" global setting, the Mac mini achieved 37.33 frames per second (fps) at 1440p and 58.11 fps at 1080p. With frame generation turned on, those numbers jumped to 62.61 fps and 96.24 fps, respectively.
If you don't mind turning the detail settings down a bit, you can achieve playable frame rates with the Mac mini. However, moving the detail slider to Ray Tracing (Medium) dropped frame rates into the 20 fps range even with frame generation turned on at 1440p.
macOS Golden Gate and Apple Intelligence
The Mac mini ships with macOS 27 Golden Gate, which was first made available to the public last week. macOS 27 is not a complete rethink of the desktop operating system formula for Apple, but it does provide a number of quality-of-life improvements for users.
One of the headlining features is new and improved Siri AI. While Siri was one of the first digital assistants to debut on a smartphone, it hasn't exactly been "smart," at least compared to its contemporaries. Siri AI now digs its fingers deeper into the operating system, allowing it to glean contextual data from your photos, mail, messages, and documents. You can access Siri AI from Spotlight (search) or using the dedicated Siri AI app. Siri AI is also vastly more useful, as it will more consistently answer general questions asked, rather than throw up its digital hands and say "Here's what I found on the web."
Apple's Shortcuts app is an incredibly powerful tool that has been available for years across the Mac, iPhone, and iPad product families. However, the granular control and seemingly limitless options can make creating a new shortcut daunting for newbies. So with macOS 27, you can now create a new Shortcut using natural language. For example, you could input, "Create a shortcut that sets the AC to 74 degrees when I leave work, and let my wife know what time I'll arrive at home," and it will take care of the rest.
Liquid Glass was one of the more controversial additions to macOS 26, with some people not liking the translucent makeover. MacOS 27 gives users more control over Liquid Glass, with sliders to adjust the intensity of the transparency effect.
Apple has also introduced plenty of system-level optimizations to improve performance across the board. For example, Apple says that AirDrop is up to 80 percent faster in macOS 27 than macOS 26, and a lot more reliable. Apps also open faster – any lagginess or stuttering that was perceptible in macOS 26 has been eliminated with this newest release. The best comparison I can make for the macOS 26 to macOS 27 upgrade is the fine-tuning that Apple did going from Mac OS X 10.5 Leopard to Mac OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard. There weren’t any major feature additions with that latter release, but there were a plethora of under-the-hood optimizations that made it much faster and more stable.
In addition, macOS 27 doesn’t install the Rosetta x86 translation software by default; you’ll need to download it when you first run a legacy x86 app. However, starting next year with macOS 28, you won’t be able to run apps that aren’t Apple Silicon-native, so Rosetta will be completely off the table.
Apple Mac mini (M6) Configurations and Warranty
The base Mac Mini comes with an M6 processor, 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD for $899. Before Apple's June 2026 price increases, the base Mac mini with M4, 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD cost $599. After the price increases, that $599 jumped to $799. Now, we're looking at another $100 increase for the base Mac Mini. There’s one standalone upgrade option: $100 extra gets you a 10 GbE port instead of the standard 2.5 GbE.
Apple also allows you to upgrade to 24GB or 32GB of RAM, along with 512GB, 1TB, and 2TB SSD options. A fully-loaded M6 Mac mini with 32GB of RAM, a 2TB SSD, and 10 GbE costs $2,399.
For people who require a bit more processing power, perhaps for AI tasks (as Apple seems so inclined to believe), the base M5 Pro Mac Mini (15-core CPU, 16-core GPU), with 24GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD, costs $1,699. However, you can go bonkers with the options, topping out with an M5 Pro (18-core CPU, 20-core GPU), 64GB of RAM, an 8TB SSD, and a 10 GbE adapter for a whopping $6,599. At that price, it’s probably worth looking at the Mac Studio.
All Mac minis come with a 1-year manufacturer warranty.
Bottom Line
The base M6 chip provides better single-core performance and nearly matches the multi-core performance of the optional M4 Pro in the previous-generation Mac mini. Compared ot the standard M4 Mac mini, the new M6 version blows it away in CPU and SSD performance.
These are the kinds of generational improvements we’ve come to expect with Apple Silicon, which seems to be firing on all cylinders these days. The new Mac mini also gets other, less-highlighted improvements, like faster standard wired networking (2.5 GbE versus 1 GbE) and Wi-Fi 7/Bluetooth 6.0 instead of Wi-Fi 6E/Bluetooth 5.4.
However, the elephant in the room is pricing for the Mac mini. Earlier this year, you could grab a base Mac mini for $599 – although availability was spotty after Q1, thanks to OpenClaw and anticipated price hikes. More importantly, over the years, going from one Mac mini generation to the next typically yielded performance benefits with no (or minimal) price increase. The AI revolution has rewritten the hardware rulebook, so we’re now faced with a new generation that is $300 more expensive than the previous model ($200 June price increase + another $100 increase for this new generation).
So in a matter of months, what was for years a screaming bargain for anyone looking for a cheap entry point into the Mac desktop ecosystem has gotten a lot more expensive. 16GB of memory and a 256GB hard drive are easier to justify at $599, but it’s a tougher pill to swallow at $899, and especially so with our review unit’s as-tested price of $1,399.
Brandon Hill is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware. He has written about PC and Mac tech since the late 1990s with bylines at AnandTech, DailyTech, and Hot Hardware. When he is not consuming copious amounts of tech news, he can be found enjoying the NC mountains or the beach with his wife and two sons.

articles.title: Jensen Huang proyecta duplicar la venta de chips de Nvidia para 2027
articles.text:
Jensen Huang, director ejecutivo de Nvidia, prevé que la compañía duplique sus ventas de chips para 2027, impulsada por la expansión de la inteligencia artificial (IA) en sectores cada vez más diversos. La empresa es el principal proveedor de aceleradores de IA, los procesadores usados para desarrollar y ejecutar modelos de esta tecnología.
El pronóstico llega después de que Nvidia anticipara, el mes pasado, un crecimiento de 70% en sus ventas para el próximo ejercicio fiscal. La compañía señaló entonces que sus ingresos podrían duplicarse si dispone de suficiente suministro para atender la demanda creciente.
PUBLICIDAD
Según Bloomberg, las acciones de Nvidia subieron hasta 2,8% en Nueva York el jueves pasado, una recuperación que ayudó a revertir las pérdidas de la semana anterior. El valor de la compañía acumula una subida cercana a 17% en lo que va del año.
El CEO de Nvidia sostuvo su visión optimista durante un acto organizado por el rey Carlos III en Escocia, pese a que aumentaron las preocupaciones sobre los posibles riesgos de la inteligencia artificial. Parte de los líderes del sector discutió la posibilidad de desacelerar el desarrollo de estos sistemas por su potencial peligro.
El directivo afirmó que las compañías tienen la responsabilidad de garantizar la seguridad de sus programas y servicios de inteligencia artificial antes de ponerlos en el mercado.
PUBLICIDAD
Por qué Jensen Huang rechaza nuevas regulaciones para la inteligencia artificial
Huang rechazó la necesidad de aprobar nuevas leyes o regulaciones específicas para el desarrollo de la inteligencia artificial durante la conferencia Dreamforce de Salesforce. Para el director ejecutivo, la seguridad de estos sistemas corresponde a la ingeniería y no al ámbito jurídico.
“La seguridad es un problema de ingeniería, no legal”, afirmó. “Estamos desarrollando software, después de todo. Estamos desarrollando sistemas de computación. Es un sistema de computación complicado, pero en definitiva sigue siendo un sistema de computación”.
El empresario se distanció de la definición de al menos un investigador de seguridad de OpenAI, que describió a la IA como una especie de “mente alienígena”. Huang sostuvo que se trata de hardware y software creados por personas, así que pueden ser controlados por seres humanos y mediante las leyes existentes.
PUBLICIDAD
Qué valor tiene la visión de Jensen Huang en la discusión sobre el avance de la IA
Huang dirige Nvidia desde antes del lanzamiento de ChatGPT y lleva años vinculado al desarrollo del hardware que sostiene la expansión de la inteligencia artificial. La compañía produce modelos de código abierto, agentes, espacios de prueba y otras herramientas destinadas al sector.
Para evitar el lanzamiento de productos inseguros, la posición del ejecutivo parte de que las fuerzas del mercado ya presionan a las empresas.
“Si no estamos seguros de la seguridad de los productos, como todas las empresas, como ustedes y yo, todas las empresas aquí presentes, si construyen un producto o un servicio y no confían en su funcionalidad, capacidad o seguridad, entonces no lo lancen. Y eso es algo muy obvio de hacer”, explicó.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuál es la responsabilidad de cada empresa en el desarrollo de IA
El director ejecutivo de Nvidia planteó que cada empresa debe decidir cuándo acelerar el desarrollo de sus productos y cuándo detenerse para corregir posibles fallas.
“Te tomas tu tiempo hasta que confías en que estás lanzando algo que el mercado va a apreciar. Las fuerzas del mercado ya están ahí. No necesitamos nuevas leyes. No necesitamos nuevas regulaciones. Solo necesitamos que las empresas decidan cuándo correr lo más rápido posible”, afirmó.
Asimismo, Huang rechazó que exista una contradicción inevitable entre la innovación acelerada y la seguridad. “Creo que innovación, velocidad y productos seguros… es una falsa disyuntiva. Definitivamente se pueden tener ambas cosas al mismo tiempo”.
PUBLICIDAD
El empresario agregó: “Corran lo más rápido que puedan. Pero si en algún momento sienten que la empresa está fuera de control, o que el producto no va a ser seguro, hagan una pausa y asegúrense de hacerlo bien”.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: À contre-courant, Jensen Huang balaie toutes les craintes sur l’IA... L’appât du gain ?
articles.text:
Pendant que de nombreuses voix dans l’industrie de l’intelligence artificielle (IA) alertent sur un possible scénario catastrophe, Jensen Huang hausse les épaules et minimise les craintes de ses pairs. Mais son entreprise a-t-elle intérêt à dire le contraire ?
Car le climat est de plus en plus alarmiste dans l’industrie. Après les agissements délibérés et dangereux de plusieurs agents IA, des employés d’Anthropic ont évoqué un risque concret et réel pour l’humanité. Dans la foulée, Dario Amodei, patron de la start-up, a publié un long essai appelant à « ralentir le rythme » du développement de l’IA. Il est soutenu par Sam Altman et Elon Musk. Mais visiblement, tout le monde n'est pas du même avis.
Le bras droit de Trump sur l’IA
Dans une interview accordée à CBS News, le patron de NVIDIA est catégorique : « Il y a 0 % de chances que ce soit la fin du monde en 2030. Faire peur aux gens n’est pas nécessaire. C’est irresponsable ». Il va jusqu’à qualifier les mises en garde d’un employé démissionnaire d’Anthropic d’« irresponsables », estimant qu’elles ne reposent sur aucune base scientifique. Pour lui, la sécurité de l’IA n’a rien d’un dilemme existentiel : c'est un « problème d'ingénierie », qui se résout avec du « bon vieux génie logiciel ».
Une posture qui lui vaut les faveurs de Donald Trump, lui qui n’entend absolument pas freiner le développement des modèles au risque de voir la Chine devancer les États-Unis. Huang est d’ailleurs attendu au dîner organisé le 24 septembre prochain en l’honneur de Xi Jinping.
Sans surprise, Huang rejette également tout appel à un renforcement de la régulation. Selon lui, les lois existantes sur la responsabilité des produits et l’accès non autorisé aux systèmes suffisent largement à encadrer les dérives de l’IA. Une position qui colle à celle défendue par Donald Trump, qui a lui-même écrit que le seul garde-fou dont l’IA avait besoin était « un président fort et intelligent ».
NVIDIA joue gros
Il n’y a rien de vraiment étonnant, NVIDIA étant aujourd’hui au cœur de toute l’industrie de l’IA. Ses puces alimentent la quasi-totalité des modèles les plus puissants, ce qui lui a permis de devenir l’entreprise la plus valorisée au monde. Son P.-D. G prévoit, d’ailleurs, d’encore doubler ses ventes de puces l’an prochain. Concrètement, plus l'industrie accélère, plus NVIDIA prospère.
En parallèle, il est bon de noter que Dario Amodei appelle à restreindre les exportations de processeurs de pointe vers la Chine. Huang, lui, plaide pour le contraire, tant le marché de l’Empire du Milieu est crucial pour les activités de son entreprise. Difficile, dans ce contexte, de savoir si le dirigeant agit en tant qu’observateur objectif, ou en défenseur de ses propres intérêts commerciaux.

articles.title: The Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete is a ridiculously clever and exceedingly competent premium hybrid robot vac for the well-heeled
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete is about as close as you can get to putting all your vacuuming and mopping duties on full autopilot. This hugely ambitious robot cleaner combines exceptional suction, clever dirt detection, rock-solid navigation, threshold crossing, impressive extendable mopping technology, and an elaborate and very handsome-looking self-cleaning dock. Granted, the X60 Pro Ultra isn’t cheap and there’s a lot of technology on board that, for some, may feel almost excessive. But if you want the ultimate hands-off cleaning experience, this is unquestionably one of the most impressive robot cleaners yet, and one that came ever so close to grasping a full five-star accolade.
Pros
- +Class-leading design touches
- +Superb vacuum perfomance
- +Highly reliable
Cons
- -Possibly too complex for some
- -Not cheap
- -Some minor obstacle-avoidance quirks
Why you can trust TechRadar
Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete review: two-minute review
Dreame’s flagship X60 Pro Ultra Complete is one of the most feature-filled, efficient and reliable hybrid robot cleaners this writer has so far reviewed — and I've reviewed many. Its class-leading 42,000Pa of suction power is certainly attention-grabbing, but the cleverness of this autonomous floor bot goes well beyond brute suction force.
Like some Roborock models, the X60 Pro Ultra is equipped with a retractable LiDAR turret that allows the unit to scoot under the lowest of furnishings with a floor clearance of just 3.5 inches (9cm). Better still, it can also tackle thresholds up to 3.9 inches (10cm) in height, so doorways and awkward transitions are much less likely to bring its cleaning mission to an abrupt halt.
Dreame has also addressed one of the biggest weaknesses of robot cleaners – getting properly into edges and corners. Where most premium bots are able to extend one of the mops by a couple of inches, this one is capable of extending it's edge-cleaning mop to an extremely impressive seven inches (18cm), and you can see the amazing results of this when it's working along skirting boards and around chair legs. Likewise, its front side-mounted sweeper brush can also reach up to four inches (12cm) into corners for a much more thorough sweep.
Dreame appears to have thrown everything it has into this flagship model, and the results are very impressive. Granted, it’s expensive, possibly over-engineered and perhaps more robot cleaner than most people actually need, but if your idea of luxury is never having to sweep or mop floors again, this model is a very tempting proposition, despite some minor anomalies in the obstacle avoidance department. The fact it comes with a surfeit of extra accessories — including spare dust bags, filters and rollers — is the icing on a very substantial cake.
Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete review: price & availability
- List price £1,299 / €1,499 / $1,699.99 (X60 Max Ultra)
- Launch date July 2026
- Availability UK and parts of Europe
At the time of writing, the Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete is available in the UK for £1,299, with retailers including Dreame, Amazon and John Lewis & Partners listing it. It is also available in most parts of Europe, priced at €1,499, with some discounts taking it to a much lower €1,199.
In the USA, Dreame is concentrating on the X60 Max Ultra Complete, a slightly different variant with lower suction power (35,00Pa) than the UK-spec X60 Pro Ultra Complete. You can purchase the Max version via the US Dreame store for $1,699.99 or Amazon where it shifts for a slightly discounted $1,614.99.
At the time of writing, the Dreame X60 Pro Ultra doesn't seem to be available in Australia yet.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
In the UK, the X60 Pro Ultra Complete is firmly in premium robot-vacuum territory, so there are plenty of alternatives worth considering. The Roborock Saros 20 is an obvious rival that offers a similarly sophisticated low-profile design for a shade under £1,000 and the Ecovacs Deebot X8 Pro Omni is another strong contender, particularly if mopping performance is a priority. Dreame’s own X40 Ultra is also worth considering if you want many of the flagship brand’s features without spending X60 Pro Ultra money.
However, for design, performance, impressive specs and the horde of spare parts it comes with, the X60 Pro Ultra Complete is difficult to ignore. While its combination of 42,000Pa of suction power, extendable cleaning hardware and highly automated dock puts it firmly at the expensive end of the market, I think it's a price worth paying.
- Value score: 4.5/5
Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete: specs
| Robot dimensions (W x H) | 13.77 x 3.5 inches / 35 x 8.9cm | 
| Cleaning dock dimensions (H x W x D) | 19.64 x 17.95 x 15.35 inches / 49.9 x 45.6 x 39cm | 
| Suction | 42,000Pa | 
| Cleaning dock bin size | 3.38 quarts / 3.2 liters | 
| Clean water tank size | 4.43 quarts / 4.2 liters | 
| Dirty water tank size | 3.17 quarts / 3 liters | 
| Navigation & obstacle avoidance | Pathfinder VersaLift ToF LiDAR paired with AI OmniSight System 3.0 + LED | 
| Carpet detection | Yes | 
| Threshold crossing | ProLeap with dual retractable legs for up to 3.93 inches (10cm) clearance | 
| Mopping functions | Dual heated rotating mops + dock-based maintenance | 
| Robot noise level | 65dB at five feet | 
Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete: design
- Whopping suction power
- Can climb tall thresholds
- Mop extends by up to seven inches
Before we take a look at design of the X60 Pro Ultra's robot and dock, I should add that, right out of the box, this model has been extraordinarily reliable and more efficient than the majority other models I've reviewed these past few months.
Robot vacuum cleaners are among the easiest of smart home products to set up and this one was one of the most efficient. Yes, it arrived in a large box but because it comes with just three main parts — the robot, the dock and its clip-on ramp – I had it on the floor and ready to map my open-plan area within minutes. And, boy, did it map it well, even to the point of accurately pre-naming the four spaces it had located – Living Room, Dining Room, Kitchen and Hall — simply by noting the type of furnishings in each room.
This was a great start, in my opinion, because most robot vacs normally settle for generic terms like Room, 1, Room 2, etc. Of course, it's extremely simple to change the names of the rooms and just as easy to divide or merge them, but to have a robot that maps a living space so accurately from the off is a major plus.
I was also pleasantly surprised to discover the true meaning of this model's 'Complete' moniker because I spotted a huge array of accessories in the box. Most floor bots only come with a spare side brush, a spare dust bag and, occasionally, a tiny bottle of floor cleaning solution. But this model comes with three extra dust bags, a spare side brush, two dust box filters, three pairs of extra mop pads, a large one-quart (1L) bottle of cleaning solution and, rare for any robot, a spare pair of roller brushes. This is a major boon given that these are all items that one would normally need to purchase further down the line of ownership. Chapeau to Dreame.
Finally, if you purchase this bot today, sometime in 2027 you'll be able to use it in cahoots with Dreame's next sci-fi offering, a staircase-climbing robot module called the Cyber X. Unveiled at IFA Berlin, this amazingly clever slice of robotic tech functions as an autonomous carrier for the X60 so it can be transported up and down stairs. Can’t wait to see that in operation.
Robot design
The Dreame X60 Pro Ultra is available in black or white and is a striking example of just how much robot vacuum design has advanced. From the outside, it remains recognisably circular, but almost every component here has been engineered to tackle many of the shortcomings that have made some robot cleaners largely frustrating to live with. In short, this is a robot designed not simply to clean the floor, but to get into more places, deal with more types of mess and spend less time getting stuck.
While not especially unique, the X60’s retractable LiDAR turret is one of its smartest design flourishes. Rather than permanently sitting proud of the robot, the turret can retract to help the machine achieve an incredibly low 3.50 inch (8.9cm) profile. That might not sound like much on paper, but it makes a substantial difference in practice, allowing the X60 to venture underneath beds, sofas, TV cabinets and any other furnishings with a minimum floor clearance of just 3.54 inches (9cm).
Dreame has also addressed another common robot-vacuum weakness: thresholds. My home doesn't have any thresholds but if it did, this is the model I'd choose because its two pop-out legs give it the ability to climb double-layered obstacles up to 3.93 inches (10cm) and single steps up to 2.04 inches (5.2cm) in height, giving it an impressive ability to move between areas of the home without requiring any makeshift ramps. It also means far fewer situations where you return home only to discover that your expensive robot has spent half the day stranded on the lip of a doorway.
The X60 Pro Ultra's class-leading figure of 42,000 Pascals of suction is colossal even by today's standards, and this is especially useful when engaging the robot's Large Particles Boost mode which gives the X60 Pro Ultra additional oomph when it encounters larger pieces of debris.
Combined with the unit's twin tangle-free rubber rollers and a retractable pressure plate that creates a semi-sealed vacuum chamber, this level of suction is particularly relevant for pet owners, where clumps of hair can present a much greater challenge than everyday dust. Moreover, the X60 Pro Ultra also features an obligatory spinning side brush which extends much further than the norm — up to four inches (12cm) — for better corner cleaning.
Many modern floor bots feature at least one mop that's able to extend by a couple inches when cleaning along skirting boards, in corners or around furniture legs. But this one takes mop extension to a whole new level of stretch by offering a reach of seven inches (18cm). When I first saw this in operation I thought a piece of furniture had ripped its arm out of a socket. The spinning mop pads, meanwhile, are thermally efficient and exert up to 15 Newtons of downward pressure, providing considerably more physical contact with the floor than a robot that merely drags damp pads behind it.
When it comes to robot vacuum cleaners, navigation and obstacle avoidance are arguably just as important as suction because all this fancy hardware is pretty pointless if the robot can’t find its way around the home.
The X60 Pro Ultra’s impressive navigation system is built around Dreame’s advanced VersaLift retractable hybrid LiDAR, which scans its surroundings using lazer beams to create detailed maps of the home and plan efficient cleaning routes. It’s also backed by AI-enhanced 3D Proactive Light Detection and intelligent obstacle recognition of around 320 object including, according to Dreame, 'tiny objects of 10mm'. We'll have to see about that.
On the battery front, this model is fitted with a 5,000mAh battery that recharges from empty to full in about 100 minutes and, according to Dreame, is capable of charging 25% of its capacity in about six minutes.
Score ref: 5/5
Dock design
The Dreame X60 Pro Ultra’s charging dock is as impressive as the robot itself. With its tall, sophisticated design and glossy facade replete with a subtle pinstripe effect, this is one robot dock you might not mind having centre stage. More importantly, it’s packed with a raft of technology that's designed to keep the X60 in readiness for action with minimal human intervention, aside from periodically discarding the dock's dust bag and servicing the two water tanks.
Speaking of which, you get the usual dual water tank combo comprising a 4.43 quarts (4.2L) fresh water tank and a smaller 3.17 quarts (3L) tank for the filthy stuff. Instead of tainting the sink area with stinky water, I always flush the contents of the dirty tank into the toilet bowl and then give the container a quick rinse under a tap. This model also comes with a liquid floor detergent dispenser situated next door to the dock's dust bag department.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
As to be expected in this day and age, the X60 Pro Ultra dock also takes care of all self-cleaning duties, including preparing the mop pads before use with scaldingly hot water. Since the mops themselves are thermally efficient enough to retain heat, the floor has a better chance of being properly cleaned. When the robot returns to the dock, the mop pads are washed with hot water — apparently 212F (100C) — before drying them using hot air to help prevent build-up of bacteria and nasty smells.
The dock is also fitted with a generous 3.38 quarts (3.2L) dust bag, which is larger than those fitted to many competing robot vacuum docks. This means that more debris can be stored before you need to replace the bag, reducing one of the few genuinely tedious jobs associated with owning a robot vacuum. The fact you get three spare bags with this specific 'Complete' model can be considered a major bonus.
Score ref: 5/5
- Design score: 5/5
Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete: performance
- Supreme vacuum power
- Very good navigation
- Average obstacle avoidance
Navigation performance
To give you some idea of how impressive Dreame's current crop of robot vacs are, I installed this model's stablemate – the extra-large Matrix10 Ultra – in our village hall where it has been running for the past eight months without any hiccups. The hall is a huge 130 square meters — two-thirds of a singles tennis court – and divided into various sections, including two toilet areas and a kitchen.
Where other robots I've installed in the hall have had issues where their LiDAR-written maps have been corrupted due to the vast size of the work space and presumably the reflective windows surrounding it, the Matrix10 Ultra has not had any issues at all. In fact, it continues to this day, having successfully completed 395.65 hours of reliable operation over an area of 25,018 square meters, equivalent to a massive 6.18 acres. Not bad for a robot vacuum cleaner!
Needless to say, this model's navigation is equally impressive in the way it has mapped my home, negotiated a lot of furniture including a cluttered dining area, and never once having got lost, trapped itself under furniture or snowplowed a loose rug.
Mind, its first mapping session did produce one amusing moment when it reached the area around our garden door. Since this model uses LiDAR to navigate, its laser beam had scanned beyond the open door towards the garden, thinking it had detected another room. All LiDAR robots do this but very few have the ability to scale a tall threshold. This one, of course, has excellent ability in that department so you can see where this is heading. In fact it was sheer luck that I happened to enter the room just as it was in the process making a beeline for the garden. You've got to laugh.
Another thing I should add is that I have had to raise the valance on the lounge sofa because the camera and laser system treats fabric valances as a solid obstacle. I personally don’t consider this a major issue because almost every LiDAR-governed robot I've reviewed has also refused to punch through a sofa or bed valance. To rectify this I now occasionally tuck the sofa's valance up out of the way so the X60 can clean underneath.
Score ref: 5/5
Obstacle avoidance
Having read the glowing headlines on Dreame's website about this robot avoiding objects as small 10mm (0.39 of an inch), I simply had to give it a go by placing some much smaller items than usual in its path, including a Hue remote, a phone cable, a small bottle of essential oil and a tiny lighter. I made sure I'd selected every option in its intelligent obstacle avoidance setting and crossed my fingers as it proceeded to travel from the hall to the kitchen.
While it deftly avoided all the objects I usually test robot vacs with — including the low circular dog chew, remote and phone cable — I was very surprised when it thundered straight over the bottle and lighter as if they weren't even there. While I don't consider this a major strike against the X60's obstacle avoidance — many other robot vacs have fared worse — I do think that if a company is going to state that their robot can avoid objects as tiny as 10mm, they really need to back it up with a level of real-world performance that matches the claim.
While the X60 is no match for the DJI ROMO when it comes to obstacle avoidance, I still think it deserves a respectable 4/5 because it has avoided everything else in its path for the last six weeks, and I have never once had to remove the roller brushes to extricate something it had tried to swallow. In short, I'd say this model's obstacle avoidance is better than average but with room for improvement.
Score ref: 4/5
Vacuuming
I've been using the Dreame X60 Pro Ultra for the past six weeks and have never had to think about it. I've never looked at a rug after hearing it perform a scheduled task and thought it needed another clean with a cordless stick vac, I've never had to untangle it from the tassels of a rug, and I’ve never had to extricate an item too big to swallow from its rubber rollers.
Nevertheless, needs must so I scattered my usual potpourri of obstreperous ingredients over the hardwood kitchen floor and a similar handful over a piece of carpet, and watched it do its thing.
For a robot vac faced with far more detritus than it would ever come across in the real world (at least I'd like to think so), the Dreame X60 Pro Ultra made surprisingly short work of cleaning up the scattered cornflakes, muesli, oats and rice, swallowing up both the fine particles and larger ones with impressive consistency, even though it needed two passes to complete the task. The X60's 42,000Pa suction rating and Large Particles Boost Mode clearly paid dividends here, though I should add that this bot is louder in volume (up to to around 68dB) when cleaning in full-power mode.
I then applied the same test to a carpeted rug and it performed just as well though, again, it required two passes – one horizontal, the other vertical – to fulfil the task. Yes, there were a few small flakes left behind on the periphery but that's because they had been flung beyond the working zone I had previously programmed.
Score ref: 4.5/5
Mopping performance
As I've stated umpteen times before, I'm no fan of robots that also mop and would much rather have a vacuum-only robot with a huge dustbin in its dock. For mopping I generally prefer sticking to my Roborock F25 Ultra wet-and-dry vac or use a paper towel to wipe up a small spill of milk.
However I can see the appeal of having a robot for hard floor-cleaning duties if it mops practically every day. And this model excels at just that, partly because of the incredible reach of its extendable mop that genuinely cleans to the edge, in corners and around table legs, and partly because its clever blue Proactive Light Dirt Detection system does seem to spot stains better than other models I've tested.
Anyway, for my extreme kitchen test I accidentally-on-purpose spilt a glass of milk and programmed the X60 to run a zone clean. After about five minutes of mop preparation, including heating the pads using hot water, it trundled over and mopped up half the milk before returning to the dock. I thought that was that until I realized it was having its mops washed in readiness for the second run I had previously programmed.
I'd say the final results were perfectly acceptable given that I would never command a robot to mop up a spill when I can perform the task a thousand times quicker with some paper towels.
The main take away here is that its day-to-day performance has definitely been a cut above many of its competitors and there's no denying the practicality of the robot's extendable mop arm which really does work wonders.
Score ref: 4.5/5
Dock performance
I have nothing but good things to say about the X60 Pro Ultra's dock. Yes, it's a pretty large item to have in a small space but, on the plus side, I think its reflective pin-striped glass-like facade is one of the most attractive finishes I've seen since the Roborock 10R.
From a functional point of view, this dock does everything from emptying the robot's dust bin and servicing the robot’s mop system with hot water, washing the mops and then drying them, to self cleaning its own mop tray at the touch of a button on the app.
Only once did the dock's suction not correctly empty the contents of the robot's bin after a full house clean, and this was because I had activated the Hair Compression setting in the app. I'm not sure how this function works but the robot's bin was so tightly clumped with loads of winter-shed hair from my two labradors that the contents refused to budge when the dock's suction kicked in. Thankfully I've had no repeats of this since switching off the Hair Compression setting and, as a result, I am not losing any sleep over it.
Score ref: 5/5
- Performance score: 4.5/5
Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete review: app functionality
- Extremely comprehensive
- Brilliant for tech nerds, not so much for luddites
- Encourages a lot of experimentation
The Dreame X60 Pro Ultra’s Dreamehome app is extraordinarily well featured, giving you an almost ridiculous level of control over what the robot does, when it does it and how it cleans each area of your home. The problem is that it can initially feel like you’ve been handed the controls to an airliner.
As per usual, once the X60 has mapped your home, the app presents a detailed map that lets you merge or divide individual rooms, define cleaning zones and set no-go areas and virtual barriers. You can specify whether particular areas should be vacuumed, mopped or given both treatments, and adjust cleaning intensity according to the room or floor type.
There are also extensive options for scheduling and short-cut tasks, along with a myriad of settings for suction power, water usage, mop behavior, carpet type, floor direction, obstacle crossing, obstacle avoidance, even if you want pet hair in the robot's bin to be compressed.
The sheer depth of the Dreamehome app is undeniably impressive, but it does come with a steep learning curve that encourages a lot of experimentation. It can also take a while to work out where everything lives, particularly if you’re the sort of person who prefers to press a couple of buttons and get on with more important things. Nevertheless, once you’ve mastered this app, it becomes one of the X60 Pro Ultra’s biggest strengths.
- App functionality score: 4/5
Should you buy the Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete?
| Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete: score card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Section | Notes | Score | 
| Value for money | While in the premium bracket, I think the Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete is fair value for money, especially given the on-board tech and huge amount of included spares. | 4.5/5 | 
| Design | Slick, sophisticated and impressively engineered, the X60 Pro Ultra and its glossy dock ooze premium quality. | 5/5 | 
| Performance | The X60 Pro Ultra delivers outstanding vacuum performance and better-than-average mopping, but its obstacle avoidance system could be better. | 4.5/5 | 
| App functionality | The Dreamehome app is impressively comprehensive, offering deep control over all aspects, but its sheer number of settings can feel overwhelming. | 4/5 | 
| Average rating | Row 5 - Cell 1 | 4.5/5 | 
Buy it if
You want great vacuum performance
Powerful 42,000Pa suction tackles stubborn household detritus with aplomb
You have hairy pets
This model has several functions designed with pets in mind
You have low furniture and high thresholds
The X60 cleans beneath very low furniture and climbs most thresholds
Don't buy it if
Your home is cluttered with tiny toys
The X60 most likely won’t evade small toys like Lego bricks
You're not very tech savvy
The X60 Pro Ultra's surfeit of features may overwhelm less technical users
Your home is on the small side
This model would be overkill, as would the large dock
How I tested the Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete
TechRadar takes its product testing very seriously so I lived with the X60 Pro Ultra for a few weeks having set up various weekly schedules and routines to gauge how efficiently it performed the tasks it was designed for. I also monitored the amount of times I had to rescue it from entanglement or some other anomaly but, aside from some minor obstacle avoidance issues, the X60 functioned reliably throughout its trial.
If only to prove its capability for cleaning up heavier doses of debris and mopping up spills, I also performed a few extreme tests that no robot should have to endure in its lifetime.
First reviewed September 2026.
Derek Adams has been in consumer tech journalism since joining London listings magazine Time Out in the early ‘80s. He’s an experienced reviewer of cordless vacs and robot vacs, indeed anything that runs on batteries or has a plug attached. Derek also writes extensively for TechRadar’s sister site T3.com between playing drums and guitar with his bandmates in Red Box.

articles.title: Box-office : démarrage record pour Resident Evil, qui ressuscite la franchise d'horreur culte
articles.text:
Box-office : démarrage record pour Resident Evil, qui ressuscite la franchise d'horreur culte
Le nouveau film Resident Evil de Zach Cregger démarre en trombe au box-office, et signe un lancement record pour la franchise cinématographique adaptée du jeu vidéo culte.
Après les cartons de Backrooms et Obsession au box-office, l'horreur continue de faire recette en 2026 avec la sortie réussie de Resident Evil. Le nouveau film adapté du jeu vidéo PlayStation vient de signer un démarrage record et de relancer une franchise cinéma qui avait du plomb dans l'aile.
L'horreur, reine du box-office en 2026
Avec 60 millions de dollars engrangés lors de son week-end inaugural en Amérique du Nord, le long-métrage de Zach Cregger (Évanouis, Barbare) vient de faire passer les adaptations de Resident Evil dans une toute autre dimension économique, oblitérant les démarrages des précédents films et ressuscitant la franchise après le bide de Bienvenue à Raccoon City en 2021 et ses maigres 41,9 millions de dollars dans le monde.
Ce nouveau volet surpasse ainsi largement les lancements du premier film Resident Evil de 2002 (17,7 millions), de Resident Evil : Apocalypse (23 millions), Resident Evil: Extinction (23,6 millions), Resident Evil: Afterlife (26,6 millions), Resident Evil: Retribution (21 millions), Resident Evil: Chapitre Final (13,6 millions) et Resident Evil : Bienvenue à Raccoon City (5,4 millions).
Mieux encore : ce démarrage canon permet à ce nouvel opus de réaliser en quelques jours le meilleur score américain de la franchise, atteignant déjà le cumul de Resident Evil: Afterlife de 60,1 millions de dollars, établi en 2010. Ce succès est aussi visible à l'international, où Resident Evil rajoute 48,3 millions à son score américain, signant un record pour la franchise adaptée du jeu vidéo, et même pour un film d'horreur depuis un an.
Son démarrage mondial de 108,3 millions de dollars met ce nouveau Resident Evil en bonne position pour aller chercher les totaux mondiaux de Resident Evil: Retribution (240,6 millions), Resident Evil: Afterlife (295,8 millions) et Resident Evil: Chapitre Final (314,1 millions). Il faut noter que le record de ce dernier est dû en partie aux recettes chinoises exceptionnelles à l'époque, qui représentaient plus de la moitié.
Avec un budget annoncé de 75 millions de dollars, ce nouveau film Resident Evil s'annonce déjà comme un succès bien rentable, d'autant que le film est très apprécié par le public et bénéficiera sans doute d'un excellent bouche-à-oreille. Sans réel concurrent sur ce créneau horrifique avant Malfaisante le 9 octobre, il sera intéressant de voir jusqu'où il monte.
Dans le reste du box-office, on notera que Les Ensorceleuses 2 avec Nicole Kidman et Sandra Bullock ne rattrape pas son démarrage très léger de la semaine dernière et que Coyote vs. Acme atteint un joli cumul monde de 80 millions. Pas mal pour un film que Warner avait destiné à ne jamais voir la lumière du jour, comme son BatGirl.

articles.title: LittleHorse adds agent controls and free serverless trial to its 'Business-as-Code' orchestration platform - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
LittleHorse adds agent controls and free serverless trial to its ‘Business-as-Code’ orchestration platform
LittleHorse Enterprises LLC, a maker of workflow orchestration software spanning multiple applications, today announced version 1.3 of its Saddle Command Center, adding no-code agent deployment, prebuilt task workers, a JavaScript software development kit, and a free serverless trial to its platform for coordinating artificial intelligence agents and conventional software.
The privately held company describes Saddle Command Center as an “action layer” that sits across agents, microservices, software-as-a-service applications and event streams. Its approach, called “Business-as-Code,” converts a business process into version-controlled, testable software represented as a graph that technical and business users can inspect and modify.
The company said it addresses the fragmentation created as companies spread processes across specialized applications, integrations, spreadsheets and manual procedures. Most enterprises have dozens of SaaS applications stitched together by manual integrations, said LittleHorse founder and Chief Executive Colt McNealy.
That fragmentation makes it difficult to adopt agents for two reasons, he said. “One is lack of context. Two is the difficulty of getting the right things to happen at the right time.”
Saddle Command Center 1.3 adds an Apache Kafka-compatible streaming engine, connectors for webhooks and data sources and a runtime for prebuilt agents and task workers. Developers can turn existing code into workflow components and connect systems through application programming interfaces, event queues or custom tasks.
The new release’s agent controls are based on what LittleHorse calls the “decision worker pattern.” An agent receives read-only access to tools and handles a task requiring judgment. Deterministic workflow code can validate its output and carry out the action, keeping authority out of the agent itself.
“What our customers started doing early on is reducing the scope of the agent to just the fuzzy tasks and then having the workflow engine orchestrate the difficult parts,” McNealy said. Without that visibility, “your token bill goes up, your reliability goes down, and you get no observability of what’s going on.”
Users can now configure an agent by choosing Model Context Protocol servers, defining a system prompt and specifying input and output structures. Saddle Command Center then deploys the model as a task worker that can be inserted into a larger workflow. The platform records tool calls and provides a stack trace for debugging. Business errors follow rules defined in the workflow, while technical errors such as network failures can be retried according to policy.
The system is also intended for long-running processes that cross organizational and application boundaries. McNealy cited a European payments provider whose merchant-onboarding process involved multiple identity services and responses that could take as long as three days.
Using LittleHorse, the provider codified error-handling and timeout procedures for calls to third-party systems and automated workflows based on the responses received. LittleHorse coordinated the steps, waits and error handling without replacing any underlying systems.
“They were able to remove a ton of manual work and speed up their onboarding time with this workflow,” McNealy said.
Saddle Command Center supports Java, Python, Go and C#, while version 1.3 adds JavaScript. The free serverless option lets developers test the platform without provisioning infrastructure.
LittleHorse was founded in 2022 by McNealy, whose father, Sun Microsystems Inc. co-founder and former CEO Scott McNealy, is an investor and adviser. It uses an open-core model, with an open-source orchestration kernel supporting the commercial platform.
The company said its software has been in production for more than 18 months, has paying customers across multiple industries and expects to book more than $1 million in revenue this year. Its enterprise sales approach often begins with a three-week Business-as-Code workshop, while software companies more commonly adopt the open-source version before buying support or hosted services. Enterprise pricing is based on processing capacity, including Kafka throughput and workflow tasks per second.
Saddle Command Center 1.3 is available now.

articles.title: China crafts working 3nm gate-all-around transistors without EUV — stacked nanosheets target 3nm without EUV, but full node remains distant
articles.text:
China crafts working 3nm gate-all-around transistors without EUV — stacked nanosheets target 3nm without EUV, but full node remains distant
But China's 3nm remains years away.
The Institute of Microelectronics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (IMECAS) has developed an experimental process flow for building stacked-nanosheet gate-all-around (GAA) transistors using immersion DUV lithography and demonstrated functional devices. The flow is intended for eventual use with 3nm-class and smaller process technologies by Chinese chipmakers that do not have access to EUV scanners, reports DigiTimes.
While IMECAS has demonstrated functional GAA devices, it has not disclosed the critical geometrical parameters that would allow comparisons to 3nm-class transistors from other chipmakers. Furthermore, the experimental process flow for building transistors is not even a defined process flow for building research chips, much less a complete 3nm-class manufacturing process.
Nonetheless, the achievement is quite important as it demonstrates that China is capable of developing its own branch of semiconductor evolution without using leading-edge tools from Western companies.
Early process integration complete
Ye Tianchun, chief engineer of China's National Major Special Project 02, said at the IC World conference in Beijing that IMECAS had completed 'early process integration' for stacked nanosheet-channel GAA transistors fabricated with DUV lithography. The researchers from IMECAS obtained devices with Ion/Ioff ratios of 9.7×10⁵ and 7.6×10⁵, both exceeding the 5×10⁵ threshold, which means gate control of the stacked sheets is working. These figures indicate that the experimental transistors can distinguish between their conducting and non-conducting states, but they say little about transistor density or whether their physical dimensions correspond to those expected from commercial 3nm-class technologies.
In particular, IMECAS has not disclosed gate pitch, metal pitch, nanosheet dimensions, transistor density, SRAM density, or other geometrical characteristics that could put its devices into perspective against 3nm-class production nodes from Intel, Samsung Foundry, or TSMC. Therefore, the achievement should be viewed as validation of a stacked-nanosheet GAA process flow based on DUV lithography rather than evidence that China has developed a 3nm process without EUV.
The most important part of the experiment is that IMECAS is investigating how GAA devices intended for future 3nm-class and more advanced technologies can be fabricated without using EUV lithography, something that nobody has done before in volume production.
GAA transistors have succeeded FinFET devices at leading-edge nodes because placing the gate around nanosheet channels provides better electrostatic control as transistor dimensions shrink. IMECAS has been developing technologies required for this transition since 2020, and its particular focus was on nodes below 3nm, which is why it now mentions 3nm as part of its announcement.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Reducing China's dependence on advanced foreign tools
It goes without saying that IMECAS' work in recent years has been focused on reducing China's dependence on tools, software, and other technologies that are designed by Western companies and therefore subject to export restrictions imposed by American, Japanese, or European countries.
Among other things, Ye mentioned architectural innovation, design-technology co-optimization (DTCO), system-technology co-optimization (STCO), and 'extracting more value' from mature fabrication technologies. For now, IMECAS' result demonstrates a DUV-based route for researching stacked-nanosheet GAA transistors intended for future 3nm-class technologies, but not a China-developed 3nm process ready for manufacturing even in the long-term future.
Even if IMECAS eventually demonstrates appropriately scaled GAA devices using DUV, or discloses critical geometry parameters of the current work, this would still be far from a production-ready 3nm-class technology. Commercial manufacturing requires integration of lithography with deposition, etching, cleaning, metrology, process control, materials, temperatures, and many other steps and parameters. For now, IMECAS has not demonstrated such a manufacturing flow.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Ce projet de Google transforme votre smartphone Android en terrain de jeu pour les agents IA
articles.text:
Avec ARTEMIS, Google propose un framework open source capable de confier un véritable smartphone Android à un agent IA. Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity ou OpenClaw peuvent ainsi naviguer dans les applications, saisir du texte ou enchaîner plusieurs actions à la place de l’utilisateur.
Après le navigateur et le terminal, les agents IA s’attaquent désormais au smartphone. Avec ARTEMIS, Google met à disposition sous licence Apache 2.0 un outil d’automatisation Android pensé à l’origine pour les tests logiciels, mais dont le serveur MCP ouvre des possibilités bien plus larges.
ARTEMIS peut fonctionner avec un vrai smartphone Android connecté au PC ou avec un téléphone virtuel lancé dans un émulateur. Une fois installé, il peut observer l’interface, ouvrir une application, appuyer sur un bouton, saisir du texte ou passer d’une app à l’autre.
Un outil de test Android qui peut aller beaucoup plus loin
À l’origine, ARTEMIS vise surtout les développeurs et les équipes chargées de tester des applications Android. On peut par exemple lui demander d’installer une nouvelle version d’une app, de reproduire un bug, de parcourir plusieurs écrans ou encore de récupérer automatiquement des captures d’écran et des logs en cas de problème.
L’intérêt est que l’agent ne rejoue pas simplement une suite de clics écrite à l’avance. Il peut observer l’interface et chercher lui-même comment atteindre l’objectif demandé.
Google montre par exemple ARTEMIS préparant plusieurs itinéraires dans Google Maps, calculant leur durée totale, puis basculant sur YouTube pour lancer un morceau. Une même tâche peut donc traverser plusieurs applications. Deux modes sont proposés. Flash privilégie la rapidité, tandis que Pro ajoute davantage de planification et de vérification.
Bien sûr, ARTEMIS n’est pas le premier système à permettre à une IA d’agir sur un smartphone. Gemini peut déjà exécuter certaines tâches multi-étapes dans des applications Android, tandis que Claude sait interagir avec plusieurs fonctions et apps du téléphone. Des outils tiers permettent également de piloter un appareil à distance.
La différence tient surtout à l’approche : ARTEMIS transforme un véritable smartphone Android en outil générique accessible à différents agents externes via MCP, sans être lié à un assistant unique. C’est justement son serveur MCP intégré qui élargit les usages. Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Cursor, Windsurf ou encore OpenClaw peuvent utiliser ARTEMIS comme un outil supplémentaire et lui confier directement des tâches sur le smartphone.
Au premier lancement, ARTEMIS installe également un service d’accessibilité dédié sur Android, visible dans les réglages et via une notification persistante. C’est notamment ce composant qui permet de lire la structure de l’interface et d’interagir avec certains éléments affichés à l’écran.
Plus de 99 % de réussite, avec quelques réserves
Google revendique plus de 99 % de réussite sur AndroidWorld, un benchmark couvrant plus d’une centaine de tâches Android en plusieurs étapes. Un chiffre impressionnant, mais auto-déclaré par le projet et qui ne constitue donc pas une validation indépendante.
ARTEMIS a aussi été rattrapé récemment par une controverse autour de l’attribution de code. La startup Minitap affirme avoir reconnu dans ARTEMIS plusieurs éléments issus de son projet open source mobile-use, dont du code et des prompts. Depuis, le README d’ARTEMIS mentionne explicitement que le projet inclut du code développé par Minitap.
Autre point à garder en tête : une issue de sécurité ouverte sur GitHub décrit une possible injection de commandes via certains paramètres transmis aux fonctions ADB. Tant que le correctif n’est pas intégré et validé, mieux vaut considérer ARTEMIS comme un outil expérimental à utiliser sur un appareil de test plutôt que sur son smartphone principal.
En bref, ARTEMIS reste avant tout un outil destiné aux tests Android. Mais avec MCP, il montre surtout jusqu’où les agents commencent à étendre leur terrain d’action : le smartphone devient à son tour une interface qu’une IA peut manipuler directement.

articles.title: Cuál es el valor en el mercado de la criptomoneda Bitcoin este domingo
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
PUBLICIDAD
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
El precio de la criptomoneda bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 80447.39 dólares. Esto quiere decir que el activo digital presentó un cambio de -0.95% en el último día, así como un movimiento de 0.0% en la última hora.
PUBLICIDAD
Por su nivel de capitalización, esta moneda digital ocupa la posición #1 entre las más populares.
El flujo histórico de inversiones impulsa a bitcoin a máximos nunca antes vistos
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
PUBLICIDAD
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
PUBLICIDAD
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.
