articles.title: Amazons neues Werbe-Tool: Eine Karte zeigt, wo deine Marke stark ist – und wo nicht
articles.text:
Amazons neues Werbe-Tool: Eine Karte zeigt, wo deine Marke stark ist – und wo nicht
Amazon Ads führt sein Tool Geographic Insights and Activation, kurz GIA, in Deutschland ein. Die Werbetreibenden sollen dabei nicht mehr nur festlegen können, wo eine Kampagne ausgespielt wird, sondern auf der Basis von Hinweisen auch, in welchen Regionen eine Marke besonders stark oder schwach vertreten ist. Daraus lässt sich ableiten, wo sich zusätzliche Werbeinvestitionen lohnen könnten. So sehen Unternehmen in einer Kartenansicht, wie gut die eigene Marke in unterschiedlichen Regionen im Vergleich zu einer Produktkategorie abschneidet.
Amazon kombiniert dazu eigene Retail-Signale mit geografischen Informationen der Werbetreibenden. Aus diesen Erkenntnissen lassen sich sogenannte intelligente Standortgruppen erstellen. Anschließend kann Amazon die Gebote einer Kampagne automatisiert anpassen. Denkbar ist etwa, gezielt mehr Werbebudget in Regionen zu lenken, in denen eine Marke bislang eine vergleichsweise geringe Marktpenetration erreicht.
Optimierung von Werbekampagnen
All das erinnert an klassisches Geo-Targeting. Der Unterschied besteht aber darin, dass Amazon Analyse und Kampagnensteuerung enger miteinander verknüpft. Zum Einsatz kommen hierbei Handelsdaten, die in einem ersten Schritt mögliche Wachstumspotenziale identifizieren. Unternehmen, die die Amazon Marketing Cloud (AMC) einsetzen, können außerdem eigene geografische Daten mit den Signalen von Amazon kombinieren. Das ermöglicht beispielsweise, Vertriebsgebiete, regionale Verkaufszahlen oder andere unternehmenseigene Informationen einfließen zu lassen.
Dabei steht GIA den Werbetreibenden zur Verfügung, die Amazons Demand-Side-Plattform Amazon (DSP) im Self-Service nutzen und gleichzeitig die Amazon Marketing Cloud einsetzen. Deutschland ist nicht der erste Markt, wo GIA zum Einsatz kommt – außerdem ist das Angebot unter anderem in Großbritannien, Frankreich, Italien, Spanien, den USA und Kanada verfügbar.
Wie üblich gibt’s zum Start ein paar Beispiele, wo das schon funktioniert. Hier zeigt Amazon einen Case von L’Oréal. Der Kosmetikkonzern setzte GIA für Werbung für ein Haaröl ein. Dabei wurden Regionen identifiziert, in denen die Marke bislang vergleichsweise schwach vertreten war, und anschließend gezielt Displayanzeigen geschaltet. Nach Angaben von Amazon lagen die Kosten pro Verkauf bei dieser Kampagne 38 Prozent unter denen einer regulären, dauerhaft laufenden Displaykampagne. Bei Neukunden seien die Kosten pro Verkauf um elf Prozent geringer ausgefallen. Konkrete Kampagnenzahlen oder Angaben zur Größenordnung der untersuchten Regionen macht Amazon allerdings nicht.
Prime-Video-Werbung wird regional
Gleichzeitig hat Amazon auch die regionalen Möglichkeiten seiner Werbung bei Prime Video verändert. So sollen Werbetreibende mit standortbezogenen interaktiven Videoanzeigen landesweite Kampagnen mit unterschiedlichen regionalen Informationen ausspielen können. Das bedeutet, derselbe Werbespot kann abhängig vom Standort der Zuschauer:innen unterschiedliche Angebote, Preise oder Informationen zu Geschäften anzeigen. Bislang hätten Unternehmen dazu für jede Region eine separate Videokampagne anlegen müssen.
Außerdem lassen sich interaktive Funktionen in die Werbung integrieren, etwa „Ans Handy senden“ oder „Jetzt anmelden“. Somit könnten Zuschauer:innen direkt aus der TV-Werbung heraus eine Aktion auslösen.
Dass für so etwas die regionalen Märkte in Deutschland inzwischen ausreichend groß sind, zeigt eine Zahl: Nach Unternehmensangaben erreicht Prime Video in Deutschland monatlich durchschnittlich mehr als 17 Millionen Nutzer über werbefinanzierte Inhalte.
Was zunächst nach zwei unterschiedlichen Meldungen klingt, ist letztlich eine durchgehende Kette: GIA könnte damit zunächst Regionen identifizieren, in denen sich zusätzliche Werbung lohnen könnte. Über Displaykampagnen und lokalisierte Prime-Video-Anzeigen wären die Kund:innen in diesen Gebieten anschließend gezielt ansprechbar. Allerdings binden sich Werbetreibende damit noch mehr an Amazons Datenschatz. Denn der Konzern kann Signale aus seinem Handelsgeschäft mit Werbeausspielung und der Reichweite seiner eigenen Medienangebote verbinden.

articles.title: GameSir Announces Official Fortnite Mobile Controller Collection
articles.text:

GameSir Announces Official Fortnite Mobile Controller Collection
GameSir, a global leader in gaming peripherals, announced its collaboration with Fortnite, introducing an all-new collection of officially licensed mobile controllers that combine GameSir's award-winning technology with one of the world's most iconic games.Launching with the GameSir G8 Plus Fortnite Edition and GameSir X5 Lite for XBOX Fortnite Edition, the collection is designed for mobile players who demand more from every match. Featuring premium controller technology that delivers console inspired performance, authentic Fortnite-inspired designs, and an in-game bonus item with every controller, the collection delivers an experience that extends well beyond the hardware.
Facilitated by IMG Licensing, the collaboration brings console-quality precision, comfort, and customization to mobile gaming—whether players are dropping into Battle Royale, Zero Build, Reload, or developer-made games.
Eric Bright, Vice President of Partnerships & Product Strategy, North America at GameSir"Fortnite has built one of the most passionate communities in gaming, and we're honored to collaborate on products worthy of that community," "Our goal wasn't simply to build another controller. We wanted to create the ultimate Fortnite experience—from the premium hardware to the authentic character-inspired designs."
Louie Sandoval, Vice President of Global Gaming at IMG Licensing"Fortnite continues to set the standard for how gaming brands connect with players through innovative products and meaningful experiences," "GameSir has built a strong reputation for delivering high-quality gaming peripherals, making them an outstanding partner for this collaboration. We're excited to see Fortnite fans around the world experience this collection."
GameSir G8 Plus - Fortnite Edition
The flagship controller for players seeking the ultimate competitive experience.
Designed for Fortnite wherever life takes you.
Fortnite has always been about expressing your unique style. Whether it's your outfit, your loadout, or your strategy, every player leaves their own mark on the Island.
The GameSir Fortnite Collection celebrates that individuality with collectible character-inspired editions built for every type of player. Whether you choose the flagship G8 Plus, the ultra-portable X5 Lite for XBOX, or your favorite Fortnite character edition, every controller delivers the premium performance GameSir is known for.
Coming Soon
The GameSir Fortnite Collection launches this fall through GameSir.com and select retail partners worldwide, including Amazon, Best Buy, AliExpress, TikTok Shop and Walmart.
Additional product details, pricing, launch timing, and the included digital in-game bonus will be announced soon.

articles.title: Cette entreprise française donne une seconde vie aux batteries de voitures électriques pour alimenter des festivals
articles.text:
PESS Energy a alimenté la moitié des 42 food trucks du Street Food Festival de Marseille avec un conteneur de 7 tonnes. Cette start-up marseillaise a rempli ce conteneur de batteries de voitures électriques de seconde vie. Il a une capacité utile de 600 kWh.
D'aucuns vous diront que le bruit et l'odeur d'un groupe électrogène font partie des charmes des festivals estivaux, mais tout de même, pour l'environnement, c'est moyen.
Il fallait trouver une solution de remplacement qui soit propre et écologique. Et cocorico, c'est en France qu'on l'a trouvée. PESS Energy assemble à Marseille des batteries mobiles, de la Bobine de 5 kWh sur roulettes au Bulk de 600 kWh. Ce conteneur de 3 mètres de long pèse 7 tonnes et il ne faut pas moins qu'un camion-grue pour le livrer sur les événements. Avec 160 kW de puissance en recharge et en décharge, il a une autonomie de 24 heures à 25 kW, ou d'environ 4 heures à pleine puissance et il est pilotable à distance.
Le Bulk trois soirs de suite au Street Food Festival de Marseille
Le coffret forain de 30 kW mis à disposition par la ville de Marseille était trop faible pour les grosses friteuses des food trucks. La moitié des 42 camions étaient en outre trop loin du point de distribution, a indiqué Rémi Pillot, fondateur de PESS Energy, à Automobile Propre. Ces camions ont tiré leur électricité du Bulk pendant trois soirs de suite.
« On a rechargé à 30 kW sur le coffret 24h/24, et de 17 h à minuit, pendant le festival, on a délivré beaucoup plus pour ne pas surcharger le réseau », a expliqué Rémi Pillot. Les plombs ont sauté à trois reprises sur le site, mais « ceux qu'on alimentait n'ont rien vu car nous avons un mode onduleur UPS », a-t-il ajouté.
Les food trucks ont consommé 1 200 kWh en trois soirs. Sur les 160 kW du Bulk, ils en ont appelé 80 au maximum et 60 en moyenne. Rémi Pillot chiffre à 1 400 euros de carburant et à 1 600 kg de CO₂ l'économie réalisée.
Rémi Pillot refuse de communiquer le tarif de location du Bulk. « À chaque devis, PESS étudie et se positionne de façon à coûter, dans le pire des cas, autant que des groupes électrogènes », a-t-il promis. L'organisateur ne fait donc pas d'économie systématique, mais ses visiteurs n'ont pas à supporter les odeurs de gazole.
Marseille est le troisième événement où PESS Energy a déployé le Bulk. L'entreprise l'avait installé auparavant à Aix-en-Provence pour un festival gastronomique, et « en pleine forêt » pour une cérémonie ministérielle. Ce site était totalement dépourvu de connexion au réseau électrique.
Des packs de seconde vie en bon état mais un marché très jeune
Il y a quelques années, les casses automobiles ne savaient pas quoi faire des packs de batteries, rappelle Rémi Pillot. Certaines en proposent désormais à la vente. PESS Energy empile huit de ces packs dans le Bulk. « C'est du réemploi, à part reprogrammer le BMS (battery management system), on ne fait rien d'autre », a précisé le fondateur.
Les packs viennent de trois sources. Des constructeurs automobiles ont écarté des packs neufs avant même de les monter sur une voiture. La start-up a aussi récupéré un pack quasi neuf sur une voiture à 34 km au compteur, mise à la casse après un choc contre un arbre. Sur les packs usés par toute une vie de conduite, Rémi Pillot ignore le style du conducteur et le nombre de recharges rapides. « C'est un peu le poker », a-t-il confié.
Le pack le plus usé du Bulk a un état de santé (SOH) de 92 %, précise le fondateur. Ce niveau est rare pour des packs de seconde vie, d'après Automobile Propre.
Rémi Pillot ne peut pas mélanger n'importe quels packs, car « c'est la plus mauvaise cellule qui détermine la capacité pack ». Or trouver des lots homogènes est difficile, si bien qu'il travaille à la création d'un « hub » de la seconde vie. Dans ce hub, chaque entreprise aurait une mission, du démontage à la certification, et un agrégateur tiendrait le stock.
Rémi Pillot économise environ 25 % sur l'approvisionnement grâce à la seconde vie, mais il estime devoir jeter un pack d'occasion sur quatre. Les fabricants chinois vendent leurs systèmes de stockage à des tarifs si bas qu'il est de plus en plus difficile de les concurrencer, note Automobile Propre. Le fondateur admet ne pas être certain que le Bulk coûte nettement moins cher qu'un équivalent neuf. Il mise sur l'impact carbone. « On économise 75 à 80 % de CO₂ par rapport à une batterie neuve », a-t-il ajouté.
PESS Energy vend aussi le Bulk sur mesure, à un tarif non dévoilé, et prépare une version de 400 kW. Enedis multiplie de son côté les points de connexion au réseau, notamment en milieu urbain, pour alimenter directement les événements sans groupe électrogène.

articles.title: ‘A sign of what RGB TVs can be’: The Samsung R95H is a fantastic TV and while it doesn’t beat elite OLED, it shows just how good next-gen mini-LED can be
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Samsung R95H is another impressive RGB TV, delivering great overall picture quality and plenty of perks for gamers. While the similarly priced flagship OLEDs still have the upper hand for now, the Samsung R95H shows how quickly RGB TV tech is advancing, and its huge potential, and it's a fantastic TV overall.
Pros
- +Brilliant overall picture quality
- +Fantastic for gaming
- +Glare-free still a hit
Cons
- -Pricey
- -No Dolby Vision
- -Still can't hit OLED's highs
Why you can trust TechRadar
Samsung R95H review: Two-minute review
Samsung’s Micro RGB lineup is its first foray into the RGB TV market, and the Samsung R95H is the flagship model in that lineup. It's an impressive TV, and a very strong performer in key areas such as movies and gaming; and, while I don’t think it quite beats the best OLED TVs, it's a good showcase for how RGB models are shaping up against the best TVs in general.
The R95H delivers great overall picture quality, with vibrant colors which also look accurate in most scenes, as well as strong contrast and refined detail. While its black levels don’t quite match those of OLED, they’re still very rich for a backlit TV. It’s not all smooth sailing, as the R95H can get overly bright, especially in Movie mode, and it’s not immune to blooming in very dark scenes. Still, its overall picture quality is of a high standard.
Sound quality on the R95H is solid for the most part, with good accuracy and detail, as well as commendable bass and solid mid-range tones. Speech is clear in most scenes I watched, and there is some sense of surround. However, the soundstage could be wider, and the volume does need to be pushed sometimes, so I’d recommend one of the best soundbars for those wanting a more of a home-theater experience.
The R95H is up there with the best gaming TVs, offering four fully-specced HDMI 2.1 ports along with a low 11.7ms input lag time for smooth gaming performance. There are tons of cloud gaming options available too, and Samsung's Gaming Hub is still an excellent feature. While its Game picture mode could be more accurate, this is still an excellent gaming TV.
Tizen is a good smart TV platform, giving you access to all the major streaming apps, as well as a plethora of AI tools for picture, sound and general usage. Its menus are generally well laid out and easy to navigate, and, while there are some frustrations, such as autoplaying Samsung TV Plus and large banner ads on the home screen, these don’t detract too much from what is a solid smart TV interface.
The R95H is a premium TV, with the 65-inch model priced at $2,799 / £2,899 / AU$4,999. This puts it at a similar price level to flagship OLED TVs, and while I don’t think it quite tops OLED, it shows how rapidly RGB tech is advancing.
A quick note on the images in this review: the TV may appear to have a red tint, but this is caused by the camera reacting to the anti-glare screen, and it not something that's discernible when viewing content on the TV.

- 85-inch: $5,499 / £5,899 / AU$9,999
The Samsung R95H is the flagship model in Samsung’s Micro RGB TV lineup, sitting above the Samsung R85H. It’s available in 65, 75 and 85-inch sizes. The launch price for the 65-inch model I tested is $3,199 / £3,099 / AU$5,299, putting it at the premium end of the market.
Since its launch in July 2026, prices have dropped across all sizes in both the US and UK. The 65-inch has dropped to $2,799 / £2,899, putting it in similar price brackets to Samsung’s flagship S95H / S99H OLED (priced at $2,899 / £2,899) and LG’s flagship G6 OLED ($2,699 / £2,999). In the US and UK the R95H is cheaper than Sony’s rival RGB, the Bravia 9 II, which is priced at $3,499 / £3,499 / AU$5,995.
Samsung R95H review: Specs

Samsung R95H review: Features
- RGB backlight
- Glare-free screen
- Samsung Vision AI and Tizen smart TV platform
The R95H uses Samsung’s ‘Micro RGB’ backlight technology, which uses LEDs that are smaller than mini-LEDs, and which consist of red, green and blue LEDs (hence RGB) rather than the traditional white in order to deliver bolder colors and brightness.
It comes equipped with the Samsung Micro RGB AI Engine Pro processor, which has features such as Micro RGB Precision Color, 4K AI Upscaling Pro and Color Booster Pro. The TV itself also has a Glare Free screen, an anti-reflection matte screen that has featured in several of Samsung's TVs, including the Samsung S95H / S99H.
In terms of HDR support, the R95H supports HDR10+, but as usual, there is no support for Dolby Vision.
For gaming, the R95H has four HDMI 2.1 ports, which support 4K 165Hz, full VRR including Freesync and G-Sync, ALLM and HDR10+ gaming. It also supports cloud gaming apps from the likes of Xbox and Nvidia GeForce Now. The R95H is also compatible with the Wireless One Connect Box, which can be used in tandem with the TV’s built-in ports, meaning there are a potential eight HDMI 2.1 ports on offer.
The R95H has a 4.2.2 channel speaker array, totaling 70W of power. Supported sound features include Object Tracking Sound+ (OTS+), Active Voice Amplifier Pro, Adaptive Sound Pro and AI Sound Controller Pro. The R95H supports Dolby Atmos, but not DTS:X.
The R95H’s smart TV platform is Samsung’s own One UI Tizen, which supports major streaming apps including Netflix and Prime Video, and for those in the UK it supports all major apps including BBC iPlayer and ITVX. There's also support for Samsung Vision AI, which enables AI features such as AI Soccer Mode Pro and Generative Wallpaper.
- Feature score: 5 / 5
Samsung R95H review: Picture quality
- Strong contrast and detail
- Bold colors
- Effective anti-glare
Starting with some brightness measurements, the R95H registered 1,977 nits and 2,066 nits peak HDR brightness in Filmmaker mode and Standard mode respectively. These are solid brightness results, but surprisingly lower than those of Samsung’s flagship OLED, the S95H/S99H, which registered 2,739 nits and 2,831 nits in the same modes respectively.
Where the R95H has an advantage over OLED is in its fullscreen HDR brightness, which hit 612 nits and 600 nits in the same Filmmaker and Standard picture modes, roughly 150 nits higher than the S95H/S99H OLED. While these numbers are solid, they're lower than those of rival RGB TVs such as the Hisense UR8, which hit over 750 nits in both picture modes, and even the Sony Bravia 7 II, which hit over 800 nits in its own Filmmaker mode.
The R95H showcases good upscaling when watching lower-resolution and SDR content. Watching various channels on Samsung TV Plus, from America’s Got Talent re-runs to news channels, the picture looked more detailed than anticipated, showing the R95H’s effective upscaling.
Moving on to the reference 4K Blu-rays I use for testing, the R95H demonstrated very good picture quality. RGB’s selling point is its color reproduction, and the R95H succeeded here. Throughout The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, colors were bold and vibrant, shown in particular whenever the Lumas were on screen. Colors also appeared accurate throughout, with the red of Mario’s overalls looking true to life. I did notice that while watching in Movie mode, there was some clipping of bright objects, and color luminance could look a little distorted at times. Dropping the brightness down to 40 improved this.
In the live-action movie, Speed Racer, I was impressed at how the R95H rendered the gaudy, saturated color scheme of the Racer household, with its vibrant greens and oranges. It captured the oversaturated look, while still delivering realistic colors. While I did prefer the Sony Bravia 7 II’s colors in my Bravia 7 II vs R95H comparison, in isolated viewing, the R95H’s colors were impressive. The R95H did, however, reproduce accurate and realistic skin tones throughout my viewing.
Measuring the R95H’s color gamut coverage, it registered a staggering 148% of the DCI-P3 color gamut, as well as a 94.1% of the BT.2020 color space. These are incredible results, rivaling the best projectors, and the BT.2020 result rivals QD-OLED, found in Samsung's flagship S95H/S99H TVs.
Switching to The Batman for higher-contrast and darker scenes, the R95H demonstrated strong contrast in almost every scene, with a great balance between light and dark tones. This was most evident in the crime scene at Mayor Mitchell’s house, and in the Batcave. The R95H also delivered excellent shadow detail, with objects like paintings on the wall of Mitchell’s house still legible even in the most shadowed areas.
I did find that while I could watch The Batman in bright conditions, thanks to the R95H’s effective glare-free screen, it was best watched in Filmmaker mode in more ambient/dimmer conditions. In Movie mode, The Batman had a tendency to look over-sharp and over-bright in places.
While its black tones weren’t quite OLED-level, the R95H did deliver some seriously rich, deep blacks in Alien: Romulus. Shots of space looked as inky as I could have hoped for, and were impressive for a backlit TV.
The R95H also demonstrated strong viewing angles, and while there was some blooming present in some scenes in The Batman and Alien; Romulus when I viewed the TV off-center, its backlight control was far more effective than you’ll see from standard LED and mini-LED TVs.
Finally, for motion, the R95H is capable of handling fast-paced scenes from movies like Speed Racer, as cars weave around the track. It showed some judder as commentators panned across the screen, but I’ve found every TV has struggled with this. For the best motion, I found setting blur and judder reduction to 3 looked smooth without venturing into soap opera-effect territory.
For sports, I watched some Major League Soccer highlights via Apple TV, and the R95H not only handled the action well but produced a very natural picture in Standard mode (my preferred picture mode for sports) that I found pleasing to watch.
- Picture quality score: 4.5 / 5
Samsung R95H review: Sound quality
- Effective OTS+ results in great sound positioning
- Decent bass and mid range
- Sound can feel contained to rear of the screen
The R95H’s built-in speaker array is a 4.2.2 channel, 70W system. It supports Dolby Atmos and has two preset sound modes: Standard and Amplify. There are AI sound features such as Adaptive Sound Pro available to use.
Watching the Batmobile chase scene from The Batman and the various race scenes in Speed Racer, with the TV set to its Amplify sound mode, I was unsurprised to hear that the R95H delivered accurate sound that was well mapped with the action on the screen, something I’ve found with a lot of Samsung TVs, thanks to its OTS+ feature. Whether it was a spray of bullets hitting the Batmobile in The Batman or the sound of the Mach 5 grinding a rail in Speed Racer, the sound accuracy was impressive.
The speakers deliver good mid-range tones throughout, as well as some punchy bass that accurately captures the rumble of the Batmobile’s engine and the roar of the race cars in Speed Racer. There were some impressive surround effects in both reference movies too.
While the speakers are generally decent, I did have to push the volume to higher levels (70+ out of 100) to get a more cinematic experience. The bass also felt flat at times, and sound did still feel contained to the rear of the screen. Turning on Adaptive Sound in the AI settings added more width, but at the cost of bass. While its sound is decent, those wanting a more cinematic experience would benefit from a soundbar.
- Sound quality: 4 / 5
Samsung R95H review: Design
- Polished frame
- Thinner than other RGB TVs I’ve tested
- Light but sturdy
The R95H takes a lot of design cues from other Samsung TVs, with a sleek, silver frame that gives the TV a premium look. Compared to other RGB TVs I’ve tested, the R95H is thinner, which again gives it an appealing look. It has a central pedestal stand that feels sturdy when attached, while the TV itself feels light for a 65-inch, and lighter than other RGB TVs I’ve tested.
The screen has a bezel-less design, giving maximum room to the pictures on screen. The R95H also has the aforementioned glare-free matte screen for easier viewing in bright conditions.
The supplied remote is the Samsung SolarCell remote, which can be recharged via the rear solar panel or via USB-C. The remote has shortcut buttons to major apps such as Netflix, as well as an AI button and mic button for voice control.
- Design score: 4.5 / 5
Samsung R95H review: Smart TV & menus
- One UI Tizen smart TV platform
- Hubs including Home and Game
- Good range of settings
As with all Samsung TVs, the R95H uses Samsung’s own Tizen OS smart TV platform, now known as One UI Tizen. Tizen has several different hubs, including the Home hub, where apps and TV shows and movie recommendations are presented, and Game hub, where cloud gaming apps are housed. There are also Daily and Art hubs, for lifestyle and art-themed apps respectively.
Tizen supports a wide array of apps, including major streaming services such as Netflix, Prime Video and Disney. In the UK, streaming services such as BBC iPlayer and ITVX are supported. It should be noted that Tizen doesn’t use Freely or Freeview for live TV, instead using its own Samsung TV Plus system.
Various AI features are supported, including the Samsung Vision AI Companion, which can be used to find specific content, or answer more general questions that you ask the AI. Also included are other AI picture and sound features, as discussed in the Features section above.
Tizen is good at offering recommendations, and the Home hub is well laid out, but as with all smart TV platforms nowadays, there's a large banner ad at the top of the screen that can be intrusive when you're trying to navigate.
Menus are well laid out and easy to navigate, and there are a good number of settings, enabling you to tailor the picture to your preferences. Tizen is fairly straightforward to use, although I did find that Samsung TV Plus would play if I lingered on the Home menu, which could be frustrating.
- Smart TV & menus score: 4.5 / 5
Samsung R95H review: Gaming
- Four HDMI 2.1 ports
- 11.7ms input lag time
- 4K 165Hz, FreeSync and G-Sync supported
The R95H has four HDMI 2.1 ports, all of which are fully equipped for gaming. It supports 4K 165Hz, full VRR including Freesync and G-sync, HDR10+ gaming and ALLM. There's a dedicated Game menu where you can adjust game-specific settings, and the Game Hub, which houses cloud gaming apps such as Xbox, Nvidia GeForce Now, and Luna.
When I measured the R95H’s input lag, it registered an 11.7ms (4K 60Hz) time. This is below the 15ms input lag time we look for, but is higher than other Samsung TVs I’ve tested, which all tend to register sub-10ms times.
Actual gameplay on the R95H is smooth, even during fast-paced action. Playing Battlefield V on Xbox Series X, the R95H easily handled the chaotic gunfights as I had to snap from target to target, showing no signs of judder or stutter. The Game picture mode rendered crisp textures and accurate colors for the most part, though I did find it favored red tones in one desert mission I played. Overall, though, the R95H is a superb gaming TV.
- Gaming score: 5 / 5
Samsung R95H review: Value
- Premium priced TV
- Similar price to OLEDs
- Good performance and features
The R95H is a premium TV, with the 65-inch model I tested available for around $2,799 / £2,899 / AU$4,795 at the time of writing. This puts it in a similar price bracket to flagship OLEDs, such as Samsung’s S95H/S99H, which costs $2,799 / £2,899 / AU$5,295, and the LG G6, which costs $2,699 / £2,999 / AU$4,995 for a 65-inch. Compared to other RGB TVs I’ve tested, it’s one of the pricier models, but is cheaper than the rival flagship Sony Bravia 9 II, the 65-inch model of which costs $3,599 / £3,499 / AU$5,995.
The R95H commands a premium price, but does deliver premium performance and features similar to those rival OLEDs and RGB TV mentioned above. Since its release, prices for the R95H have dropped, and I anticipate they’ll continue to drop from now on, improving its value proposition. For now, I don’t think it can quite outshine rival OLEDs for the money, but it's close, and this is still a very good TV.
- Value score: 4 / 5
Should I buy the Samsung R95H?
| Samsung R95H |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | The Samsung R95H has a stacked feature set, including a ton of smart and AI features, and dedicated gaming features. Dolby Vision is still not supported though. | 5/5 | 
| Picture quality | Vibrant, detailed and delivering strong contrast, the R95H's picture quality is excellent. It doesn't beat OLED, and there is still some blooming, but picture is very good. | 4.5/5 | 
| Sound quality | Accurate, well-mapped sound with good detail and clear speech. Bass can be hit-and-miss, though, and the soundstage can feel narrow. | 4/5 | 
| Design | Slimmer than most RGB TVs, with a sleek, polished design. Looks like a premium TV. | 4.5/5 | 
| Smart TV and menus | Tizen is a vey good smart TV platform with plenty of great features, and it's easy to use. Some annoying quirks do remain, though. | 4.5/5 | 
| Gaming | Fully kitted out with ports and features, and with top-notch performance to match, the R95H is a great TV for gaming. | 5/5 | 
| Value | A premium-priced TV in the same price bracket as some of the best OLEDs, but has the features and performance to mostly justify the price. | 4/5 | 
Buy it if...
You want brilliant picture quality
The R95H's picture is vibrant, colorful and detailed. Add in strong contrast, rich black tones and a glare-free screen, and the R95H's really impresses. 
You want a TV for gaming
The R95H is packed with all the gaming features you could need, and delivers terrific performance to match. 
You want to watch in a bright room
The R95H's glare-free matte screen makes watching in bright rooms easy, doing a great job at eliminating reflections. 
Don't buy it if...
You're on a budget
The R95H is a flagship TV and carries a premium price. While it has excellent features and performance, cheaper RGB TVs and OLEDs with similar features are available.  
You want Dolby Vision HDR
The R95H, like all Samsung TVs, doesn't support Dolby Vision HDR. 
You want the very best picture quality
While the R95H boasts very good picture quality, it still doesn't quite beat the best OLEDs for me. 
Also Consider
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Samsung R95H | Samsung S95H/S99H | LG G6 | Sony Bravia 7 II | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price (65-inch) | $3,199 / £3,099 / AU$5,299 | $3,299 / £3,199 / AU$5,299 | $3,299 / £2,999 / AU$4,999 | $2,599 / £2,299 / AU$3,299 | 
| Screen type | Micro RGB | QD-OLED | OLED | RGB LED | 
| Refresh rate | 165Hz | 165Hz | 165Hz | 120Hz | 
| HDR support | HDR10+/HDR10/HLG | HDR10+/HDR10/HLG | HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision | Dolby Vision/HDR10/HLG | 
| Smart TV | One UI Tizen | One UI Tizen | webOS 26 | Google TV | 
| HDMI ports | 4x HDMI 2.1 | 4x HDMI 2.1 | 4x HDMI 2.1 | 4 (2 x HDMI 2.1) | 
Samsung S95H (US and AU) / S99H (UK)
The Samsung S95H/S99H is Samsung's flagship OLED and offers the same gaming features as the R95H, as well as the same smart TV interface, for near-enough the same price. Where the S95H/S99H has the advantage is in its richer-contrast picture quality and detail. If you want OLED, this is the TV to choose. 
Read our full Samsung S95H review (US and AU) / Samsung S99H review (UK)
LG G6
LG's flagship OLED for 2026, the LG G6 supports Dolby Vision HDR support and offers OLED quality picture compared to the R95H. In terms of price, they're near-identical, and both do a offer a full list of smart and gaming features. Your choice will come down to LG vs Samsung preference. 
Read our full LG G6 review
Sony Bravia 7 II
Sony's 'more affordable' RGB TV delivers excellent picture quality, with colors that actually rival, and sometimes beat, the R95H. Plus, it's a lot cheaper. It does lack the same level of features and gaming performance, and isn't as strong performing in bright rooms. This choice will come down to budget. 
Read our full Sony Bravia 7 II review
How I tested the Samsung R95H
- Tested over a few weeks
- Tested in varying light conditions in our testing lab
- Measurements taken using Portrait Displays Calman software
The first step of my testing was casual viewing to establish the best pictures modes. For sports and daytime TV, Standard worked best, and for movies and TV shows, I switched between Movie and Filmmaker depending on the content.
After this, I did my critical viewing using reference 4K Blu-ray scenes to test color, contrast, motion and detail. I also used SDR broadcast TV to test upscaling, as well as sports to test the R95H's sports viewing.
Next, I tested the R95H using specialized measuring equipment, including a Murideo Six G 8K metal test pattern generator, Klein K-10A colorimeter and Jeti Spectral 15VA spectroradiometer and Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software.
To test brightness, I took SDR and HDR brightness measurements using white window patterns in sizes 1-100%, focusing on peak (10%) and fullscreen (100%) measurements.
After this, I tested color and grayscale accuracy in SDR, using Delta-E values (the margin for error between the test pattern signal source and what is displayed on screen.)
Next, I tested HDR color gamut coverage, using the BT.2020 and UHDA-P3 color spaces. The closer to 100%, the better.
Finally, I measured the R95H's input lag using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Input Lag Tester.
We also do two new tests as part of our testing. The first is the HDR EOTF, which shows the accuracy of a TV's brightness across its range, using 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000 nits targets. Then, there is the Spectral Power Distribution test, which measures how a TV recreates colors.
- First reviewed: September 2026
- Read TechRadar's reviews guarantee
James is the TV Hardware Staff Writer at TechRadar. Before joining the team, he worked at a major UK based AV retailer selling TV and audio equipment, where he was either telling customers the difference between OLED and QLED or being wowed by watching a PS5 run on the LG 65G2. When not writing about the latest TV tech, James can be found gaming, reading, watching rugby or coming up with another idea for a novel.

articles.title: Intelligent HMI at the Edge: AI and Human-Machine Interaction - EE Times
articles.text:
Next-generation HMI systems are evolving beyond the touchscreen into intelligent, context-aware experiences powered by edge AI
The interfaces through which people operate machines have grown progressively more capable over several decades. Mechanical knobs and switches were succeeded by membrane keypads, and those in turn by the capacitive touchscreens now standard on thermostats, appliances, medical equipment, and industrial control panels. Each generation increased the flexibility of the interface and reduced the effort required to use it.
The next transition is now underway, and it represents a more significant departure than those that preceded it. Users increasingly expect the device to share the work rather than wait passively for input. They expect it to register their approach, interpret a spoken instruction, and respond to the conditions of the surrounding environment. A thermostat that activates only on a screen tap appears dated alongside one that wakes as a user approaches and adjusts the temperature in response to a spoken request.
Delivering this class of experience is not a matter of industrial design. It is an engineering problem that spans sensing, signal processing, machine learning, connectivity, and graphics, and these elements have historically been difficult to integrate within a single platform. Here we’ll examine why intelligent HMI has become the prevailing design objective, why the underlying AI is migrating from the cloud to the device itself, and what is required to develop such a system without devoting the opening months of a program to hardware and software integration.
Why Traditional HMI Architectures Are Reaching Their Limits
The touchscreen addressed genuine limitations of earlier interfaces. A single display could replace a panel of dedicated buttons, reconfigure itself for different functions, and receive updates in software well after the hardware shipped. For an entire generation of products, that capability was sufficient.
It is no longer sufficient, for reasons unrelated to the quality of the display. A touchscreen depends on deliberate, hands-on input. The user must be within reach of the panel, must look at it directly, and must navigate whatever menu hierarchy the designer has defined. In a kitchen where hands are wet or gloved, on a factory floor where an operator is already holding a tool, or in any setting where the user stands across the room, that interaction model fails.
Touch interfaces are also inherently reactive. The device remains idle until it is touched. It has no awareness of whether anyone is present, who that person is, or what they intend to accomplish. All context must be supplied explicitly through taps and swipes. As products acquire additional functions, their menu structures deepen and interaction slows, the opposite of what users have come to expect.
What designers now require instead is an interface that assumes part of the cognitive load. An intelligent HMI senses its environment, interprets user intent, and responds in a manner that more closely resembles interaction with a person than operation of a machine. Achieving this requires equipping the device with sensing capabilities it has not previously possessed.
What Makes an HMI Intelligent?
The defining characteristic of an intelligent HMI is that it perceives its surroundings through more than one channel. Infineon describes this as a multi-sensing approach. No single sensor captures sufficient context in isolation; it is the combination of several modalities that produces an interface capable of responding with apparent awareness.
Voice is typically the most prominent of these channels. With on-device speech recognition and small language models, a product can respond to a wake word and execute spoken commands without reliance on a paired phone or a network hub. Natural language reduces a deeply nested settings menu to a single spoken instruction.
Vision contributes a different form of awareness. A camera paired with a trained model can determine that a person is present, count the number of people within view, or distinguish a user from the background. This capability supports applications ranging from a display that activates when a user looks toward it to safety functions that depend on confirming whether an operator is correctly positioned.
Radar addresses what cameras and microphones cannot. A 60 GHz radar sensor detects presence and motion without capturing an identifiable image, which makes it well suited to privacy-sensitive environments and to low-power, continuous monitoring. It functions in darkness, operates through certain materials, and requires no deliberate action on the part of the user.
Environmental and motion sensing complete the picture. Temperature, humidity, and data from an inertial sensor provide the system with context regarding its physical conditions and orientation. None of these channels is novel in isolation. What distinguishes an intelligent HMI is the fusion of these inputs, performed on the device and in real time.
Why AI Is Moving from the Cloud to the Edge
For much of the past decade, the default location for executing a machine learning model was the data center. Training required that level of compute, and inference tended to follow training. For an HMI, however, that arrangement carries substantial costs.
The most immediate is latency. A voice command that must travel to a remote server and return introduces a delay the user perceives, and the round trip degrades a natural interaction into a halting one. Performing inference locally removes the network from the path, so the response is bounded only by the time the device requires to compute it.
Privacy and security follow closely. An HMI that processes audio, video, or presence data handles precisely the categories of information about which users are most sensitive. Retaining that data on the device, rather than transmitting it to a third party, reduces the attack surface and avoids an entire class of compliance and trust concerns before they arise.
Reliability is more consequential than it may initially appear. Many of the products that benefit from intelligent HMI operate in locations with poor or intermittent connectivity, including industrial facilities, basements, and remote installations. A system that depends on the cloud to interpret a voice command ceases to function the moment the connection is lost. A system that performs inference locally continues to operate regardless.
Power efficiency is the final factor. Edge AI has become practical largely because the underlying silicon has advanced to meet it. Dedicated neural processing units now execute useful models within the power budget of a battery-operated or always-on device. That development, more than any other, has moved on-device intelligence from a research demonstration to a feature that product teams can bring to market.
The Engineering Challenge of Building Multi-Sensing AI HMI Systems
If the case for an intelligent, edge-based HMI is this clear, the reasonable question is why such systems are not already commonplace. The answer is integration.
Developing one of these systems requires combining a substantial set of subsystems that were not designed to interoperate by default. The sensing hardware alone comprises microphones, a camera, a radar sensor, and environmental and motion sensors, each with distinct interfaces, timing requirements, and driver dependencies. The compute element must provide a processor able to run graphics and multiple inference workloads concurrently without degradation. The AI must be selected, trained, quantized, and optimized to fit the memory and power envelope of an embedded target. Connectivity, generally both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, carries its own firmware development and certification burden. And the display and graphics stack must unify the result into a coherent experience.
Each of these constitutes a project in its own right. Undertaken individually, they represent months of effort that must be completed before a team writes a single line of the application that actually differentiates the product. Engineers spend that time resolving clock-tree issues and driver conflicts rather than designing the experience they set out to create. Hardware integration, software bring-up, model deployment, and connectivity each introduce their own risk, and schedule pressure increases with every dependency. For many teams, this initial cost is the reason an intelligent HMI remains on the roadmap rather than reaching production.
Accelerating Intelligent HMI Development with Integrated Edge AI Platforms
The means of avoiding that initial cost is to begin from a platform on which the integration has already been completed. Infineon developed the PSOC™ Edge E84 HMI Kit for this purpose: a hardware evaluation platform that consolidates the sensing, compute, connectivity, and display elements of an intelligent HMI within a single application-centric package.
The kit is built around the PSOC™ Edge E84 microcontroller, which pairs an Arm Cortex-M55 core with Helium DSP and an Ethos-U55 NPU operating at up to 400 MHz for demanding inference workloads with a lower-power Cortex-M33 core and Infineon’s NNLite NPU for always-on tasks that must minimize power consumption. A dedicated 2.5D GPU renders the graphics, and a secure enclave performs cryptographic operations, while ensuring a robust root of trust for secure boot, authentication, and key management. This architecture allows a design to run a demanding vision or voice model when required and to transition to an efficient always-listening or presence-sensing mode when it is not.
Surrounding the processor, the board integrates the sensing channels described above rather than leaving them for the developer to assemble. It provides a 4-inch capacitive touch display, a USB camera, two analog and four digital microphones, an audio amplifier and speaker, a 60 GHz XENSIV™ radar sensor, a six-axis inertial sensor, and a humidity and temperature sensor. Wireless connectivity is supplied by an onboard Murata module incorporating AIROC™ Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and the supporting Octal-SPI NOR flash and HYPERRAM™ memory are already in place.
Hardware represents only half of the bring-up effort, so the platform pairs the board with Infineon’s ModusToolbox™ software and DEEPCRAFT™ AI Suite. Drivers, example code, reference applications, and out-of-the-box demonstrations are included with the kit, as are companion mobile applications for iOS and Android. The preloaded thermostat demonstration illustrates the complete stack in operation: it responds to the wake phrase “Okay Thermostat,” accepts spoken commands such as a request to lower the temperature, and uses the radar sensor to determine when a user approaches or departs, dimming the display during periods of inactivity and restoring it upon detecting presence.
The significance of this configuration lies not in the component list itself but in what that list removes from the development schedule. With the sensors, processor, connectivity, and software already integrated and validated together, a development team can forgo platform bring-up and begin with the element that differentiates the product, which is the application. In practice, this translates into faster prototyping, reduced integration effort and risk, and a materially shorter path from concept to a production-ready product.
The Future of Human-Machine Interaction
The thermostat demonstration represents a starting point rather than a limit. The same combination of sensing and on-device intelligence applies across consumer appliances, smart-home controls, industrial operator panels, touchless public kiosks, and the expanding category of service and consumer robots that must perceive and respond to people.
The trajectory of these systems is consistent. Interfaces are becoming more conversational, relying on natural language in place of menu hierarchies. They are becoming context-aware, adapting to who is present and to the conditions around them. They are becoming increasingly touchless, driven by voice, gesture, and presence rather than physical contact. And they are becoming more personalized, adjusting their behavior to the individual user. Each of these developments rests on the same foundation: multiple sensing modalities supplying AI that executes on the device itself.
For engineering teams, the relevant conclusion concerns not any single feature but the allocation of design effort. The demanding and largely undifferentiated work of integrating sensors, silicon, and software is increasingly a starting condition rather than a task to be undertaken. The differentiation resides in the application built on top of it.
Getting Started
The PSOC™ Edge E84 HMI Kit provides a means of evaluating that foundation directly. It combines voice, vision, radar, environmental sensing, connectivity, and an edge-AI-capable processor on a single board, supported by the software and reference designs required to begin development immediately. For teams preparing to move an intelligent HMI from roadmap to production, it offers a practical point of entry. To learn more and begin evaluation, visit the Edge E84 HMI Kit webpage.

articles.title: Moneyview IPO to open on September 24
articles.text:
Moneyview IPO to open on September 24
The IPO will close on September 28, and the company's shares are proposed to be listed on the NSE and BSE on October 1, according to a public announcement on Monday.
Digital lending platform Moneyview Ltd is gearing up to launch its Rs 1,092-crore initial public offering (IPO) on September 24.
The price band has been fixed at Rs 32-34 per equity share, valuing the company at nearly Rs 6,000 crore at the upper limit.
The IPO will close on September 28, and the company's shares are proposed to be listed on the NSE and BSE on October 1, according to a public announcement on Monday.
Moneyview's IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth Rs 750 crore and an Offer for Sale (OFS) of 10.05 crore equity shares, valued at Rs 342 crore at the higher end of the issue price, by existing shareholders. This takes the total issue size to Rs 1,092 crore.
Of the Rs 750 crore fresh issue proceeds, Rs 325 crore will be used to support the company's lending operations, while Rs 250 crore will be invested in augmenting the capital base of its NBFC subsidiary. The remaining funds will be utilised for general corporate purposes.
On the financial front, Moneyview reported a profit after tax of Rs 242 crore in FY26 and revenue of Rs 3,351 crore during the year. For the quarter ended June 2026, the company's profit after tax stood at Rs 174 crore and revenue at Rs 1,065 crore.
The company's lending business has continued to grow, with loan disbursals rising 31 per cent to Rs 23,099 crore in FY26. Disbursals stood at Rs 7,152 crore in the first quarter of FY27, up 40 per cent year-on-year. Its assets under management (AUM) stood at Rs 22,520 crore as of June 30, 2026.
Founded in 2014 by IIT Delhi graduates Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, Moneyview operates as a digital-only, credit-led fintech platform offering financial products across borrowing, transactions, investments and protection. Its flagship digital personal loan business, launched in 2017, remains a key contributor to its operations.
The company said its technology and artificial intelligence-led model enables a largely unassisted digital customer journey and allows it to offer personalised financial products at scale.
Moneyview has a user base of more than 140 million and claims coverage across 99 per cent of pincodes in India.
Beyond personal loans, the company has expanded into products and services including earned wage access, home loans, loans against property, digital gold and UPI transactions.
Axis Capital, BofA Securities India, IIFL Capital Services and Kotak Mahindra Capital Company are the book-running lead managers to the issue.

articles.title: Google dévoile les Googlebooks, 5 ordinateurs portables destinés à enterrer les Chromebooks
articles.text:
En mai dernier, Google a dévoilé le Googlebook, soit sa nouvelle plateforme de PC portables destinée à enterrer le Chromebook. Aujourd’hui, l’entreprise de Mountain View dévoile les spécificités de cette nouvelle marque, mais surtout les cinq premiers modèles de Googlebook. Constructeurs impliqués, spécificités, date de disponibilité, prix : on vous dit tout.
Passer facilement d’un smartphone Android à un ordinateur portable, et inversement
Google explique que le Googlebook est « conçu pour notre façon de travailler aujourd’hui ». En d’autres termes, nous commençons à travailler sur le téléphone avant de poursuivre sur l’ordinateur, ou inversement. C’est tout le principe de cette nouvelle plateforme de PC portable : passer facilement d’un appareil à un autre.
Comment cela se traduit-il dans les faits ? Lorsque vous lancez la configuration d’un Googlebook, les paramètres de votre smartphone Android, vos mots de passe enregistrés, vos réseaux Wi-Fi et vos messages sont transférés sur le Googlebook, avec un chiffrement de bout en bout. Point important à préciser : les Googlebook sont basés sur Android, tout en étant associés aux fondations desktop de ChromeOS, ce qui implique la même architecture de sécurité. L’utilisateur a ainsi un accès direct aux applications du Play Store « dont beaucoup sont optimisées pour les grands écrans et l’utilisation d’une souris et d’un clavier », précise l’entreprise américaine.
Quelles fonctionnalités pour ces nouveaux ordinateurs portables ?
Sans surprise, les Googlebook ont été conçus autour de l’intégration de l’IA Gemini. Un bouton sur le clavier permet d’ailleurs d’y avoir un accès direct. Au niveau des fonctionnalités, nous pouvons citer Cast My Apps (les applications du smartphone sont affichées sur l’écran de l’ordinateur et il est possible d’interagir avec celles-ci), Continue On (vous pouvez reprendre sur l’ordinateur une activité commencée sur un smartphone Android et inversement) ou encore Files – Quick Access (accéder aux fichiers du smartphone depuis l’ordinateur).
Nous pouvons aussi citer l’intégration de Magic Pointer (utiliser Gemini directement à partir de ce qui est affiché à l’écran, par exemple pour organiser un calendrier ou traduire du texte), Rambler (transformer des notes ou pensées dictées à l’oral en texte structuré) et Create My Widget (créer des widgets personnalisés en les décrivant simplement en langage naturel).
Cinq modèles de Googlebook pour le lancement
Pour le lancement du Googlebook, Google s’est associé à cinq constructeurs : Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP et Lenovo. Chacun d’entre eux propose son propre Googlebook. Au niveau des performances, Google annonce avoir travaillé avec Intel, Qualcomm et MediaTek. Il est ainsi possible de choisir entre les processeurs Intel Core Ultra Series 3 et Snapdragon X Elite, qui sont « associés à des NPU avancés offrant plus de 45 TOPS de puissance d’IA exécutée directement sur l’appareil ». Notons également le retour de la Glowbar, soit une fine barre lumineuse intégrée au châssis de l’ordinateur qui s’allume au démarrage, s’anime pour indiquer le niveau de charge de la batterie et réagit avec des animations lorsque vous parlez à Gemini. Google précise que chacun des ordinateurs dispose d’un écran tactile, d’un clavier rétroéclairé et d’un pavé tactile haptique. Côté audio, l’entreprise américaine promet « un son cinématographique », avec jusqu’à six haut-parleurs et une prise en charge du son surround Dolby Atmos. Voici les cinq modèles de Googlebook.
L’Acer Googlebook 14 est le seul ordinateur convertible de la gamme. Il peut être utilisé comme ordinateur portable ou comme tablette. Ses caractéristiques techniques sont les suivantes : processeur Intel Core Ultra 5/7 Series 3 (Panther Lake), 16 Go de RAM et au moins 256 Go de stockage, écran tactile OLED 2,8K de 14 pouces avec une luminosité de 500 nits, le tout dans un châssis en aluminium et magnésium de 13,9 mm d’épaisseur pour un poids de 1,13 kg. Son prix débute à 899 dollars.
L’ASUS Googlebook 14 présente quant à lui les caractéristiques suivantes : processeur Intel Core Ultra 5/7 (Panther Lake), 16 à 32 Go de RAM et au moins 256 Go de stockage, écran tactile OLED 2,8K de 14 pouces avec une luminosité de 500 nits, le tout dans un châssis en aluminium et magnésium de 14 mm d’épaisseur pour un poids total de 1 kg. Son prix débute à 1 299 dollars.
Le Lenovo Googlebook 15 est davantage axé sur la productivité avec son écran de 15,3 pouces. Il présente les caractéristiques suivantes : processeur Intel Core Ultra 5 Series 3 (Panther Lake), 16 Go de RAM et au moins 256 Go de stockage, écran tactile OLED 2,8K, son Dolby Atmos, le tout dans un châssis en alliage de magnésium et en carbone de 15,95 mm d’épaisseur pour un poids de 1,28 kg. Son prix débute à 1 299 dollars.
Le HP Googlebook 14 mise quant à lui sur l’élégance, avec un processeur Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite, 16 à 32 Go de RAM et au moins 256 Go de stockage. Il embarque un écran tactile OLED 2,8K de 14 pouces avec une luminosité de 500 nits et se distingue par son châssis entièrement en aluminium de 14 mm d’épaisseur pour un poids de 1,24 kg. Il dispose également d’un capteur d’empreintes digitales et d’une authentification faciale. Son prix débute à 1 299 dollars.
Enfin, le XPS Googlebook de Dell est présenté comme « un équilibre parfait entre hauteur, poids et écran ». Il affiche les caractéristiques suivantes : processeur Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite, 16 à 32 Go de RAM et au moins 512 Go de stockage, écran tactile 2,5K de 13,4 pouces avec une luminosité de 500 nits, le tout dans un châssis en aluminium usiné de 12,7 mm d’épaisseur pour un poids de 1 kg. Il dispose également d’un capteur d’empreintes digitales. Son prix débute à 1 199 dollars.
Ces cinq ordinateurs portables Googlebook seront disponibles à partir du 5 octobre sur le Google Store et chez certains revendeurs. Chaque ordinateur inclut un abonnement de 12 mois à Google AI Pro, avec 5 To de stockage cloud et les outils Gemini Advanced de Google, ainsi que 3 mois d’abonnement à YouTube Premium, Adobe Photoshop et CapCut. Google annonce jusqu’à 10 ans de mises à jour et d’ajout de nouvelles fonctionnalités. Il reste maintenant à voir si les ordinateurs portables Googlebook parviendront à concurrencer le Macbook Neo. Dans tous les cas, Google promet d’offrir (enfin) une expérience plus fluide entre les smartphones Android et les ordinateurs Windows.

articles.title: Ya disponible la nueva Huawei MatePad Air 12: muy ligera, con un pantallón OLED antirreflejos y más de 10.000 mAh de batería
articles.text:
Huawei sigue aumentando su catálogo de tablets con un nuevo modelo que ya podemos comprar en España. Se trata de la MatePad Air 12, una tablet que pesa poco más de 500 gramos y que destaca especialmente por su pantalla OLED. Su PVP es de 799 euros, pero tiene un pequeño descuento de lanzamiento: sale por 749 euros en la tienda oficial de Huawei (también en Amazon). Y en ambas tiendas viene con el M-Pencil Pro de regalo.
HUAWEI MatePad Air Tablet 12" OLED PaperMatte, 8+256GB, con M-Pencil Pro
Una tablet que es ideal para leer, estudiar o dibujar
Esta nueva tablet de Huawei lleva el apellido Air, lo que ya nos indica que es un dispositivo ligero y muy manejable: tiene 5,3 milímetros de grosor y pesa 509 gramos. Para poner esto en contexto, la podemos comparar con el último iPad Air M4 de 11 pulgadas, que es 0,8 milímetros más grueso y 45 gramos más ligero. Todo teniendo en cuenta que la MatePad tiene 12 pulgadas, claro.
Uno de sus puntos estrella es, sin duda, la pantalla. Es un panel OLED de 12 pulgadas con 2.800 x 1.840 píxeles de resolución, 144 Hz y 275 ppi. Además, esta utiliza la tecnología MatePad de Huawei, lo que en la práctica se traduce en dos puntos clave: reduce los reflejos y ofrece textura de papel que la hace ideal para escribir con el lápiz óptico de Huawei (que, recordemos, viene de regalo si aprovechamos la promo de lanzamiento). Todo junto hace que sea una pantalla muy versátil, ideal para ver contenido multimedia, leer o dibujar.
Esta versión de la tablet cuenta con 8 GB de RAM, 256 GB de almacenamiento y una suite completa para tomar notas, escribir o dibujar. Su procesador es un Kirin T93C y cuenta también con un sistema de seis altavoces para poder disfrutar de pelis o videojuegos. Para terminar, cabe destacar que tiene una batería de 10.100 mAh que promete 16 horas de reproducción de video con HDR local y carga rápida de 66 W.

articles.title: "C'est un cataclysme" : Cédric Villani et 24 autres médaillés Fields se disent secoués par la percée mathématique de l'IA
articles.text:
"C'est un cataclysme" : Cédric Villani et 24 autres médaillés Fields se disent secoués par la percée mathématique de l'IA
Trois jours après qu'OpenAI a annoncé avoir résolu l'un des problèmes du millénaire grâce à 10 000 agents d'IA autonomes, 25 lauréats de la médaille Fields, dont Cédric Villani et Terence Tao, alertent sur un possible "effet destructeur" de l'intelligence artificielle sur la recherche en mathématiques.
Le 8 septembre 2026, OpenAI a annoncé qu'un essaim d'environ 10 000 agents autonomes, propulsés par un modèle interne non accessible au public, avait trouvé une singularité dans les équations de Navier-Stokes en trois dimensions. Le problème, vieux de plus d'un siècle, figurait parmi les sept problèmes du prix du millénaire du Clay Mathematics Institute, chacun doté d'un million de dollars. OpenAI a déclaré ne pas avoir l'intention de réclamer le prix. La preuve, formalisée dans l'assistant Lean, attend encore une vérification indépendante.
La communauté mathématique a été soufflée. Cédric Villani, médaille Fields 2010 et spécialiste des équations aux dérivées partielles, qui affirmait encore en juin que les LLM "ne sont pas intelligents et ne comprennent rien de ce qu'ils disent", a reconnu avoir été ébranlé.
	
J'ai été secoué. Une ambiance de fin de l'histoire. C'est un cataclysme comme jamais les maths n'en ont connu.
25 médaillés Fields cosignent une tribune dans Le Monde
Le 11 septembre, vingt-cinq lauréats de la médaille Fields ont publié une tribune dans Le Monde, parmi lesquels Terence Tao, Pierre-Louis Lions, Hugo Duminil-Copin, Peter Scholze et Artur Avila. Ils y alertent sur un possible "effet destructeur" de l'IA sur la recherche mathématique et appellent les entreprises d'IA à "répondre urgemment" aux questions que leur technologie pose à la discipline.
Leur formule centrale : "Les objectifs des entreprises d'IA et ceux de la communauté mathématique divergent profondément."
Isabelle Gallagher, présidente de la Société mathématique de France et elle-même spécialiste des équations de Navier-Stokes, a résumé le malaise dans un témoignage bref : "Le dopage a fait irruption dans notre métier." Sur son blog, David Madore, enseignant-chercheur à Telecom ParisTech, va plus loin, évoquant une "destruction des mathématiques en tant qu'activité humaine".
Une discipline ébranlée jusque dans ses doctorants
Le séisme ne touche pas que les sommets de la discipline. Jean Abou Samra, doctorant en deuxième année à Budapest, témoigne d'un trouble plus intime : "L'usage de l'IA contredit toutes mes motivations et valeurs. J'ai toujours envie de rester dans la recherche, même si ce qui se passe m'interroge. Surtout, je me demande s'il y aura encore des emplois pour moi après ma thèse."
Sur Radio Classique le 15 septembre, Villani a détaillé sa position : il interdit à son doctorant d'utiliser les outils d'IA générative pendant la durée de sa thèse. "Pendant la formation, il faut travailler dur pour remodeler son esprit, son cerveau", a-t-il déclaré, ajoutant que "le chemin est encore plus important en sciences, et en mathématiques en particulier, que le résultat lui-même".
L'annonce d'OpenAI a par ailleurs été ternie par une controverse de priorité. La veille de la publication, le mathématicien Tristan Buckmaster (New York University) et Levent Alpöge, chercheur chez Anthropic, ont révélé qu'ils travaillaient sur le même problème depuis un an, en utilisant eux aussi des modèles de langage, dont Codex d'OpenAI. Buckmaster s'est publiquement interrogé sur des similarités entre ses travaux et ceux du modèle d'OpenAI.
Sam Altman, lui, a revendiqué sur scène à Dreamforce que son modèle interne "surpasse les meilleurs mathématiciens au monde", compressant trois étés de progrès en quatre phrases.

articles.title: Google y Nvidia se asocian para impulsar el uso responsable de electricidad en centros de datos de IA
articles.text:
Google, Nvidia y la empresa de gestión energética Emerald AI lanzaron la Alianza para la Gestión Energética de la IA (AEMA), una coalición que busca desarrollar capacidades de carga flexible en los centros de datos dedicados a la inteligencia artificial. La iniciativa propone que estas instalaciones dejen de ser meros consumidores de electricidad y se conviertan en participantes activos de la red eléctrica, mediante la reducción temporal de su consumo en momentos de alta demanda.
A los tres miembros fundadores se sumaron Anthropic y una serie de socios de lanzamiento provenientes de los sectores energético y de infraestructura digital. Entre ellos figuran The AES Corporation, Constellation, Generate, National Grid, NRG Energy, Analog Devices, Calibrant Energy, Camus, ClearPath, encoord, Fluence, GridUnity, PassKey Inc., RWE, Splight, Verrus y Voltus.
PUBLICIDAD
El mecanismo de respuesta a la demanda podría liberar 100 gigavatios
El concepto central de la alianza es la respuesta a la demanda, una práctica que las empresas de suministro eléctrico utilizan desde hace décadas con grandes consumidores industriales, como fábricas que aceptan reducir su actividad o recurrir a generadores de respaldo a cambio de una compensación económica durante picos de consumo. Según AEMA, aplicar este esquema a los centros de datos de IA permitiría conectar hasta 100 gigavatios adicionales de capacidad al sistema eléctrico.
El fundamento técnico radica en que las redes eléctricas se diseñan para soportar picos de demanda que ocurren solo durante una fracción del año.
Tyler Norris, director de innovación en el mercado energético para IA e infraestructura y primer presidente del consejo de administración de AEMA, explicó en una publicación en LinkedIn que reducir el consumo neto de la red a menos de 100 horas al año puede liberar docenas de gigavatios de capacidad, sin necesidad de esperar entre cinco y siete años —o más— por las actualizaciones tradicionales del sistema.
PUBLICIDAD
Google ya integró un gigavatio de capacidad de respuesta a la demanda
Norris citó como antecedente que Google demostró la viabilidad de este modelo al integrar 1 gigavatio de capacidad de respuesta a la demanda a nivel nacional en Estados Unidos. La compañía probó por primera vez estas capacidades con el Omaha Public Power District en 2024 y, el año siguiente, anunció acuerdos similares con Indiana Michigan Power (I&M) y la Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA).
Recientemente, Google firmó contratos adicionales con Entergy Arkansas, Minnesota Power y DTE Energy que también incorporan mecanismos de respuesta a la demanda en sus contratos energéticos a largo plazo.
En respaldo a la nueva alianza, Google publicó dos informes con hojas de ruta concretas. Uno, elaborado por The Brattle Group, ofrece un plan técnico para convertir en realidad operativa la reciente orientación bipartidista de la Comisión Federal Reguladora de la Energía (FERC).
PUBLICIDAD
El segundo, a cargo de Aurora Energy Research, presenta un modelo de centros de datos flexibles en el sistema ERCOT combinados con recursos “front-of-meter”, es decir, ubicados del lado de la red antes del medidor del consumidor.
El eje de la alianza
La tecnología de Emerald AI ocupa un lugar central en la alianza. El software de la empresa coordina las solicitudes de las empresas de suministro eléctrico con los centros de datos, que pueden pausar tareas no críticas o transferir cargas hacia instalaciones donde la red cuenta con margen disponible. Esta propuesta se presenta como alternativa a los generadores diésel de respaldo, a los que recurren actualmente muchos centros de datos durante los picos de demanda.
PUBLICIDAD
Emerald AI no es la única compañía que desarrolla este tipo de herramientas: Google trabaja en sus propias soluciones internas, y Enel X permite a los centros de datos aprovechar sus sistemas de alimentación ininterrumpida para suavizar los picos de demanda eléctrica. Un estudio de Goldman Sachs estimó que limitar el uso máximo de la red al 90% durante algunas horas podría liberar 76 gigavatios de capacidad adicional.
Más allá de la coordinación técnica, AEMA también se propone ayudar a las empresas tecnológicas y a las compañías eléctricas a identificar nuevos emplazamientos para centros de datos, un proceso que hasta ahora ha resultado complejo para ambas partes.

articles.title: VZMORE Introduces V-Cooling Vapor Chamber Thermal Architecture for Mini PCs
articles.text:
Monday, September 21st 2026
	
	
	
	
VZMORE Introduces V-Cooling Vapor Chamber Thermal Architecture for Mini PCs
Combining vapor chamber cooling, vertical airflow and intelligent thermal management, V-Cooling improves thermal efficiency, sustained performance and acoustic performance in compact computers. Mini PC brand VZMORE has introduced its proprietary V-Cooling thermal architecture, bringing vapor chamber technology—commonly used in flagship smartphones, high-performance laptops and gaming consoles—to its Mini PC products. The system is designed to reduce heat buildup, performance loss and operating noise during sustained workloads.
Traditional Mini PCs often rely on single- or dual-heat-pipe cooling, which can concentrate heat around the processor and limit sustained performance. V-Cooling uses a large vapor chamber to spread heat rapidly and evenly across the cooling area. Compared with conventional dual-heat-pipe solutions, it increases heat-spreading area by approximately 40% and thermal conductivity efficiency by approximately 50%, helping reduce localized hot spots and support more stable processor performance.VZMORE also optimizes the overall industrial design around thermal requirements. The system combines wider high-density cooling fins, vertical airflow, 360-degree bottom air intake and intelligent thermal management. Fan blades made from a polymer material help reduce vibration and operating noise, improving the balance between cooling and acoustics.
Under high-load operation, VZMORE Mini PCs can operate at noise levels as low as approximately 38 dB—around 12 dB lower than the approximately 50 dB produced by some conventional Mini PCs. This creates an acoustic environment closer to a quiet library and a less distracting desktop experience.
"A Mini PC should offer more than a smaller form factor," said a VZMORE representative. "V-Cooling is designed to help compact computers remain stable, quiet and reliable under demanding workloads. Although the cooling module costs approximately three times as much as a conventional dual-heat-pipe solution, we believe the long-term user experience justifies the investment."
