I would not expect nvidia 5090 performance for my radeon 9070 oc and i would not expect 1080p performance for this 720p radeon 9050 4gib vram graphic card.
Such card is usable for these days overblown windows 95 style desktops like windows 11 pro, 10 pro, kde, gnome and for basic tasks like libreoffice or using gimp with 2d acceleration. maybe some cpu offloading for watching youtube videos etc. I would not recommend such cards with these days gamers kiddy monitors, like the aoc one i tested, 150hz or more with 1080p or similar hz vs resolutions.
Someone at these companies needs to embrace the concept of performance-per-dollar and pursue it, especially at the low end.
People who settle for buying a product like this likely don't have the money to buy anything better.
For me this card was never a gaming card, it's a media pc / office pc option for those where the iGPU in the CPU isnt up to the task.
AMD clearly learned something from their prior mistakes no?
Is it a good product overall? No, because right off the bat, it imposes limitations. But we are talking about a low-end product in today's reality. Honestly, what do you expect? Especially when the low-end market is dead. And back when we used to say the low-end market was dead, we meant graphics cards up to $100. That threshold eventually rose to $150, and later to $200. Seriously, has any other company released anything modern and better? The way the market is now, you have to look above $250 to find current-generation products. At lower price points, you only find options that are 3, 5, 10, or 15 years old. People are still buying relics like the GT 730, GT 1030, and RX 580.
It all comes down to the price. OEMs surely asked for a 4GB card because they wanted something that yields a higher profit margin. If an RX 9050 or an RTX 5050 ends up starting at $300 and up, this one will probably sit slightly above $200. An unthinkable price, but that is the current state of affairs. Once upon a time, an RX 570 8GB was selling for under $150. But that was then. Are we forgetting what is happening today?
AMDLeather Jackets Unboxed said
That being said, it's better to use the bigger percentage, instead of saying that A is 50% slower than B, it's better to say B is 100% faster than A.
As everyone else, I don't get why AMD didn't rename the graphics card to something else. Yes, the core is the same, but unlike the 9060 XTs, where both the 8 GB and 16 GB versions use the same memory bus width, the 4 GB of the 9050 version only uses half of it, along with half of the Infinity Cache.
Also giving it PCIe 5.0 x16 interface seems very weird, seeing that the AMD Radeon RX 6500 XT has PCIe 4.0 x4, so eight times less bandwidth to the CPU. This will surely help hide the meager 4 GB of VRAM, but only when using it in a compatible platform with plenty of fast system memory, which is an issue as this is an entry level card.
This should have been an AMD Radeon RX 9040 with 75 W total board power to run from the PCIe slot only.
I am not going to do it here.
Calling the 4GB card a 9030 may have helped, but someone would've trashed on it regardless for being a 4GB card with AMD in the name. This card is indeed a waste, having less than 8GB of VRAM is too limiting for anything but the least demanding titles and you may as well just use an iGPU.
5050/60 even more so at ~$300.
This has to be $170 to make sense and even then it's a bad idea to buy one.The OEM is irrelevant. OEMs are desperate for any GPU. AMD sets policy and experiences the effect of that, they're not some mom and pop store desperate for customers. Multi-billion Corp. This isn't a 9050, it differs in more than just VRAM quantity, so shouldn't be called a 9050. Very simple.
The different laptop variants of NVIDIA 3050 cards is another conversation, but if there's a ~40% performance difference like there is here, that's not power/cooling related then they should be held to the same standard.
As if two wrongs make a right (even giving that benefit of the doubt). Oh, and there's a 9050-4GB page now, with no benchmark results promised or anything else. So they're excused by default, the customer is the one responsible for making sure they did their due diligence, they aren't obliged to let people know it's not a 9050 beyond that.
And at $170 a year ago, it wouldn't have made sense either, because the RX 6600 with 8GB of VRAM was going for around that price. But again, I ask: are we forgetting what's happening in the market? I think we all know what's going on in the market today, and we shouldn't be commenting based on yesterday's reality.
The reference to OEMs is not irrelevant at all. We've known and heard about this for years—decades, even—how OEMs demand new names, and companies will oblige. Not just AMD, which has its back against the wall regarding the gaming market right now, but even the mighty Nvidia itself will do OEMs a favor just to make the sale. For instance, I was showing @Dr. Dro the case of the MX 550, which based on its architecture should have been called the MX 470. He didn't answer me. Even top-tier companies release embarrassing models. The GTX 1630 from 2022, built on a 2019 architecture and offering the performance of a GTX 1050 from 2016, is a prime example. As for the naming of the card itself, I completely agree with those saying it should be called the RX 9040, just like how the 6GB RTX 3050 should have been called the RTX 3040 based on its performance.I guess you agree with this kind of tactics
The B570 is $259, however who knows what driver support it'll get in the long term, since Intel has all but abandoned any new dGPU development in favor of selling them as AI cards.
A RTX5050 starts at $353, no the low profile version doesn't count, neither do MC bundles, and a 5060 is close to being $500. $500 for a entry level 8GB card, crazy times we're in and things will probably get worse as the companies buying all of the RAM and GPU's are doing things like selling us back gaming in the cloud with limited play time.
Apples and oranges. Of course, the topic is the current gen card, not something released half a decade ago.Intel have been very good with drivers both for iGPU (for a long time) and dGPU (more recently), they're also ahead of AMD in upscaling and FG tech. B570 has gone from like $220 to $250 recently, and could be had for cheaper at times. Still more compelling.2587 instead of 2620-50 boost MHz it's going to cost... 1% perf? LP versions absolutely count, especially as many people looking at entry level want to upgrade a office or prebuilt PC with limited space, and can be had for $300 online, delivered.
Why is it you get to pick and choose what "counts"?$440 on Amazon. Cheaper on Ebay (new). Not hard to check these things. What is hard is believing the misrepresentation isn't deliberate.
You get to pick what counts then? People outside the US need to realize Microcenters stores aren't everywhere.A $19 difference,lol. I personally wouldn't buy PNY because of their recent reputation on denying warranties, or a dumb mishap with placing a serial number sticker on the PCI-e contacts, PNY cards are probably cheaper for a reason. What is difficult to believe is your defending a $400+ low end card when it should be $200 at most.

articles.title: Beyond the hype: Who actually needs a local stablecoin?
articles.text:
This is Follow the Money, our weekly series that unpacks the earnings, business, and scaling strategies of African fintechs, financial institutions, companies, and governments. A new edition drops every Monday.
Over the past six years, several local stablecoins pegged to African currencies have sprung up with one clear proposition: to put African money on-chain.
South Africa has ZARP and ZARsc. Nigeria has cNGN, while Tanzania has nTZS. ZARP, launched in 2019, had about R74.6 million ($4.6 million) worth of tokens in circulation as of September 21, backed by R92.8 million ($5.7 million) in reserves. cNGN’s supply crossed ₦3.75 billion ($2.82 million) as of September 21, according to figures reported by the issuer.
The local stablecoin industry has spent much of its time explaining how putting African currencies on a blockchain could make payments faster, cheaper, and more interoperable. The pitch skips the harder question: who actually needs them on-chain badly enough to use them?
Dollar-backed stablecoins already have something that could take years for local stablecoins to replicate: a global market, network effect, deep liquidity, and a reason for people to hold or use them. In emerging markets, including Africa, users hold dollar-backed stablecoins to protect savings, pay suppliers, move money across borders, or access global markets. In many cases, what they want is exposure to dollars, the underlying currency.
The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) estimated the combined stablecoin market at about $320 billion at the end of May 2026, with about 99.4% of that value tied to the dollar. A local stablecoin does not have an equivalent source of built-in demand.
On the other side of that equation are the rails that already exist today. In parts of Africa, consumers have established ways to move local currencies within their borders. Bank transfers work. Mobile money works. Payment processors have spent years stitching these systems together.
This compounds the chicken-and-egg problem for local stablecoin issuers. Users need a reason to hold a local token before merchants have a reason to accept it. Merchants need enough users and liquidity before accepting it becomes worthwhile. Liquidity providers need enough trading activity to make money, but more trading activity requires more users, restarting the cycle.
The B2C case is weak
Local stablecoins often target integration with cryptocurrency exchanges, which provide distribution for these digital currencies. For example, cNGN, in its early days, sought integration with startups such as Busha and Quidax, while incentivising smaller exchanges through token grants. The strategy was aimed, in part, at retail consumers.
But the retail case, particularly for last-mile payments or currency conversion, is weak.
If a retail user holds Tether’s USDT, wants naira, and can convert directly into a bank account, adding a naira stablecoin in the middle adds another transaction rather than obvious value. It creates an additional leg in the transaction.
The wholesale case is more nuanced, and potentially more compelling.
On the wholesale, or business-to-business (B2B), side, a local stablecoin has to answer three questions before it becomes useful: who wants to hold it, who will accept it, and who will provide liquidity when either side wants to enter or exit?
The first question is especially difficult. A Nigerian who wants dollar exposure has an obvious reason to hold USDT or USDC. A Tanzanian business making a payment to China has a reason to want dollars. An importer, trader, or payment company can use a dollar-backed stablecoin beyond its home market because the other side of the transaction is more likely to recognise it.
A Tanzanian shilling-backed stablecoin does not have the same cross-border network simply because it represents the underlying currency.
But it can still play a useful role as the local leg of a transaction.
Purely as an illustration, a Tanzanian importer could convert shillings into nTZS, move the nTZS on-chain, convert it into USDT, and eventually pay a supplier in China. The local stablecoin has done something useful in that chain: it has provided an on-chain representation of the shilling that connects local liquidity to a global digital asset market.
This is particularly relevant in African markets where directly on-ramping—converting from fiat to digital currencies—is difficult.
The Chinese supplier does not need to want nTZS. A local stablecoin does not necessarily need to become the money used by both sides of a transaction. It can serve as the local leg of a transaction whose other leg is a dollar-backed stablecoin.
Move up the financial stack, and the picture changes.
I spoke with David Machuche, founder of NedaPay and its Tanzanian shilling-backed stablecoin nTZS, in July, days before the product kicked off participation in the Bank of Tanzania’s regulatory sandbox.
He said much of the early demand for nTZS was coming from payment companies, developers, and businesses managing cross-border liquidity, rather than consumers looking for a new way to pay for groceries.
Consider a payment service provider (PSP) moving money across several African markets. It may hold local bank accounts, liquidity relationships, and operating balances in each country, with cash sitting idle while it waits for transactions to settle. A local stablecoin could turn part of that inventory into an on-chain asset.
Market makers have their own reason to show up. They quote buy and sell prices for nTZS against shillings or USDT, earning from the difference between those prices. Machuche said market makers can set spreads ranging from 0.1%–0.4%, depending on how they price their liquidity, while swaps settle within seconds. TechCabal could not independently confirm these figures; nTZS saw only a handful of on-chain transfers in the 24 hours before publication, and pricing runs through NedaPay’s internal market-making rather than a public order book.
However, purely as an illustration, at a 0.1%–0.4% spread, a liquidity provider moving $1 million would generate $1,000–$4,000 in gross revenue. Do that 100 times a month, and it becomes $100,000–$400,000 in gross spread revenue.
Circle, the US-based issuer of the dollar-backed USDC stablecoin, said USDC traded with spreads below 0.01% on major exchanges 99% of the time between January and December 2025. Data intelligence firm Kaiko’s 2023 analysis found that USDT pairs had some of the tightest spreads in crypto, while some less-liquid stablecoin pairs had spreads of 0.08% or more.
If market makers see enough activity from merchants and payment companies moving large volumes, the opportunity to earn money from the spread could give them a reason to stay, helping to solve the liquidity problem.
During its initial rollout, Machuche noted that nTZS had about 6.2 million tokens on-chain and roughly 390 holders, as of July. That figure has now crossed 9.66 million, according to AfriFlux, an on-chain intelligence platform, since the stablecoin launched in April.
The opportunity for local stablecoins, then, is to find and operate in pockets where dollar-backed systems are less efficient. Targeting a niche wholesale market may be a more realistic problem to solve than chasing retail adoption.
On-chain foreign exchange
On-chain foreign exchange (FX) gives local stablecoins another possible role: they can become the local-currency leg in a market where the other side is a dollar-backed stablecoin or another local stablecoin.
Across Celo and HyperFX, cNGN is already being used this way. It has integrated with HyperFX, an on-chain FX protocol built by Nigerian startup Polytope Labs, which runs on Hyperbridge.
A business can deposit cNGN and request USDC, for example. A liquidity provider or solver on the other side provides the USDC from its own inventory, while the transaction settles through smart contracts rather than a series of manual transfers.
The point is not for the counterparty to hold cNGN. It needs USDC, dollars, or another currency. cNGN provides the naira liquidity that enters the market, while the other side provides the foreign currency.
Noblocks, a Nigerian payments infrastructure company, is one example. HyperFX said on September 17 that Noblocks had helped move more than ₦573 million ($430,910) in cNGN into naira through 45 orders, putting the average order at about ₦12.7 million ($9,545). The size of those transactions points to a market being used for larger flows rather than everyday retail payments.
According to AfriFlux, HyperFX settled $3.83 million across 1,309 orders between June 1 and September 19, with 1,058 orders filled. The broader opportunity is to connect local currency liquidity to the much larger pool of dollar stablecoins already used for cross-border transactions.
Yield can manufacture demand—but at what cost?
Building network effects for stablecoins is difficult. If the retail use case does not have an obvious reason to exist, yield is one way to manufacture demand.
People respond to incentives. Yield can give users a reason to hold a token even when they have no immediate use for it.
Fiat-backed stablecoin issuers often invest a substantial portion of their reserves in relatively safe assets, such as government securities and bank deposits, which generate income. Purely as an illustration, an issuer with ₦100 million ($75,223) in reserves earning 12% a year could generate ₦12 million ($9,027) in gross income. Some of that income could be passed on to holders as a reward.
But there is a trade-off. A stablecoin that pays users simply for holding it could compete with bank deposits. Banks rely on deposits to fund lending and other financial activity, so moving large amounts of customer money from bank accounts into stablecoins could reduce the pool of deposits available to banks.
Regulators are drawing a line around passive yield. In the United States, negotiations over the CLARITY Act moved towards restricting rewards that function like interest on stablecoin balances while allowing some activity-based rewards. The bill failed to advance in the Senate on September 15.
Kenya’s virtual asset regulations prohibit interest and benefits tied to how long a stablecoin is held. Nigeria’s proposed framework for digital assets, issued on August 20, also prohibits virtual asset service providers from paying interest without approval from the capital markets regulator and proper disclosure to customers.
Tanzania has taken a more cautious approach: its current sandbox conditions require separate approval for yield-generating activity.
Yield can create holders. It cannot, on its own, create a reason to use the token.
Where will local stablecoins solve a pain point?
Local stablecoins need serious scaffolding around them to work: exchanges, wallets, market makers, banks, and redemption channels. Without that infrastructure, supply does not equal demand. Retail adoption can follow once the layer works well enough; it does not need to come first.
There is also a regulatory case for local stablecoins. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned that widespread use of dollar stablecoins could indirectly accelerate digital dollarisation and put pressure on monetary sovereignty. As dollar stablecoins become more widely used, regulators may have an interest in keeping more digital payments denominated in local currencies.
Local stablecoins give regulators a potentially more visible and controllable alternative, provided reserves, issuance, and redemption can be properly monitored.
A few African regulators, including Nigeria and Kenya, have signalled they want to keep a close watch on stablecoins, both local and foreign. In Nigeria, where a local stablecoin is already operating, specific rules could spur demand or hold it back.
Local stablecoins can be useful where they connect local currency liquidity to markets that already have demand: cross-border payments, on-chain FX, treasury management, and wholesale settlement, including intra-African trade cases where local currencies are difficult to access or convert directly.
In those markets, the token does not need to replace the naira or shilling. It needs to make moving, exchanging, or settling the underlying fiat currency easier.
None of this means African currencies do not belong on-chain. It means the question worth asking is narrower than the industry’s pitch suggests: not whether a naira or a shilling can become a token, but whether enough institutions moving real money have a reason to keep using it once the incentives are removed.

articles.title: Moteurs hybrides : Stellantis s'attaque au pire défaut de la conduite urbaine
articles.text:
Le groupe franco-italo-américain accumule les revirements sur la voiture électrique, où il a clairement pris du retard. Un dépôt de brevet montre que le constructeur met des ingénieurs et de l’argent sur l’hybride.
Le document, repéré à la mi-septembre 2026 par le média américain CarBuzz, décrit une manière de faire travailler moteur thermique et moteur électrique plus « proprement » qu’aujourd’hui. De quoi gommer, en théorie, les petits à-coups qu’on ressent parfois en pleine relance.
Sur un hybride, moteur thermique et moteur électrique doivent se passer le relais en permanence. Le vrai souci tient au temps de réaction. Le conducteur accélère, des capteurs le détectent, le calculateur envoie ses ordres, le système répond. Ces échanges filent presque à la vitesse de la lumière, mais ça reste une réaction, et une réaction prend toujours un peu de temps. Surtout pour un moteur thermique qui ne réagit pas aussi rapidement qu’un moteur électrique. Ce délai minuscule suffit à provoquer les micro-secousses qu’on sent parfois passer dans la transmission.
Le brevet déposé auprès de l’office américain propose de passer de la réaction à l’anticipation. Un nouveau calculateur combinerait un filtre de Kalman (un algorithme mathématique qui prédit le comportement d’un système malgré les incertitudes) avec une prédiction sur un horizon donné, qui fixe jusqu’où on peut anticiper.
L’objectif : caler les impulsions du moteur électrique sur celles du thermique, réduire les chocs dans la transmission et lisser la conduite. Le système vise surtout les hybrides dépourvus d’embrayage pour débrancher le moteur, autrement dit ceux qui roulent avec une transmission à variation continue, l’eCVT.
Un brevet déposé, pas une voiture à vendre
Précisons que le brevet protège une idée, mais il ne garantit pas un produit, et beaucoup ne dépassent jamais le stade du papier. Stellantis en dépose d’ailleurs plusieurs autour de l’hybride en ce moment, entre un turbo électrique signé SRT, un autre système de commande cet été et même des supercondensateurs dérivés de Lamborghini.
Le groupe n’a pourtant presque plus d’hybrides au catalogue américain, après avoir abandonné ses hybrides rechargeables aux États-Unis et retiré ses modèles 4xe..
En Europe, la feuille de route n’est pas plus limpide. Jeep prépare sa riposte avec une gamme mêlant électriques et hybrides, après avoir lancé sa Wrangler en version 100 % électrique. Et Stellantis commence tout juste à adopter le full hybrid, cette architecture que Renault et Toyota exploitent depuis des années.
Miser sur l’hybride quand Toyota écrase tout
Sur le papier, remettre de l’hybride au catalogue tombe bien, puisque la demande grimpe. Sauf que Stellantis souffle le chaud et le froid depuis des mois. Le groupe a renoncé au thermique comme à l’hybride pour sa future gamme de petites voitures inspirée de la 2CV. Côté américain, le V8 HEMI du Ram a même perdu son hybridation 48 volts pour 2027.
Ce dernier renoncement est en partie poussé par une réglementation américaine sur la consommation. Début 2026, le constructeur justifiait un virage favorable à l’essence par 22,2 milliards d’euros de charges exceptionnelles. Difficile, dans ces conditions, de savoir sur quel pied danse le groupe.
Pendant ce temps, Toyota domine l’hybride sans partage. Le japonais table sur un record de plus de 5 millions d’hybrides vendus en 2026, du jamais-vu pour lui. C’est précisément ce savoir-faire que Stellantis espère rattraper, voire dépasser, avec ce genre de brevet.
Sauf que Toyota, justement, traîne lui aussi sur le 100 % électrique, à force d’avoir tout misé sur l’hybride. Parier gros sur cette technologie suppose qu’elle restera la référence encore longtemps, alors qu’elle reste une étape avant l’électrique. Un calculateur plus malin rendra peut-être l’hybride plus agréable, il ne changera pas cette trajectoire de fond.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Quelles sont les meilleures voitures électriques ? Notre guide d’achat
            
Un système capable de gommer les à-coups d’une hybride est uen bonne idée. Encore faut-il qu’une voiture l’embarque un jour, ce qui n’a rien d’acquis avec un simple brevet. Le vrai chantier de Stellantis est ailleurs : décider combien de temps il veut encore raisonner en hybride, quand son retard, lui, se joue sur l’électrique.

articles.title: Bun Rewrites 535K Lines of Zig into Rust in Four Months, Eliminates Numerous Memory Leaks
articles.text:
Bun creator Jarred Sumner recently announced that Bun, the JavaScript/TypeScript runtime, bundler and package manager has been rewritten from Zig to Rust. The rewrite seeks to eliminate recurrent memory safety vulnerabilities via Rust’s borrow checker. The AI-assisted rewrite was released after 4 months of work instead of the estimated one year.
Sumner summarizes the motivation behind what started as a spike:
A large percentage of bugs […] are use-after-free, double-free, and “forgot to free” in an error path. In safe Rust, these are compiler errors and RAII-like automatic cleanup with Drop. Compiler errors are a better feedback loop than a style guide.
Historically, rewrites are a terrible idea. […] Bun is 535,496 lines of Zig. A rewrite in another language would take a small team of engineers a full year. It would mean freezing bugfixes, security fixes or feature development for that time.
Fortunately, Bun’s own test suite is written in TypeScript which means it doesn’t depend on the runtime’s programming language.
What if, instead, I spend a week testing if Anthropic’s new model can rewrite Bun in Rust?
At first, I didn’t expect it to work. A few days in, a high % of the test suite started passing and I saw how much the new Rust code matched up with the original Zig codebase. My opinion went from “this is worth trying” to “I’m going to merge this”.
Sumner executed an automated all-at-once port leveraging for most of the rewrite a pre-release version of Claude Fable 5 orchestrated across approximately 50 dynamic workflows. The Zig would be transpiled into Rust (possibly using unsafe Rust that could be refactored later) and validated against the existing extensive test suite of more than one million assertions. A porting guide would help Claude map Zig patterns & types to Rust patterns & types. Adversarial agentic code reviews would further detect issues before they make it to the final port. The implementation loop would be improved after each error by improving the implementation process rather than manually fixing the implementation artifacts (e.g., the code).
The constant process improvement revealed useful patterns. The planning phase is critical to success and must result in key challenges being anticipated and mitigated. PORTING.md (describing the mapping from Zig to Rust) and LIFETIMES.tsv file (describing lifetimes of every struct field in the codebase) were key success factors for the port.
An implementer would then use those files to translate Zig files into Rust code. The implementer agent would be faced with two adversarial reviewer agents running in isolated context windows with access only to the file diffs, with their only task being to discover bugs and behavioral divergences. Sumner emphatically explains:
The implementer doesn’t review. The reviewer doesn’t implement.
Suggestions and issues found by the reviewer agents were dealt with by a fixer agent.
The implementation process efficiency massively leverages the parallelization of the implementation tasks. That however requires addressing concurrent updates of the shared codebase, and the starvation of limited computing resources.
The effort was ultimately distributed across four workspace shards running 16 agents each, operating 64 Claude instances in parallel. At peak velocity, the system generated roughly 1,300 lines of code per minute and logged up to 695 commits an hour.
Getting to the full test suite passing required $165,000 worth of tokens — to be contrasted with Sumner’s estimate of human engineering effort:
Pre-merge, this took 5.9 billion uncached input tokens, 690 million output tokens, and 72 billion cached input token reads — around $165,000 at API pricing. By hand, I think this would’ve taken 3 engineers with full context on the codebase about a year.
Having what became over 1 million lines of code pass the test suite was then followed by further testing and validation, which surfaced further issues.
The mechanical nature of the port introduced 19 subtle semantic regressions rooted in syntactic similarities between Zig and Rust. 11 rounds of security review from Claude Code Security fixed several security issues. 24/7 coverage-guided fuzzing of every parser in Bun resulted in 15 PRs.
According to the Bun team, the resulting Rust implementation in Bun v1.4.0 resolved 128 longstanding bugs present in v1.3.14 while delivering noticeable dividends. Native memory leaks were addressed. In-process bundling tests running 2,000 consecutive Bun.build() operations plateaued stably at 609 MB in Rust rather than climbing past 6.7 GB. HTTP throughput increased by 2% to 5%.
Bun v1.4.0 was finally released in August 2026.
Zig creator Andrew Kelley published a sharply critical reaction titled “My Thoughts on the Bun Rust Rewrite,” which included the following comments:
There’s a dichotomy being presented here where you have to either choose a “style guide” or a programming language feature in order to avoid bugs. The sleight of hand misdirects the reader away from the main way bugs are eliminated: by dedicating engineering resources to it. […]
The argument for shipping all the million lines of unreviewed code is that the test suite is good enough to catch everything. Then why are you saying you have so many annoying bugs in the Zig code? What happened to the test suite being sufficient to catch everything? It’s not sufficient to catch bugs in Zig code but it is sufficient to catch bugs in 1 million lines of unreviewed slop?
Concurrently, user vitaminCPP posited that merging over one million lines of machine-transpiled code establishes Bun as a crucial industry canary for whether massive, LLM-generated codebases can remain maintainable over the software engineering lifecycle.
Developers are encouraged to read the full article, which contains in-depth technical explanations and accompanying illustration and graphics.

articles.title: Belgium’s NewSchool VC closes maiden fund at €10 million to back B2B technology startups | EU-Startups
articles.text:
NewSchool VC, a Belgium-based venture capital fund that invests in B2B pre-Seed technology companies, has closed its first fund at its €10 million target. The firm announced a €6.1 million first close for NewSchool Fund I in September 2025.
Around fifty investors back the fund, including six family offices, among them The Millers Office, as well as entrepreneurs from the Belgian business scene. These include Willem Delbaere and Roeland Delrue (Aikido Security), Jean-Louis Van Houwe (Monizze) and Luc Coopman (Cobofisk). Christophe Morbee, founder of NewSchool, contributed 25% of the fund himself.
“I invested as an angel for years, but felt it was time to build a real structure around it. I love entrepreneurship, investing, and sharing what I know about marketing, sales, HR and finance with founders. That’s what led me to launch a full-fledged fund,” said Morbee. 
Founded in 2025 by Morbee, who spent years as an angel investor before launching it. He’s also the CEO of besox, a Belgian payroll and HR administration provider for SMEs. “That journey, from a first idea to a company that keeps growing well past the startup phase, shapes the fund’s investment philosophy. Through besox, with its roughly 4,000 SME clients, the fund also opens doors for its portfolio companies to find early customers,” the VC fund mentioned in the press release.
The solo-GP fund invests between €100k and €500k in B2B technology companies at the pre-Seed and Seed stages, focusing on AI, SaaS, cybersecurity, robotics and compliance+.
It has made 32 investments to date, 75% of which are based in Belgium, with the remainder spread across Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Switzerland, France, and the United Kingdom.
Notable names in its portfolio that have since raised follow-on rounds are Ravical, Warren, Spotable and Donna. The fund recently invested in the Swiss company Talentir and in Paris-based Outline.
“Europe is an engineer’s continent, with technically strong teams. What’s often missing is someone who takes charge of go-to-market, sales and storytelling. That’s where we focus, alongside the capital we provide. There’s still enormous room to automate old industries. We see plenty of opportunity there for the years ahead,” concluded Morbee.

articles.title: Nouvelle cyberattaque en France : les données de près de 2 millions de Français compromises
articles.text:
Une nouvelle fuite de données frappe la France. L’Agence nationale pour la formation des adultes (Afpa) a en effet été victime d’un piratage informatique. L’organisme, spécialisé dans la formation professionnelle continue, explique avoir ouvert une enquête dès que deux hackers ont revendiqué le vol de ses données.
Les investigations ont mis en évidence « une potentielle extraction de données qui serait liée à une faille sur l’outil qu’on utilise pour gérer nos hébergements », indique Pierre Prady, directeur adjoint de l’agence, à l’AFP. L’outil piraté est géré par un éditeur tiers, extérieur au système d’information de l’Agence nationale pour la formation des adultes. Selon la direction, il n’y a « a priori pas eu d’impact sur les services et systèmes d’information » de l’agence elle-même.
À lire aussi : Facturation électronique – une fuite de données frappe une plateforme comptable en pleine réforme
1,7 million de victimes potentielles
Pour le moment, l’ampleur exacte de la fuite est encore incertaine. Les investigations réalisées par les équipes de l’Afpa estiment qu’1,7 million de personnes sont potentiellement touchées. L’organisme dit continuer à « examiner l’étendue des données et des personnes concernées pour ensuite les prévenir ».
Parmi les informations compromises, on trouve les noms, les adresses postales et, éventuellement, les numéros de téléphone. Par contre, aucune donnée sensible, comme des coordonnées bancaires ou des numéros de Sécurité sociale, n’a « a priori » été dérobée. Néanmoins, les cybercriminels disposent d’assez d’informations pour orchestrer des arnaques de phishing ou des tentatives d’usurpation d’identité.
Une fois revendues sur des forums clandestins, ces données permettent à des escrocs de construire des messages frauduleux crédibles, en se faisant passer pour l’Afpa, un organisme public ou un service administratif, afin de soutirer des informations plus sensibles… ou directement de l’argent. Les victimes sont invitées à se méfier de tout appel, SMS ou mail qui prétend provenir de l’agence.
À lire aussi : L’Éducation nationale encore piratée – c’est déjà la troisième fuite de données de 2026
Le piratage de l’Afpa s’ajoute à la très longue liste des entités françaises victimes d’une fuite de données, qui comprend déjà les impôts, plusieurs opérateurs, et des mutuelles. Selon Cybermalveillance, la plateforme de cybersécurité de la France, près de la moitié des Français ont été piratés au cours de l’année.

articles.title: Tesla é julgada por acusações de discriminação racial contra trabalhadores negros nos EUA
articles.text:
A Tesla começou a enfrentar nesta segunda-feira (21), na Califórnia, um julgamento sobre acusações de discriminação racial contra trabalhadores negros em sua fábrica de Fremont. O processo, aberto em 2022 pelo Departamento de Direitos Civis do estado, aponta problemas que incluem assédio, desigualdade salarial e falta de oportunidades de promoção.
A empresa nega as acusações e afirma que não tolera discriminação no ambiente de trabalho. O julgamento será conduzido pelo juiz Peter Borkon, sem participação de um júri, e está previsto para terminar em 30 de outubro.
Acusações envolvem a fábrica de Fremont
De acordo com o processo, trabalhadores negros eram alvo de assédio praticado por outros funcionários, incluindo insultos raciais e pichações. A agência também sustenta que a Tesla não adotou medidas suficientes para impedir ou interromper essas condutas.
O processo ainda aponta diferenças salariais em relação a outros funcionários e acusa a empresa de restringir oportunidades de promoção. Segundo a agência, trabalhadores negros também estariam concentrados nos cargos de menor remuneração e em funções consideradas menos desejáveis.
A acusação descreve a fábrica de Fremont como racialmente segregada, justamente pela concentração de funcionários negros nesses postos de trabalho.
Indenizações não têm limite na Califórnia
Como o julgamento não terá júri, caberá a Borkon decidir se a Tesla violou as leis estaduais de direitos civis. Na Califórnia, diferentemente da legislação federal, não existe um limite para as indenizações em casos de discriminação no trabalho.
Uma condenação pode resultar em pagamentos de muitos milhões de dólares. A dimensão do processo é ampliada pelo número de trabalhadores envolvidos e pelo histórico de acusações contra a empresa.
A Tesla também responde a uma ação da Comissão de Igualdade de Oportunidades de Emprego dos Estados Unidos e a dezenas de processos individuais apresentados por trabalhadores.
Tesla já enfrentou outros processos
Em outro processo, Borkon decidiu no ano passado que mais de 6 mil trabalhadores negros não poderiam processar a Tesla como um grupo. A decisão reverteu uma determinação anterior.
Leia mais:
- Tesla Cybercab: robotáxi de Elon Musk é apresentado de forma discreta e sem preço
- Sem volante nem pedais, Cybercab vira alvo de investigação
- China está prestes a ganhar carros solares, mas tecnologia não é bem o que parece
A empresa já chegou a acordos em algumas ações individuais. Em um dos casos, um ex-operador de elevador da fábrica de Fremont recebeu US$ 137 milhões (cerca de R$ 701 milhões) após decisão de um júri, mas o valor foi reduzido posteriormente.
A empresa já negou irregularidades e afirmou que não tolera discriminação, além de dizer que demitiu funcionários envolvidos em condutas inadequadas.
O julgamento coloca agora as acusações do Departamento de Direitos Civis da Califórnia contra a Tesla nas mãos de um juiz, que decidirá se a empresa violou as leis estaduais de direitos civis.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Kash Patel says that AI use at the FBI has 'increased by 605%' since he became director — claims that every major tech player is 'embedded' in the agency
articles.text:
Kash Patel says that AI use at the FBI has 'increased by 605%' since he became director — claims that every major tech player is 'embedded' in the agency
A seemingly unsupported figure that nevertheless may be grounded in truth.
FBI Director Kash Patel just stated in an interview that he's responsible for a "605% increase" in the bureau's usage of AI. The problem is that while the pattern-recognition abilities of AI models make them an ideal candidate for use in law enforcement agencies, and It's a reasonable expectation that entities like the FBI would leverage the technology, it's hard to pin down what the 605% figure refers to.
The statement came up in an interview on Fox News, where Patel also said that AI, "when used lawfully, is a critical tool to triage data," remarking that the technology can be invaluable to assist in protecting children from school shootings. He credits AI as being instrumental in following up a lead to stop a shooting in North Carolina and "a half dozen other states" since his swearing-in.
It's hard to tell what Patel's seven-fold increase in AI could be referring to, as there appears to be little hard data about how much, and in what ways, AI is integrated into the bureau. Yet, there are a few leads that may help corroborate his claim.
The most recent details come from a February 2026 report about the DOJ's AI use case inventory in 2025, showing 50 of those attributed to the FBI, with nine marked as "high-impact." However, a more recent statement by the agency's Chief AI Officer Katie Noyes, in August, pinned approved use cases at 139, or close to three times the January amount.
Last year, the U.S. General Services Administration approved Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT as approved products, making them available to government agencies. Earlier this year in May, the Pentagon struck eight deals with AI companies as well. A few months ago, the FBI posted a procurement document asking for vendor proposals for $88 million's worth of AI servers, seemingly indicating that the agency is looking to expand its services.
But that may well be changing, as just a few days ago, on September 15, Patel claimed during a Senate hearing that he can directly contact major AI player's CEO, noting that "every single one of them has complied with our request and worked with us on law enforcement matters." Perhaps most importantly, he said that having access to vendors' models would make it easier to crack down on AI-assisted crime, seeing as criminal enterprises are rolling their own models, helped by distillation attacks.
The FBI now classifies AI-related crimes with its own descriptor, too, and highlights investment, romance, and employment as common areas of malfeasant activity in its latest Internet Crime Report. And in an op-ed published last May, Patel attributed a 30% increase in missing child locations and a 20% rise in child abuse arrests to the use of artificial intelligence tools, including facial recognition.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
He also wrote that the "FBI now uses new AI tools to generate call transcriptions, provide concise synopses and even help correlate contacts with other received complaints," highlighting that messages collected under a search warrant can take weeks to be processed by a cadre of analysts, something that AI can do with ease.
All told, these developments do seem to indicate that the bureau is indeed leveraging AI tools, even if Patel's "605%" figure needs a basis for comparison.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Can John Ternus find Apple’s next big thing?
articles.text:
Today, I’m talking with Mark Gurman, who is the world’s best-sourced Apple reporter — both as Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent and the host of the upcoming podcast Power On.
Can John Ternus find Apple’s next big thing?
Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent Mark Gurman on Siri, Tim Cook’s legacy, and what to expect from new CEO John Ternus.
Earlier this month, Apple hosted its annual iPhone hardware event, virtually every detail of which was reported ahead of time by Mark. But this event was special, for a number of reasons.
It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior. It was also the debut of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable smartphone. The timing of those two things was not at all coincidental, as you’ll hear Mark explain. Apple takes these hardware events — and the stories they tell — extremely seriously.
This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture. Furthermore, what all that tells about Ternus’ plan to navigate Apple from what you might call the iPhone era into the AI era.
Okay: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman on the future of Apple. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Mark Gurman, you’re the chief Apple correspondent and the managing editor of consumer technology at Bloomberg. Welcome to Decoder.
Good to be here finally. Thanks for having me. And it’s been a while, so it’s good to catch up on all things Apple.
Yeah, I’m really excited to talk to you. Obviously, Apple just had its big event. They announced the iPhone Duo. It was John Ternus’s first event as CEO. This is a Decoder episode, so we’ve got a new CEO, and we’ve got a new org chart inside of Apple.
There’s been a lot of shuffling. You’ve been chronicling them very, very deeply over the past few years. Let’s just start with the event. I have a very basic question for you.
Sure.
Do you ever get nostalgic for a time when you didn’t know what was going to happen at the iPhone event?
Do I ever get nostalgic?
Do you ever wish that you, Mark Gurman, were about to be surprised?
Honestly, I never think about it that way. I’m just fixated on delivering the goods and delivering the news. And people love their Apple. People want to know everything that’s coming down to the last minute, so I’m here to provide it for them.
The thing with me, and I don’t know if most people know this about me, but I hope people know this about me, is that I’m a huge Apple fan through and through, and I’ve always been. And I’m so lucky to be able to cover a company that I love, a company that I am obsessed with, and a company whose products I use. There are so many people who cover companies that they couldn’t care less about. That’s not me.
So I do what I do because I love Apple and I love covering Apple. I love the community around it, and I love talking about it. And it’s always fun to get a peek at the future and help keep not only myself informed, but people informed around me.
That actually leads me to a lot of things because I’ve known you forever. We’ve been working in and around the same spaces forever. You got your start as an Apple blogger at the Apple rumor sites.
There’s a whole culture around Apple that has grown up and changed over the years, and you can trace it to different eras of hardware, to different CEOs, to different sizes of the company. This was the first event with John Ternus as CEO. Apple announced a big new product in the iPhone Duo.
Do you sense that the community is changing? How do you think that community has changed over the years? And do you think Ternus is going to lead to a difference in what that community feels like?
I have to say, this event really didn’t feel much different than a Tim Cook event. They felt pretty interchangeable. It could have been Tim up there introducing it. It could have been Ternus up there introducing it.
The one thing I will say that did feel slightly different is that Ternus came out swinging with a point of view on AI. The first thing he came out with was about the intelligent personal hub. Now, here’s the big difference between Tim Cook and John Ternus in terms of their management style. You’re inside Apple, you’re an executive, you’ll come to him with an idea, you’ll come to him with a viewpoint, a decision, an opinion, and he’ll just pepper you with more questions. He won’t make a singular decision in many cases. It’s very much communal decision-making, collaborative decision-making.
John Ternus, if you come to him and you want him to make a decision, he’ll make a decision. He’ll have an opinion. Now, you may hate his opinion; you may completely disagree with him, but he has a viewpoint. But that’s the big difference between talking to people about Ternus and Tim.
Ternus comes out talking about his view on AI. I may disagree with it. A lot of people may disagree with it. They may think the OpenAI or Anthropic approach is superior, but at least he came out and had a viewpoint.
Apple’s been at this AI game now for two years since they launched Apple Intelligence at WWDC in 2024, and it’s been a mishmash of things. They haven’t really come out with a very strong narrative and viewpoint, and they finally did. So, as I said, whether you agree with it or not, they did do that. And I thought that was a really interesting way to kick off the keynote.
All right, we’re just going to get into the weeds of Apple nerds disagreeing about things.
Okay, let’s do it.
I sat through that event, and I appreciated the same thing that you saw, which is, “Oh, we’re telling a story.” John Ternus is on the stage, and the first thing he’s doing is telling a story about this product and how it fits into the universe of technology. And then I took a beat, and I was like, oh, but they’re also just making sure that he’s successful at his first event by playing Apple’s greatest hits.
Because an “intelligent personal hub” is just a replay of Steve Jobs saying the iMac was the digital hub. At the very end of the event, Ternus said, “There’s one more thing, and it’s the iPhone Duo.”
There was just a part of all of that that, to me, felt like Apple saying, “Look, our new CEO can put on the clothes of the old CEO. He can do this same dance that you’re expecting.” Underneath it, what I felt was, to your point, that I don’t buy the story about the intelligent hub.
No, I don’t buy it either.
Because any of the things we’re seeing AI do are happening in cloud services. It’s the same week that Meta launched Muse, right?
Right.
You can feel what you want about Meta launching Muse, but Mark Zuckerberg is giving everybody 8GB of storage and 8GB of RAM in the cloud, and Muse can go do a lot of things that AI on the iPhone absolutely cannot do at this point in time.
I just felt like there was a part where they were playing it really safe with John by having him basically show up and be the new lead singer of Journey. You can’t get it wrong if you’re going to do “Lights.” If you’re going to show up on stage and do “Don’t Stop Believin’,” you’re going to be fine for a minute. And it’s all the stuff that comes after that’s going to really show his real personality. But it sounds like you thought that that’s his point of view.
Well, it’s a couple of things. At a very high level, Apple’s going to tell a story around what they have. If Apple invented ChatGPT, they would’ve invented ChatGPT, and they would’ve told a good story around that. Apple has gone as far as it’s able to, at least for now, on AI. So it’s telling the story, the best version of that story that they can with what they have to work with, with the bird they have in hand. So that’s the one thing.
I agree with you on the intelligent personal hub, and how that compares to the iMac back in ‘98. And it feels like they’re trying to sell this pivot from the Mac as the center of everything with the peripherals around it; then you got to iCloud in 2011, the center of everything with the peripherals around it. Now, it’s this Intelligence right at the center with everything around it.
But what’s so fascinating is that Apple held a major product launch event in September of the year 2026 and did not introduce a single notable new AI feature. The first 15 minutes or so of the keynote was simply a replay, a re-narrativization of what they introduced over the past two years with Apple Intelligence. And so they tried to just tell that story in a more concrete way.
The other thing is they don’t have any AI devices at the very core, and so they need to prop up the iPhone as their AI device because they don’t have an alternative. But of course they’re only going to do that until they have that killer device, and then they’re going to change that whole narrative.
So it’s a very narrative PR and marketing-driven company. And I’m not saying that to be critical. I mean, if I ran the company, obviously I’m going to tout what I have. I’m not going to veer from that. But it is interesting how they’re playing this. And I agree, they did play it very safe. There’s nothing safer than John Ternus introducing a new iPhone. It’s like the safest thing you can do. No major new AI product, no smart home hub, nothing in the spatial space, just straight down the middle.
Yeah, it seems like that next wave of smart home products, which we’re expecting later this year... I say, “We’re expecting.” I’m expecting it because that is something you have reported.
[Laughs] I am expecting it, yes.
Mark Gurman is expecting new products from Apple. That is the first cut at some truly AI-native devices. Because you have Siri AI and it is functional now in a way that it previously was not functional, you can try some new classes of devices.
There are about a half dozen AI-native devices coming in the next year and a half or so. The first will be the smart home hub, which is basically an Amazon Echo Show but Apple-style. It will have a square screen and an entirely new operating system. The idea is: what would a Siri AI operating system look like? This is that: intercom, video conferencing, proactive intelligence.
So you walk up to it, it recognizes who you are, and it will show content personal to you. It will know who is speaking. Obviously, the Amazon Echo can do that, but Apple’s doing it in its own Apple-y way with AI-based Face ID.
They’re working on a home security system. They’re working on another version of the smart home hub that I just talked about that is attached to a robotic arm. So you put it on your desk, and it can move around. It’s actually a category that’s pretty popping in Asia and in China right now.
Then you’ve got the wearables, the smart glasses. I still believe those are going to be introduced and shipped in 2027, so not too far from now. Trust me, you’ll be wearing them. This brings me to the last thing I want to talk to you about, which is Apple and privacy. The things you’re describing with AirPods are science fiction ideas that have been around forever. I tried Microsoft HoloLens 10 years ago, and they were doing augmented reality demos that are very much the things you’re describing. They had me change spark plugs in an ATV. I’ll never forget doing this with their big silly glasses on my face.
The problem has been one: it’s very hard to shrink that technology and have the appropriate battery life. And then the other problem is, well, you’ve got a camera pointed at everything around you all the time, and people don’t like that.
I’m always joking that I think the killer app for Meta’s glasses is facial recognition. If you just gave me a pair of glasses that would tell me everyone’s names and faces at events, I would be the single greatest politician in world history.
The problem with that is that it requires a worldwide surveillance database of everyone taking each other’s pictures all day long. And that is probably not an appropriate trade-off for me to be the greatest politician in the world. But I’m just letting you know, I think that product would be cool for my personal benefit. The social cost would be too high.
This is Apple’s brand — privacy — and they’re up against people calling the Meta glasses pervert glasses. They’re in a world where people hate Flock cameras and all the surveillance that’s happening online. They’re doing watchOS 27 with an always-on listening feature that just does transcripts. It doesn’t record or store any audio, but–
Still a surveillance device. I’ll be honest with you. I can’t believe they did it.
I can’t believe they did it.
I can’t believe they did it.
Right? It’s just listening, and you can double-click it, and it’ll show you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you without their permission.
First of all, read the room.
It doesn’t even light up.
No, I know. No, that’s not true. It does light up. But read the room.
I was told it doesn’t light up.
Okay. First of all, we can get into this, but I was not at the Apple event for obvious reasons. I haven’t been at one since 2019.
Well, you already know what’s going to happen.
Well, I didn’t have the briefings.
Yeah.
But according to the literature on their website, when you’re doing that feature, it lights up with a microphone icon when you do the live rewind. Maybe it doesn’t light up for the Siri Recap — I don’t think it does for the all day listening — but the last 15 seconds things, it supposedly shows a microphone. But Nilay, is this podcast a video?
Yeah.
Okay. I’m wearing an Apple Watch. Can you see anything on my screen?
Right, it’s crazy to me.
So I can’t believe they did that because, really, you’re going to take a backlash like this and then do it again with a visual intelligence six, nine months from now?
And then you’re going to do it with a pair of smart glasses, and you’re going to walk into all of the other things.
Yeah.
It feels like Apple knows that there’s a next generation of user interfaces coming that is AI-powered that requires an amount of ambient capture, whether that’s just listening so you can talk to it or whether it’s visual so you can see the world around you. And they haven’t solved the social privacy aspect.
Nope.
There are white papers about how Apple might have solved the technical database privacy aspect, right?
Yep.
They’ve got Private Cloud Compute, and they’re going to encrypt the data. They’re not going to store this and that. And I don’t think any of that’s going to overcome the social privacy aspect.
They didn’t do a good job on articulating the social aspect of it at all. They could’ve shown more demos. They could’ve discussed it a bit deeper. I know they only have very limited time in the keynote, but I don’t think they spent enough time breaking things down here. I quite frankly think they did not do a good job rolling this feature out.
I ask myself, would I be comfortable using this feature? Yeah. But then if I tell everyone around me in the last week, “Hey, I’ve been recording you the whole time,” they’re going to freak out, and they’re not going to trust Apple. So it’s a really interesting one. I’m pretty shocked they did it.
What are the net new Apple Watch buyers because of this feature? What is the bigger challenge, doing this feature or not doing this feature? And I think that doing this feature is a bigger drawback than not doing the feature. Here, there is no cost of not doing something.
Well, there is a cost if you think there’s about to be a wave of AI devices that are doing always-on transcripts and meeting recordings, and OpenAI is going to do something. I mean, we have seen a wave of startups that do this.
But we’re not there yet, right?
Right.
This could’ve waited six months.
So you can just foreclose it. This is like Microsoft stuff. You’re like, “Here’s a preview of a feature. Don’t even consider that stuff. Eventually this will get good,” and you’ve just foreclosed the competitor.
Well, the other thing is they had nothing else for the watch, so they had to just do something, right? This is the weakest Apple Watch update we’ve seen in a long time, and they’re lost as to what to do next. Now they’re recalibrating it. They’re going to have a major watch revamp at the end of next year and so forth, but they have to do something.
If it were me, I would have ripped off the bandaid at the same time with all the audio plus visual intelligence stuff next year. Do it all together and have a really coherent privacy story.
But do you think that stuff is compatible with Apple’s reputation for privacy? This is the real question I’m getting at: they might not have told the right story about the Apple Watch.
Apple is going to have to tell the right story about AirPods with cameras in them in a world where people are shooting spray foam at Flock cameras because they don’t want them in their communities. There’s a connection between these two ideas, and it doesn’t seem like Apple knows how to tell that story.
Well, clearly not, because they haven’t done it. But here’s the story on the AirPods. They can’t record actual video. They can’t take actual pictures. They have an extremely low frame rate. I’m talking about a few frames per second.
The actual data that gets input into them, it’s like… Have you ever used a Roomba, and when you look at the app, what does the Roomba see? It’s like wireframes of the environment. It would not be able to tell you and me apart. It’s just seeing two people.
Then how can it do the brands of tomato sauce in the aisle?
Well, in terms of non-people, it’d be able to do that, and it could read text. So it’d be pretty heavily reliant on reading text and seeing color and whatnot. But being able to differentiate between two people would be very difficult. It’s almost like a fake reproduction of what’s around you. I don’t have a good explanation for it, but I’m sure if they wanted to, they’ll give a good one.
I’m not sure they’re going to break it down. They might just say, “Just trust us. We’re Apple. It’s not taking pictures. It’s not taking video. It doesn’t know what it’s seeing to some extent.” So we’ll see how they play it. But I would’ve done all this stuff together, ripped off the bandaid and spent a lot of time focused on it. There was no need to do this audio intelligence feature at the end of ‘26 when you could have done it at the end of ‘27.
Unless you’re trying to slowly boil the frog, right? You’re going to get people mad about this, and then you’re going to do the next one the next time.
Right.
It just seems like this next generation of devices involves some kind of ambient listening that we are not ready for as a society. People are really mad about Meta glasses. What are you going to do about it?
They soiled the water for Apple and a lot of other companies. Meta being the first mover on this created an industry-wide problem. And I think even though Apple has such a strong privacy stance, there are people who don’t believe them. There are people who don’t care what they have to say. There are people who are going to be angry about the Apple glasses and whatnot.
I think Apple, to some extent, is on such a high horse with its privacy message that it came away surprised that there would be some backlash to Apple doing this. They think, I believe, that people are overblowing it when it comes to Apple and everyone should just be focused on Meta. And just because Meta has done a poor job protecting people’s privacy doesn’t mean we’re going to. So we’ll see what happens.
One thing: when I talk to the folks there, they never make the connection between Apple and Meta in the sense that Meta’s apps run on Apple’s phones. People are mad about Meta, and they still think the phones, Apple’s phones, are listening to them, and they can’t quite make that connection because it undoes a lot of their own messaging. If you believe your iPhone is listening to you, that’s not just Meta’s problem. It is also Apple’s problem.
They kind of have to actively ignore that relationship because otherwise everything else falls apart. And I think that’s why there’s this blind spot. If people’s watches start generating transcripts, it’s exactly the same relationship as “my iPhone is listening to me, and that’s why I saw an ad for a vacation that I only talked to my friend about.”
I’m curious what they’re going to do. I have a feeling they’re just going to bulldoze their way through it. They’re going to just try to tell a good story. They’re going to do a ton of PR briefings about it. They’re going to do a ton of white papers about it, and get as nerdy and in-depth as they can on this stuff.
You know what they’re going to do? They’re going to throw out a lot of comparisons. I even heard Ternus do this in one of the interviews, in Apple’s statement on some of these features. I could totally imagine them saying, “Why is it any different recording from smart glasses if you could just hold your phone up and record people?” With the audio intelligence feature, one thing I didn’t even think of is the Apple Watch-
It’s very funny you just mentioned that because that is exactly what Mark Zuckerberg just said to our friend Alex Heath.
Oh, that’s funny.
“How is it different from a phone?” This is the industry’s approach. I think the answer is that people are like, “Yeah, I can see you doing that, and I feel very comfortable telling you to stop.” There’s something different about that.
I didn’t even realize this. Someone pointed this out to me the other day. It’s like your Apple Watch has had the Voice Memos app for, I don’t know, eight years at this point. Who stopped anyone from recording their whole day with the Voice Memos app on the Apple Watch anyway? This is just a more privacy-centric version of that. So Apple’s solving a problem here. They’re not creating one. So it just depends on how you look at these things. I think they’ll bulldoze their way through it. It’s going to be a problem, but I think they’ll be fine.
All right. Last two before I let you get out of here. We’ve talked around the iPhone Duo a lot. We’ve mentioned it a lot. It’s the thing that just came out. We haven’t talked about it. What do you think of it?
I think it’s incredible. I think, and this is a bold take, that foldables will become the new normal within a decade. If you look at the market share of smartphones at the end of 2006, smartphones had like 6 percent of the market. Now they have 85 percent of the market. It went over 50 percent of the market after five to six years.
The iPhone itself was not the source of that, but the iPhone got everyone into the smartphone game. I think the iPhone Duo is going to do the same for the phone market. I think it’s going to become the new normal.
Even though Apple is a late mover to foldables?
Yeah. I think the Apple brand is that strong, really. I really do. I think the fit and finish, the software integration, is going to get people really excited about this category. I think that the Apple Upgrade program, the leasing program, will eventually expand internationally. I think that’s going to get people in it.
I think that at some point they’re going to stop advertising sticker prices and focus on the monthly prices, and they’re going to get people locked into this thing. They’re going to have a family of iPhone Duos over time. You’ll see every phone maker just transitioning, transitioning to foldables. Samsung: half the line is already foldables. Very soon the candy bar style is going to become legacy.
That’s a big prediction. Although I will say their iPhone handoff feature, where you can move a number between phones, seems to point to a future where I, for example, have the folding phone for work and then a much smaller, lighter phone for the weekends with the family. You can see that vision taking shape only because it’s now easy to port a number between devices, just whenever you want, which I think is incredible.
Last question. We’ve talked a lot about Apple, its culture, and its set of products. What do you think its biggest challenges are in the new era under John Ternus, and what do you think its biggest opportunities are?
I would say that I think the biggest challenge and the biggest opportunity are the same thing. Ternus’ Apple for the next three to five years is still Tim Cook’s Apple, right? That’s just the reality. He’s still going to be there in the background. He’s still going to loom large, and the product pipeline is still going to be coming out of an era that started under Tim Cook.
But in five years from now, they are going to need to start thinking of what actually replaces the iPhone as the next thing. We went from the Mac to iCloud to AI as the center. What is Apple’s new thing after the phone? What is Apple’s new thing after the current generation of AI? And Ternus’ tenure as CEO, I think, will go down as a success if he’s able to find that next new centerpiece. He’s got a few years before he needs to start cooking on that, but I’m talking about something that can be in development for 5 to 10 years.
Tim Cook never had the opportunity to have his new centerpiece of the company. He never had the opportunity to put his stamp on products at the company for two reasons. Both things that he tried to do as his centerpiece failed spectacularly. Obviously the Vision Pro, but the car — the car, that was Apple’s multi-trillion-dollar market cap opportunity, and they just blew it. Ternus will need to successfully hit that.
I’d actually put a third thing on that list. It was the very beginning of the Cook era, with Jobs literally on his deathbed, and he said he’d figured out TV.
Oh, yes.
He had to spend however long pretending he knew what that meant because I don’t think it had been solved. And so there was this first wave of “Apple’s going to redefine TV” because the last page of the Isaacson biography had a Jobs quote on it.
They haven’t even done a new Apple TV box in four years.
That’s a long time. It’s funny because you don’t need one. It never occurs to me that I need to upgrade this thing, but maybe there’s going to be some AI feature.
Well, Siri AI. They’ve been waiting for the Siri AI update. This could be a whole other podcast, but Siri AI has been the gate to all of these new product categories. The AirPods were supposed to be out already, the Apple TV, the HomePod, the smart home hub… all these devices were supposed to come out. Apple couldn’t do any of them until Siri AI. Now Siri AI is here, so the floodgates are open.
All right. Well, Mark, we’re going to have to have you back on the show to talk about those floodgates and all these new products very soon. I can’t believe you haven’t been on until now. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.
Yeah. And obviously I’d love to have you on my new podcast, Power On Podcast, launching very shortly. So thanks in advance.
Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
Decoder with Nilay Patel
A podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems.

articles.title: Vous avez trop de réunions ? Ce petit badge qui enregistre et résume vos réunions grâce à l'IA perd 51 € pour la rentrée
articles.text:
Les assistants qui enregistrent et résument automatiquement les réunions se multiplient depuis l’essor des LLM. Plaud fait partie de ces marques qui ont misé sur un objet physique plutôt qu’une simple application. Un petit boîtier que l’on porte sur soi et qui capte la voix, avant de confier la transcription à l’IA (Gemini, GPT, Claude…).
Pour sa rentrée, Plaud propose le NotePin à 118,90 € au lieu de 169,90 €, soit 51 € de réduction. L’offre concerne uniquement les versions argent et violet, jusqu’au 24 septembre 2026 à 8 h 59, heure française. Le gris cosmique reste au tarif plein.
Comment fonctionne le Plaud NotePin ?
Le NotePin est un enregistreur vocal que l’on porte sur soi, à peine plus gros qu’une pile AA. Il pèse 16,6 g et se glisse au poignet, autour du cou, en clip ou sur un vêtement grâce à une épingle magnétique, selon les accessoires fournis. Une pression prolongée lance l’enregistrement, avec une vibration pour confirmer que l’appareil a bien démarré.
Ses deux microphones captent la conversation, conservée dans les 64 Go de stockage. Plaud annonce jusqu’à 20 heures d’enregistrement continu et 40 jours en veille. De quoi envisager plusieurs rendez-vous entre deux recharges, tout en gardant son téléphone disponible.
Les fichiers sont ensuite synchronisés avec l’application Plaud. Celle-ci peut transcrire les échanges, distinguer les intervenants et produire un résumé adapté : compte rendu de réunion, points à retenir ou tâches à effectuer. La marque annonce la prise en charge de 112 langues. Le boîtier assure donc la captation ; le traitement passe par les services de Plaud.
Ce modèle vise avant tout les conversations en présentiel. Il ne possède pas le capteur de vibrations permettant au Plaud Note d’enregistrer directement les appels depuis un téléphone. Pour des interviews principalement téléphoniques, ce n’est donc pas le modèle le plus adapté.
À ce prix, le Plaud NotePin est-il une bonne affaire ?
Gemini (via meet) ou d’autres logiciels savent déjà transcrire un enregistrement et en tirer un résumé. L’intérêt du Plaud NotePin est de rendre toute la démarche plus pratique. Une pression sur le badge lance l’enregistrement, sans sortir son téléphone ni ouvrir une application. Les fichiers sont ensuite synchronisés avec Plaud, où l’on retrouve l’audio, la transcription et le compte rendu. Cela réduit les manipulations entre le dictaphone, le transfert du fichier et l’outil d’IA.
Cette offre prend des airs de déstockage puisque le Plaud NotePin a désormais un successeur : le NotePin S, lancé en début d’année. Les deux modèles sont très proches. À 118,90 €, le premier NotePin permet donc d’économiser surtout d’économiser 60 € face au S, en acceptant quelques concessions sur les commandes et les accessoires.
Le vrai point à prendre en compte reste toutefois l’abonnement. Les 300 minutes gratuites représentent cinq heures de transcription par mois : cinq réunions d’une heure suffisent à les épuiser. Le forfait Pro, qui porte ce quota à 20 heures mensuelles, coûte 110,99 € par an.
