articles.title: On a calculé combien coûte un chargeur branché 24h/24 : le résultat va vous étonner
articles.text:
On a calculé combien coûte un chargeur branché 24h/24 : le résultat va vous étonner
Selon un mythe, les chargeurs de smartphones consomment beaucoup d’énergie, même si les terminaux n'y sont pas branchés. Afin de terrasser cette hydre à sept câbles, nous avons mené une petite expérience pour obtenir des données chiffrées et rétablir la vérité.
De nombreux articles alarmistes prétendent que même lorsqu'ils ne sont connectés à aucun appareil, les chargeurs de smartphones "représentent jusqu'à 11 % de consommation d'énergie dans une maison". Sceptiques face à ce chiffre somme toute impressionnant, nous avons mesuré nous-mêmes la consommation de 7 chargeurs
Les meilleures offres électricité du moment :
Notre protocole de test
Pour ce faire, nous avons utilisé un panel varié de chargeurs : un chargeur d’ordinateur portable Asus de 65W, et 6 chargeurs de smartphones de 10W, 18W, 33W, 68W, 100W et 120W. Nous n’avons utilisé que des chargeurs fournis avec les appareils, de marques connues (Huawei, Motorola, Honor, Xiaomi). Tous les chargeurs étaient branchés sur la même multiprise, elle-même branchée à un compteur de coûts d’énergie.
Xiaomi Redmi 13
Realme GT 6
Afin d’obtenir les conditions de test les plus réalistes possibles, nous avons également branché des câbles USB sur les chargeurs, certains d’origine, d’autres issus d’une boîte, retrouvée dans l’obscurité d’un placard de la rédaction.
Une fois le banc d’essai mis en place, nous avons lancé un enregistrement des données sur 12 heures (entre 18:00 et 6:00).
Les résultats
Après avoir exporté et traité les données de l’appareil de mesure dans un tableur, la consommation totale des 7 chargeurs sur 12 heures s’élève à une valeur "faramineuse" de 0,07Wh, soit 51,1Wh par an. Cela représente environ la capacité de la batterie d’un ordinateur portable d’entrée de gamme, tel que le VivoBook Go 15 d’Asus. En termes de coûts, en considérant un prix moyen du kWh de 0,2516€ (tarif Base d’EDF), cela reviendrait à dépenser 0,013 € par an soit 1,3 centime d’euro par an. C’est effectivement très peu, et nous devons reconnaître avoir du mal à imaginer la provenance des fameux 11% des dépenses en énergie.
Une marge d'erreur pas si gênante que cela
Mais nous devons reconnaître avoir commis une erreur dans nos mesures. Lors de l’exploitation des mesures, nous avons consulté la documentation du compteur d’énergie (ce qui aurait dû être fait en amont, on vous l’accorde). Nous nous sommes alors rendu compte que le fabricant annonce une plage de mesure de puissance de 0,3 W à 3 680 W, avec une tolérance de plus ou moins 0,3 W pour des puissances inférieures à 3 W. Or, pendant toute la durée du test, l’appareil n’a jamais enregistré de valeur supérieure à 0,25 W (à part un pic très bref de 0,434 W au début).
La seule conclusion que nous pouvons en tirer est que la puissance délivrée n’a jamais été supérieure à 0,6 W (valeur minimale mesurable de 0,3 W plus l’intervalle de tolérance de 0,3 W). Nous avons donc refait nos calculs en supposant que les chargeurs consommaient 0,6 W en permanence.
Mais même dans ces conditions "extrêmes", et même si les résultats sont différents, la conclusion reste très similaire. Avec une puissance totale continue de 0,6 W, sept chargeurs branchés « à vide » consomment 7,2 Wh sur 12 heures, ou 5266,9 Wh sur un an. Soit un coût à l’année de 1,33 €. Le prétendu gouffre financier n’est donc en réalité qu’un petit nid de poule.
Conclusion et risques
Ainsi, à moins que vous ne dépensiez que 12,09 € d’électricité par an, vous pouvez laisser vos chargeurs branchés sans qu’ils ne représentent 11% de votre facture EDF.
Cependant, il existe d’autres raisons pour lesquelles vous pourriez vouloir débrancher votre chargeur lorsqu’il n’est pas utilisé. Par exemple, certains chargeurs no-name (qui ne sont pas construit par des marques reconnues) peuvent ne pas respecter certaines normes de sécurité. Nous pensons par exemple aux chargeurs vendus sur des sites comme AliExpress ou Wish, promettant des puissances énormes à des prix défiant toute concurrence. Ces chargeurs ont tendance à chauffer, parfois même lorsqu’aucun appareil n'est branché dessus. Cette chauffe peut, sur le long terme, endommager des composants à l’intérieur, voire provoquer des incendies dans certains cas extrêmement rares.
Les chargeurs que nous avons utilisés pour cette expérience proviennent tous de marques reconnues, et nous n’avons constaté presque aucune chauffe (environ 1,5 °C de plus que la température ambiante) après avoir été branchés, à vide, pendant plus de 24 heures.
Ainsi, comme pour les alimentations d’ordinateurs fixes, nous ne saurions trop vous recommander d’opter pour des chargeurs de qualité, ou au moins de marques connues. Si votre appareil est livré sans chargeur, vous pouvez vous en procurer un chez un fabricant connu de smartphone ou d’ordinateurs portables, ou chez une marque telle que Ugreen, Anker ou Baseus.

articles.title: From new smart glasses to Muse updates and beyond, these are the 7 big things to expect at Meta Connect 2026
articles.text:
7 things to expect at Meta Connect 2026 — from camera-less smart glasses to Meta Ray-ban glasses updates
New glasses, improved AI, and more
It’s almost time for Meta Connect, with the brand hosting its annual event on September 23 and 24. Here, we’re expecting to see several new devices, with a focus on smart glasses.
Software updates are also likely, including to Meta Muse, but between the RAM crisis and a privacy backlash against the company’s smart specs, this might not be an entirely rosy affair.
So below, we’ve detailed the seven major things to expect at Meta Connect 2026 — covering both the good and the bad.
1. Camera-free Meta smart glasses
While smart glasses like the Ray-Ban Meta can be extremely useful, they’re also facing a major backlash right now, with many people worrying about them being used as spy glasses to photograph and video people without their knowledge or consent. As a result, Meta might respond by launching camera-free smart glasses.
These are rumored to land at Meta Connect, and would likely focus on conversational interactions with Meta’s AI chatbot. It makes sense for Meta to launch these, though how useful or appealing they will be when the AI can’t see what you’re looking at remains to be seen.
2. The Project Phoenix mixed reality headset
We’ve been hearing for a while that Meta is working on a mixed reality headset codenamed Project Phoenix, and while this reportedly won’t launch until 2027, we might get an official look at it during Meta Connect.
From what we’ve seen so far, this might look more like smart glasses than the Meta Quest 3S headset, despite featuring both AR and VR functionality. However, Project Phoenix has been pictured with a cable running down from it, suggesting that perhaps the battery and/or processor are external, thereby allowing for a slim design.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
We don’t know much else about this yet, but that might change at Meta Connect.
3. New Oakley and Ray-Ban glasses
We’re probably due a second generation of the Oakley Meta glasses by now, and there’s also a chance we’ll see the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3, though it might be too soon for them at this year's Connect.
The Oakley Meta specs are sportier than the Ray-Ban line, with things like wrap-around designs and better water resistance, so expect the second generation to continue with that focus.
As for the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3, leaks suggest these could have better battery life, smarter AI, and improved audio.
4. A global launch for the Meta Ray-Ban Display Glasses
The Meta Ray-Ban Display Glasses are currently only available in the US, but hopefully at Meta Connect we might see these display-packing specs go global.
It’s certainly about time — originally these were planned to get a wider launch in early 2026, but thanks to "unprecedented demand and limited inventory" this was delayed.
But if you’re hoping to get your hands on them you’ll also have to be prepared to pay a lot, as in the US they retail for $800, so you can expect similarly high pricing elsewhere.
5. Price hikes
Alongside new and improved products, we might also see new and not at all improved prices for some things, thanks to the ongoing RAM crisis.
In other words, don’t be surprised if prices for new generation models of the likes of Oakley Meta and Ray-Ban Meta glasses are higher than the current generation.
In the case of Ray-Ban Meta glasses we already saw a price hike for the second generation, so another for the third would be extremely undesirable, but may also be unavoidable.
6. A Meta Muse AI update
Meta Muse — Meta’s AI agent that can send emails, fill out forms, shop, and do other tasks for you — only launched recently, but as a major new service it’s likely to be getting a lot of attention from Meta, so improvements are probably already in the works.
Meta Connect then would be a prime time to find out about any upcoming changes — and perhaps even for Meta to roll out a software update for it or a new model. Or perhaps Meta will announce availability in countries other than the US, so that more of us can try it.
7. Updates addressing the privacy backlash
As well as launching some camera-free smart glasses, Meta may use Connect to announce some software updates aimed at addressing privacy concerns in its existing specs.
Already, the company has rolled out an update that will stop the glasses recording if you cover the LED once a recording has started, but Meta may well be cooking up additional changes to further prevent surreptitious photography and video recording.
Indeed, Meta's VP of Wearables Alex Himel recently said "we’re going to keep rolling out updates like this to make sure the capture LED can reliably alert bystanders when photos or videos are being captured for someone’s gallery." So while it’s unclear what exactly those updates will be, we might learn about some of them at Meta Connect.

articles.title: Dragos Completes NetRise and runZero Acquisitions Following Accenture Deal
articles.text:
Accenture’s majority investment in Dragos has now closed, and Dragos followed it on Monday by announcing that it has completed its acquisitions of NetRise and runZero.
The moves are part of Accenture’s $4.1 billion OT cybersecurity push announced in June.
Dragos will continue to operate independently with Robert M. Lee serving as its CEO. Lee has also been named chairman of the board. There will be new board members from Accenture, and Dmitri Alperovitch is returning to Dragos’ board.
Key executives — including runZero CEO HD Moore, NetRise CEO Thomas Pace, and NetRise CTO Michael Scott — are joining Dragos alongside their teams to lead platform integration.
NetRise contributes firmware-level insight into device exposure and software supply chain visibility, while runZero, founded by Metasploit creator HD Moore, adds asset discovery, exposure assessment and attack surface intelligence.
Dragos said the acquisitions add exposure management and software supply chain security to its platform alongside existing OT asset visibility and threat detection.
“Organizations across electric, oil and gas, manufacturing, data centers, and other critical infrastructure sectors need to defend every system that can influence a physical process. That extended environment is xOT. NetRise, runZero, and Dragos defend it together,” said Lee.
Financial terms of the NetRise and runZero acquisitions have not been disclosed, but it was previously reported that of the total $4.1 billion deal value, Accenture acquired its majority stake in Dragos at an enterprise valuation of $3.25 billion.

articles.title: This new ultra-compact FPGA Game Boy clone costs just $90
articles.text:
The takeaway: Game Boy enthusiasts with physical cartridge libraries who are unwilling to pay $240 for an Analogue Pocket might want to consider the recently launched FPGB Mini. Although it isn't quite as versatile as Analogue's well-regarded handheld, it still plays ROMs and cartridges with virtually perfect emulation accuracy at less than half the price. It's also barely larger than a Game Boy cartridge.
FunnyPlaying has launched a smaller version of its budget-priced rival to the Analogue Pocket. Slightly cheaper but with the same software capabilities, the FPGB Mini might be as small as a faithful Game Boy clone will ever get.
Most retro handhelds, like Ayaneo's products, emulate the Game Boy and other classic systems entirely in software, typically running Android or Linux. In contrast, devices like the Analogue Pocket, Game Bub, or FPGB use FPGA-based hardware emulation.
FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays) are integrated circuits whose logic isn't hard-wired at the factory. As such, they can be reprogrammed at the hardware level for various purposes, including imitating retro game consoles. This lets them emulate retro devices essentially flawlessly with low TDPs, meaning longer battery life.
However, following recent price hikes, the Analogue Pocket retails for $240, while the Game Bub starts at $249 and climbs to $300 for its limited-edition color. FunnyPlaying, meanwhile, sold through its initial batch of 20 early-bird FPGB Mini units at just $69, and even its standard $89 MSRP significantly undercuts the competition.
Despite measuring just 113 × 64 × 22 mm, only slightly larger than a Game Boy cartridge, the FPGB Mini is a fully featured emulation handheld. Its 2.98-inch, 800×720-pixel IPS screen displays at exactly five times the original Game Boy's resolution, its 1800 mAh rechargeable battery promises four to six hours of gameplay, and a microSD slot (up to 32GB) handles digital ROMs and firmware updates while USB-C takes care of charging. With a USB-C adapter, it also supports Game Boy link cables.
Compared to the Analogue Pocket, the FPGB Mini's main drawback is that it doesn't support Game Boy Advance games or emulators for other retro consoles. Its tiny form factor also prevents inserting cartridges with extra hardware features such as rumble.
Also Read: GPUs vs. FPGAs: What's the Difference?
The FPGB Mini's first batch sold out within minutes, but it's expected to restock on FunnyPlaying's online store, which also sells custom and replacement screens, motherboards, batteries, and other components for official Game Boy models. Natalie the Nerd's shop is another well-regarded source for Game Boy parts and documentation.

articles.title: Intel Ends Its $100,000 Bug Bounty Program
articles.text:
Sunday, September 20th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Intel Ends Its $100,000 Bug Bounty Program
Intel has officially suspended its Bug Bounty Program, which offered security researchers compensation for finding and reporting security vulnerabilities. The program is now marked as suspended on the Intigriti platform, but Intel has not provided a detailed explanation for this decision. Previously, Intel organized a series of bounties for those discovering bugs and vulnerabilities, divided into four tiers. In tier one, the highest payout was $5,000; tier two offered $10,000; tier three provided $30,000; and the most severe bugs in tier four could be compensated with $100,000. Tier four was intended for major vulnerability disclosures, like Spectre or Meltdown, which were significant security issues a few years ago.
Although Intel hasn't explained why it suspended the bug bounty program, a likely reason is that modern technologies are advanced enough to explore, find, and report possible vulnerabilities. For example, AI can analyze modern software and hardware protection layers, identify potential weaknesses, and quickly develop a solution to patch them. Intel's internal tools are probably utilizing various AI systems to discover new ways to exploit Intel machines and simultaneously fix them before anyone can take advantage.As some readers may recall, modern operating systems like Windows 11 are so exposed to bugs and issues discovered by AI tools that Microsoft released nearly 1,000 patches for vulnerabilities in a single monthly update. This suggests that the operating system now operates under the assumption that its kernel could be compromised, leading to the introduction of new security layers like Virtualization-based Security (VBS). VBS employs hardware virtualization to create Windows hypervisors that dedicate isolated virtual environments and conceal kernel controls. Hence, Intel is probably using tooling that identifies these issues with AI, and traditional bug bounty programs are no longer as efficient as machines can be.

articles.title: Xiaomi acaba de matar a IKEA: así es su nueva mesita de noche con hilo musical, cargadores y mucho más
articles.text:
Xiaomi se acaba de sacar de la manga uno de los productos más sorprendentes del año. Y sí, rivaliza directamente con varias secciones de IKEA. En otras palabras: es un mueble. Pero no uno cualquiera, sino uno pensado para toda la comunidad tech. La compañía china ha presentado una mesita de noche completamente renovada y actualizada a los tiempos que corren. De hecho, su función principal ya no es guardar el mando de la televisión y tu ropa interior: ahora hace mucho más e incluso te ayuda a descansar.
Su diseño está increíblemente cuidado y, como casi todas las cosas que hace Xiaomi, cuenta con una parte tecnológica impresionante. Para que te hagas una idea, se trata de una mesita de noche que se debe conectar a la corriente a través de un enchufe. ¿Para qué? Para alimentar su sistema de iluminación variable, el hilo musical y los cargadores que lleva integrados.
Xiaomi se ha cansado de que tengas el cargador enchufado y esté dando vueltas por todos lados: su nueva mesita de noche cuenta con un cargador Qi integrado en la parte superior que recarga tu dispositivo de forma inalámbrica con hasta 15 W de potencia. Además, también incluye un USB C y un USB A, ambos de 18 W para cargar otros dispositivos.
En la zona inferior se encuentra una tira LED que puede variar en temperatura de color e intensidad, para darle un toque de luz al cuarto o que se activa por sí sola cuando te levantas al baño en mitad de la noche. Ahora bien, lo mejor es su hilo musical: cuenta con un altavoz Bluetooth integrado para que puedas reproducir sonidos para dormir o alarmas para despertarte.
La mesita de Xiaomi tiene hasta un sensor de huellas
A simple vista puede parecer una mesita normal, pero esconde otro detalle interesante que la hace prácticamente perfecta. En la zona central oculta un cajón que se desliza tras pulsar un botón, verificar tu huella o poner un PIN numérico. Tú eliges si quieres que sea accesible solo por ti o no.
Xiaomi asegura que es resistente a manipulaciones, aunque no se trata de un sistema tan avanzado como el de una caja fuerte. Aun así, se puede utilizar como cajón privado para que ninguna persona que entre en casa pueda abrirlo de forma sencilla.
Ahora las malas noticias. Xiaomi ha puesto a la venta esta mesita de noche solo en China. Su precio ronda los 180 euros al cambio, una cifra elevada para tratarse de una mesita, pero que tampoco es inaccesible teniendo en cuenta todas las funciones que incluye.

articles.title: Autonomous NATO strike drone uses Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano to independently pick and bomb targets — Swedish startup's attack drones run small AI model, require no human input and zero external comms
articles.text:
Autonomous NATO strike drone uses Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano to independently pick and bomb targets — Swedish startup's attack drones run small AI model, require no human input and zero external comms
Targeting AI ran autonomously on non-frontier models.
Drones built with small, non-frontier computer-vision models autonomously identified and attacked targets in a recent demo, Ars Technica reports. Scaleout Systems, a Swedish AI startup, used a low-cost loitering munition from BAE Systems Bofors to strike a target as part of the Affordable Loitering Modular Ammunition (ALMA) program. BAE’s Winter Demo 2026 had the drone detecting and geolocating targets before ranking an armored engineering vehicle highest, autonomously flying to it, and dropping an explosive.
Scaleout’s demo video, “Technical Demo: Onboard Edge Intelligence for Autonomous UAV Missions,” shows the company’s drone spotting potential threats with AI, with all processing handled onboard. Beyond a button press to start the system, manual input is optional; the designated pilot remained a failsafe controller. The mission flew under human-set parameters to engage an armored engineering vehicle and required about 200 seconds of recon, with the full mission completed in under 320 seconds. The mission completed without needing communication, supporting Scaleout’s claim of resilience against electronic warfare.
The report referred to the munition as a “kamikaze drone,” but the program’s own term, “loitering munition,” is more descriptive. Most of the mission is spent searching, ranking targets, and waiting to strike. The company combines Scaleout Edge and “federated learning” in a “Tactical Computer Vision Network (TCVN).” Devices train AI locally and share model updates for rapid adaptation. Scaleout’s project, FEDAIR, is part of NATO’s DIANA accelerator, receiving 100,000 euros of development funding, training, and test access.
In a February post, Scaleout described a separate “arctic strike demonstration” at BTC Karlskoga, Sweden. The mission was flown at -18 degrees Celsius, about 0 degrees Fahrenheit, in the snow. There, an Airolit S1 airframe ran the YOLOv8 Nano object-detection model on Nvidia’s Jetson Orin Nano. Scaleout claimed a framerate of 30 fps at around 20 m/s, with a target latency of 30 ms or less and about 30 ms sustained in the field. Ranging without a depth sensor is possible using a pinhole camera model combined with known object size.
Scaleout’s follow-up June 30 post, “Resilient Edge AI for ISR: Inside Our Swedish Air Force Demonstration,” spoke of another test with Scaleout Edge “already deployed under an active licence.” The network used two ground nodes under a cloud-hosted Scaleout Edge control plane. The first was ALPHA, a forward-deployed node at the air base with a stable link, and the second BRAVO, a lab node in Uppsala whose connection was first degraded, then cut entirely. BRAVO kept inference and active learning at full frame rate while offline, logging detections locally, then backfilled on reconnect in priority order for heartbeat, critical alerts, drift, model updates, and telemetry. This test mimics the impact of external interference.
The demonstrations, license, and funding come before any official NATO procurement order or actual combat deployment. Concerns about lethal autonomous weapons are being addressed by a UN expert group. Its recent report concluded that human judgment and control are required to comply with the laws of war; its recommendations will be reviewed in Geneva in November. Still, Scaleout’s demonstrations show autonomous target selection running on the airframe, and in the February test it ran on a board hobbyists can buy. Whether BAE Systems Bofors moves ALMA from demonstration to procurement remains to be seen.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Shane Downing is a Freelance Reviewer for Tom’s Hardware US, covering consumer storage hardware.
-
