articles.title: Microsoft patent describes in-game advertising triggered by boss fights, loading screens, and cutscenes
articles.text:
What we know so far: Microsoft has filed a patent application for a system that would place ads in PC and console games during breaks the game itself identifies. Instead of interrupting play on a fixed schedule, the system would use game data to find a natural break, such as after a boss fight or while a new level loads.
The filing points to a possible ad-supported model for PC and console games that is less disruptive than the approaches commonly used in mobile titles.
The application, published as US 2026/0260258 A1 and titled "Contextually Aware Management of Interactive Software Application Access," describes a way to support free-to-play games without inserting ads at random points in a session.
Under the proposed system, players would receive an initial period of ad-free access. That could be a set amount of time, such as 30 minutes, or an allowance tied to game progress, such as completing a full level.
As that period nears its end, the system would wait for the game to reach a suitable pause point. The patent identifies examples including the end of a boss fight, a completed quest, the end of a cutscene and a loading screen.
The game would send an event to a content-management system when one of those moments occurs. The system could then pause the player's interaction, display video or static promotional material, and resume the game after the ad has run.
Viewing the ad would give the player another block of uninterrupted access. The patent calls that block a credit, which would delay the next gameplay suspension.
The key element is the use of game-state data. Instead of relying on a timer alone, the proposed system would use game-engine information to determine when an ad can run with less chance of interrupting active play.
That would require a game to provide signals about events such as level completion, checkpoints, menus, transitions and other points when the player is not actively engaged in an important task. The advertising platform could use those signals, along with the player's remaining credit, to decide whether to show promoted content.
The filing does not identify a specific Microsoft game, Xbox service or product plan. A patent application also does not mean the technology will be commercialized. It does, however, show one way Microsoft is considering ad-supported access for interactive software.
Advertising is already common in mobile games, where ads often run between levels or after failed attempts. Applying a similar model to PC and console games is more complicated because game sessions can be longer and less structured. A fixed-timer interruption could cut into combat, dialogue or another important part of a game.
Microsoft's proposed approach would try to avoid that by tying ad delivery to in-game events. The result would be a system in which a player earns more play time by viewing an ad at a moment chosen by the game's own state.

articles.title: Así se filtró la clave pirata más famosa de Windows XP
articles.text:
Si eres de la generación de usuarios que creció con Windows XP, hay un alto porcentaje de probabilidades de que hayas usado la clave FCKGW-RHQQ2-YXRKT-8TG6W-2B7Q8 para instalarlo. Millones de personas que compraban o compartían versiones pirata del sistema operativo encontraban esta serie de letras y números escrita sobre el CD. A más de dos décadas de volverse popular, uno de los ingenieros que ayudó a diseñar el sistema anticopia de Windows XP reveló cómo se filtró esta clave.
Dave Plummer, exingeniero de Microsoft, publicó los detalles técnicos detrás de la filtración más famosa en la historia de Windows. Plummer, quien también desarrolló el Administrador de Tareas que todavía usamos hoy en día, mencionó en su cuenta de X que trabajó en Microsoft como uno de los responsables de la protección anticopia de Windows XP.
El antiguo empleado de Redmond explicó que no participó en las matemáticas que validaban las claves de producto, sino en la integración de ese sistema dentro de Windows. Su trabajo consistía en verificar qué tipo de disco usaba cada usuario, por lo que incluyó un bloque de datos oculto de unos 10 MB para diferenciar los discos para empresas (volumen) de los discos de retail.
Si no estás familiarizado con estos términos, los primeros se usan para que los administradores de sistemas puedan instalar el sistema operativo en múltiples equipos. Estas licencias por volumen ayudan a que el proceso sea más rápido cuando se hace en decenas o cientos de equipos, ya que usar una clave por equipo tomaría días o semanas. En contraste, los discos de retail tenían asignada una clave única que se validaba al instalar Windows XP en un ordenador de casa.
Cómo se filtró la clave FCKGW de Windows XP que todos usaron
De acuerdo con Plummer, la clave FCKGW solo funcionaba en discos de volumen que contenían ese bloque oculto de 10 MB. Si alguien intentaba usarla en un disco retail normal, la activación fallaba porque faltaba esa pieza. Hasta aquí todo va bien, pero el problema llegó cuando esa versión se filtró en internet con todo y clave.
Cinco semanas antes del lanzamiento de Windows XP, el grupo de piratería Devilsown publicó una imagen ISO completa de Windows XP Pro Corporate junto con la clave FCKGW. A partir de ahí, la comunidad comenzó a distribuir el archivo y a escribir la clave en las copias grabadas que se volvieron populares a comienzos de esa década.
Según Plummer, el origen de esta fuga fue un socio de hardware o fabricante OEM que recibió los discos finales antes de tiempo. Entre la lista de sospechosos se menciona a Dell, aunque también se ha dicho que Intel tuvo que ver, luego de que el fabricante apareciera en filtraciones posteriores. El exingeniero de Microsoft no está seguro de quién fue el responsable, pero señaló que la empresa tuvo que trabajar más para contener la filtración.
La respuesta oficial llegó con el Service Pack 1, que comenzó a bloquear los identificadores de producto asociados a las claves FCKGW. Después, con el Service Pack 2 y el programa Windows Genuine Advantage, Windows XP se volvió más agresivo e impidió las actualizaciones en equipos señalados como piratas.
Un detalle curioso es que ese bloque de datos oculto provenía de los archivos de Microsoft Bob. Este proyecto fallido de los años noventa evolucionó y se convirtió en el Clippy de Office.

articles.title: Kanin Energy raises $138 million for waste heat to power development | BetaKit
articles.text:
Calgary cleantech company Kanin Energy has secured significant capital for its “energy-as-a-service” (EaaS) business.
The news: Kanin announced a $138-million CAD new equity financing round on Sept. 16. The round was led by Chicago’s S2G Investments and Canada Growth Fund (CGF), both of which supplied $50 million USD (around $69 million CAD). Capital will support the development of Kanin’s waste-heat-to-power (WHP) projects in both the US and Canada.
From the source: “Rising power prices, grid congestion, and reliability constraints are pushing industrial companies to rethink how they source power. Waste heat has largely been an underused solution,” Marisa Sweeney, a principal at S2G Investments, said in a statement on the firm’s investment. “We view this as a category with real staying power.”
The context: Kanin operates out of both Calgary and Houston, with a focus on decarbonizing industrial waste heat through WHP projects that capture high-temperature exhaust and convert it to power without creating additional emissions. With several projects in development south of the border, Kanin is operating on an “energy-as-a-service” (EaaS) business model, where customers pay for energy services rather than the infrastructure itself. Kanin says investment from S2G and the Canada Growth Fund represents a significant milestone, as the company looks to scale its EaaS business model and expand its commercial pipeline.
Final thought: A beneficiary of several Canadian accelerator programs, including Plug and Play Alberta, MaRS, Canadian Tech Accelerator, and Foresight Canada, Kanin has leveraged the support it has received from accelerators and prior investment to quickly develop its footprint in the US market. Still, recent gains have come at a price. In an exclusive with Axios, CEO and founder Janice Tran said that, under the conditions of the raise, the company had ceded control of its board to investors to get the deal over the finish line. Tran cited increased difficulty for non-AI startups to access funds and the impacts of US-Canada tariff policies as reasons for the move.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.

articles.title: China’s DRAM Specialist CXMT Eyes NAND Flash Entry - EE Times
articles.text:
The NAND flash market is likely to have a new player, and it’s from China. ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), which has already shaken up the DRAM market, is reportedly preparing to enter NAND flash to capitalize on a global memory shortage driven by surging demand from AI servers. Data centers need more solid-state drives (SSDs)—built around NAND flash—to store AI workloads.
According to Reuters, the company is setting up an R&D production line for NAND chips at its new fab in Beijing. Moreover, CXMT has established a research institute in Beijing, where projects include the development of NAND flash technology. Reuters also quoted an unnamed startup in China that is currently in talks with CXMT to use its NAND chips in storage products for AI systems and supercomputers.
First and foremost, it’s noteworthy because CXMT is moving beyond its core DRAM business. China’s twin memory stars, CXMT and Yangtze Memory Technologies Corp. (YMTC), have so far operated strategically in two major memory segments: CXMT is China’s largest DRAM manufacturer, and YMTC leads the NAND market in China.
However, in April this year, Reuters reported that YMTC had sent low-power DRAM samples to customers as it weighed entry into CXMT’s core market. YMTC expects customer feedback by the end of 2026, which will help it decide whether to start DRAM production. Now CXMT is considering a foray into the NAND flash market.
On the surface, it may seem that CXMT and YMTC are readying to move into each other’s memory turf. However, both CXMT and YMTC are backed by China’s national semiconductor fund and local governments. CXMT grew with backing from Hefei, the provincial capital of Anhui province in eastern China; YMTC expanded with backing from Wuhan, the provincial capital of central Hubei province.
A flash window of opportunity
A closer look at CXMT and YMTC encroaching on each other’s memory territories shows it’s about more than sparking direct competition in China’s domestic market. CXMT’s entry into NAND could inevitably generate friction over domestic equipment distribution, cleanroom tooling quotas, and specialized engineering talent from regional institutions. However, it also eliminates single-supplier vulnerabilities for memory consumers in China.
Memory industry leaders Samsung and SK Hynix have maintained commanding positions across both DRAM and NAND markets, and Micron has followed suit, though it initially lagged in NAND flash. The dual-memory portfolio allows chipmakers such as Samsung to absorb market downturns by continuously shifting capital between DRAM and NAND operations.
Both CXMT and YMTC likely want to become one-stop shops for DRAM and NAND, just like their bigger rivals Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix. The timing couldn’t be better, amid a global memory shortage driven by AI server demand that industry executives expect to persist through at least 2027.
Both CXMT and YMTC could gain global market share by competing aggressively on price as memory supplies remain tight. However, according to the Korean newspaper Chosun Ilbo, that represents a longer-term competitive threat for global rivals rather than an immediate supply response.
At a time when the memory troika—Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix—has prioritized capital spending on DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM), limiting additions to NAND flash capacity and worsening shortages in this segment mark a window of opportunity for China’s largest memory chipmaker.
But the question is: How viable is this move? CXMT has neither announced a full commercial capacity target nor a publicly detailed production timetable.
Can CXMT pull it off?
Apparently, CXMT’s NAND plan is a work in progress. NAND flash is among the most capital-intensive undertakings in the semiconductor industry. It requires distinct tooling configurations and chemical supply chains, as well as completely different patent architectures compared to DRAM.
NAND manufacturing entails specialized process technology, production equipment, quality controls, and long-term design validation. Therefore, moving from an R&D line to commercially competitive volume production would involve substantial technical and financial challenges.
While the company is awash in cash after a blockbuster IPO, access to advanced chipmaking tools still poses significant challenges amid U.S. export controls. On the technical front, the shift from DRAM fabrication to vertical 3D NAND manufacturing creates steep operational challenges. DRAM relies on precise lateral photolithography to pattern dense capacitor networks at tiny dimensions, while 3D NAND devices are manufactured vertically.
So, CXMT, which spent the past decade developing a competitive DRAM technology, will most likely spend the next decade expanding beyond DRAM and into the NAND flash realm. This strategic expansion into flash memory also marks an inflection point in mainland China’s broader campaign to solidify semiconductor self-reliance across critical supply chains.

articles.title: Vous aimez les pubs sur Disney+ ? Parce qu'il y en aura aussi dans les formules Standard et Premium
articles.text:
Elle est déjà loin l’époque où la publicité était totalement absente des plateformes de streaming. Aujourd’hui, elle est envahissante. Dans un mail adressé à ses abonnés et intitulé « Mise à jour des Conditions générales d’abonnement », Disney+ annonce plusieurs changements dont un qui saute aux yeux. Désormais, tous les abonnements, y compris Standard et Premium, incluront bientôt de la publicité. Déjà que la formule Premium devenait compliquée à justifier…
Pour la rentrée, BNP Paribas propose une offre de bienvenue étudiante avec carte Visa incluse, paiements sans frais à l’étranger, prêt à 0,99% et jusqu’à 175€ d’avantages offerts (80€ offerts + 1 an gratuit à Esprit Libre).
    À lire aussi : 
    Vous passez 30 minutes à chercher quoi regarder ? Disney+ a enfin la solution
De la pub dans une formule à 16 €/mois…
Après la disparition de la 4K, du HDR10+ et du Dolby Vision de la formule Premium, celle-ci avait quasiment perdu tout intérêt. Alors attendez d’apprendre que la publicité pourra envahir tout Disney+ suite aux changements des conditions générales d’abonnement. Autant dire que cette annonce ne tombe pas au meilleur moment pour la plateforme de streaming qui enchaîne les déboires.
La firme aux grandes oreilles (qui sifflent) indique à ses abonnés que du contenu promotionnel, des messages de parrainage et des publicités seront diffusés avant ou après la lecture d’un programme. Cela concerne tous les abonnements, y compris les formules Standard (10,99 euros par mois) et Premium (15,99 euros par mois).
Une annonce qui survient tout juste un an après la dernière hausse des tarifs de Disney+. Peut-être échapperons-nous justement à une nouvelle augmentation grâce à cette stratégie de la pub omniprésente, mais on doute qu’elle soit au goût de tous les abonnés.
Ces changements entreront en vigueur dans les 30 jours à compter de la réception du mail, qui date du 13 septembre. Pour celles et ceux qui n’acceptent pas ces changements, Disney+ indique que les abonnés annuels à qui il reste plus d’un mois d’abonnement peuvent résilier dans les 30 jours suivant la réception du mail en contactant le support via téléphone ou le chat. Les abonnés ayant souscrit via leur FAI peuvent gérer leur abonnement directement auprès de celui-ci.

articles.title: Dérapage chez Google : Gemini a piraté 3 entreprises pendant un test qui a mal tourné
articles.text:
C’est au tour de Gemini de déraper ! Google vient de reconnaître que son IA a accédé sans autorisation aux systèmes de trois entreprises. L’incident remonte au mois de mai dernier, lors d’un test de cybersécurité réalisé par Irregular, une start-up israélienne. Spécialisée dans l’audit de sécurité des modèles d’IA avancés, la société s’est déjà retrouvée impliquée dans des incidents analogues, avec ChatGPT, l’IA d’OpenAI. Ces incidents s’étaient soldés par le piratage de la plateforme open source Hugging Face.
Dans les trois incidents recensés par Google, Irregular testait Gemini dans un environnement totalement fermé, peuplé d’entreprises fictives, qui était censé être coupé d’Internet. Par inadvertance, la prison numérique s’est retrouvée connectée à Internet. Une fois en ligne, le modèle d’IA a agi de façon autonome et s’est introduit dans les systèmes de véritables entreprises.
À lire aussi : Six ChatGPT hors de contrôle – OpenAI reconnaît plusieurs nouveaux dérapages « préoccupants »
Quand Gemini devine le mot de passe d’une entreprise
Dans le premier cas, Gemini devait extraire des informations depuis le logiciel d’une entreprise fictive portant le même nom qu’une société réelle. Ayant obtenu un accès involontaire à Internet, le modèle a deviné correctement le mot de passe de la véritable entreprise et s’est connecté à ses services. Google indique que le modèle s’est arrêté dès qu’il a compris qu’il ne s’agissait pas de l’environnement de test.
Dans deux autres cas, Gemini a recherché sur le web des dépôts publics contenant des identifiants de connexion, puis les a utilisés pour accéder aux serveurs des entreprises. Là encore, le modèle a cessé son action une fois qu’il a identifié qu’il s’agissait de cibles réelles et non d’une simulation.
« Lors d’une évaluation standard, le modèle a trouvé des informations publiques en ligne et deviné des identifiants pour accéder à des sites qu’il pensait faire partie du test. Dans les trois cas, le modèle s’est arrêté », déclare Heather Adkins, vice-présidente en charge de l’ingénierie de sécurité chez Google.
Google n’a pas divulgué l’affaire pendant des mois
La responsable a ajouté que « ces événements soulignent l’importance d’entraîner des modèles d’IA puissants à agir de manière responsable ». Irregular a signalé les intrusions à Google fin juillet, après avoir découvert qu’OpenAI avait, de son côté, piraté Hugging Face lors d’un test comparable. Pendant plusieurs mois, Google n’a pas jugé nécessaire de réaliser de divulgation publique. Le géant de Mountain View souligne que Gemini n’a causé aucun dommage aux entreprises concernées. Le groupe affirme néanmoins avoir prévenu les trois sociétés touchées et avoir travaillé avec Irregular pour faire évoluer son protocole de test.
Cet épisode s’inscrit dans une série d’incidents similaires au cours de ces derniers mois. En juillet, le modèle Claude d’Anthropic s’était échappé de son environnement de test pour pirater trois organisations, peu après que ChatGPT a mené des cyberattaques contre plusieurs services en ligne. Ces incidents ont poussé les géants de l’IA à plaider pour un moratoire sur le développement de l’intelligence artificielle. Pour Dario Amodei, PDG d’Anthropic, il faut impérativement lever le pied avant que des agents autonomes ne fassent de sérieux dégâts. Dans ce contexte, OpenAI, Google et Anthropic se sont mis à travailler main dans la main sur un outil commun de supervision des risques de l’IA.

articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max review - a bigger upgrade than it appears - Tech Guide
articles.text:
- Design
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are bigger upgrades than they appear. Apple has improved the tentpole features – performance, battery, Apple Intelligence and the camera to make it a pro-level device that's tailor-made for a high-end user and content creator.
It might not look like it from the outside but the new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max has had some solid upgrades including an upgraded camera, better battery life, Apple Intelligence and improved performance.
And what puts more focus on these new devices is the fact that there was no entry-level iPhone 18 announced.
These are always popular with customers because they are more affordable yet still packed full of features and an excellent camera.
So if the iPhone 18 Pro is more than what you need or can afford then you’ll have to wait till early next year to buy your next iPhone.
The cheapest iPhone 18 Pro is $2,099 for the 256GB variant. The cheapest iPhone 18 Pro Max is $2,299 (256GB).
DESIGN
Design-wise, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max is identical to the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max.
Apart from improved colour-matched aluminium and a range of new colours, including white, black, glacier and the new hero colour, burgundy – they are physically identical.
In fact cases for the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max will fit perfectly on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
The only change you can see is the smaller dynamic island – it’s about 25 per cent smaller – at the top of the Super Retina XDR display. But it can still display the same amount of information as before.
It’s smaller because of the Face ID Sensor has been moved under the display near the time.
There is a different pixel pattern here so the infrared sensor can still shine through and hit your face and register your identity to unlock the iPhone.
PERFORMANCE
The new iPhone 18 Pro series is powered by the A20 Pro chip that’s built on the latest 2nm technology with a new CPU, a GPU with even more cores, and a dual 16-core Neural Engine.
Apple took its inspiration for this new chip from the M series to offer improved heat dissipation that unlocks noticeable performance gains.
Speaking of heat dissipation, there is a new vapour chamber that has three times more surface area.
And with the new packaging of the A20 Pro chip, which places the memory layout and the silicon side by side, it is attached directly to the larger vapour chamber.
The result is your iPhone doesn’t feel warm very often.
During our review we found the iPhone 18 Pro Max hardly raised the temperature even while charging and using intensive and multiple apps.
Apple says it will provide 40 per cent better sustained performance and prevent thermal throttling during intense workloads.
iOS 27
The new iPhone 18 Pro series comes preloaded with iOS 27 which brings Apple Intelligence and Siri AI directly into the foreground.
One thing we noticed when setting up the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max was that our device was being indexed by Siri so that it could know everything about us (from our messages to our emails and photos), so it can present information when needed even if we don’t ask for it.
For example you may be calling about a hotel confirmation and on the screen you’ll see all the emails that you exchanged with that hotel. Information like confirmation numbers and dates is literally at your fingertips.
Some other Apple Intelligence features include editing images, communicating through messages and mail and browsing in Safari.
One example of a Safari feature is being updated about the price of an item that you may have seen. You can receive a notification the second the price drops on that item.
And the great thing is that you don’t need to upgrade to the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max to get these features.
If you have an iPhone 15 Pro or later you can upgrade your device to iOS 27 and enjoy these Apple Intelligence and Siri AI upgrades.
CAMERA
The biggest improvement has come to the Pro camera aboard the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which has a new 48MP Fusion main camera with variable aperture to improve low-light performance and achieve greater depth of field.
The variable aperture can be seen on the 48MP Fusion main camera, which is the lowest camera in the arrangement.
It has six laser-cut blades that are controlled by a new mechanism to transition between four aperture settings: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0.
If you look closely enough you can see the aperture changing as you move through these stops.
This benefits in two ways – a better result low-light situations and creating a greater depth of field.
At the lowest setting, f/1.8, this opens the aperture and lets in 50 per cent more light.
On auto mode the camera will intelligently select the best aperture for what you are shooting but you can access it and assume manual control to suit the shot you’re trying to capture.
But it also helps create more depth of field.
When the aperture narrows to f/2.8 or f/4.0, you’re getting much better detail in the background.
At f/1.48 and f/1.8 you can see greater depth of field – in other words a more blurred background.
In the past the iPhone achieved this computationally rather than physically with the lens and the light.
Now with this variable aperture you can really dig into the settings and be even more creative with your images.
If you look at the images we shot at the various aperture stops, you’ll see the background is a lot more blurred at the higher end (f/1/48, f/1.8) with more detail visible when the aperture is narrowed (f/2.8 and f/4.0).
The other great effect with the variable aperture is the starburst effect.
When you switch to f/4.0 and point it at a light source, you’ll see the starburst effect that’s created by the unique shape of the blades.
Another camera improvement includes being able to take time-lapse videos in 4K and Dolby Vision HDR.
Bottom line, Apple has delivered arguably the best camera you can find on a smartphone, thanks to its habit of bringing real camera features into the iPhone rather than trying to pass it off with gimmicks and software.
That’s why this is the go-to iPhone for anyone interested in photography and creating high-quality images and videos.
BATTERY
The iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max have had their biggest year to year leap in battery improvement.
The improvements come about because of the silicon upgrade that create efficiencies within the device, resulting in longer usage.
Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max has up to 43 hours of video playback and up to 34 hours with the iPhone 18 Pro.
Since we received the phone last week, we’ve seen the battery improvements quite clearly, resulting in up to a day and a half of use before needing to recharge.
PRICE
The iPhone 18 Pro is priced at $2,099 (256GB), $2,499 (512GB), $3,299 (1TB) and $4,499 (2TB).
At 256GB and 512GB the iPhone 18 Pro models are $100 more expensive than last year’s models.
And the 1TB model is $500 more expensive than the iPhone 17 Pro at the same capacity. Last year Apple didn’t offer an iPhone17 Pro with 2TB capacity.
Pricing for the iPhone 18 Pro Max is $2,299 (256GB), $2,699 (512GB), $3,499 (1TB) and $4,699 (2TB).
The 256GB and 512GB iPhone 18 Pro Max models are also $100 more expensive than the same capacity iPhone 17 Pro Max.
But the 1TB model and 2TB models are $500 and $900 more expensive, respectively than the iPhone 17 Pro Max at those same capacities.
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are ideal for the customer who wants the best camera on an iPhone or has been waiting a few years to upgrade.
If you have an iPhone 17 Pro or iPhone 17 Pro Max there’s no need to upgrade but if you’re rocking an iPhone 15 or older, then the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max are well worth a look.
VERDICT
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are bigger upgrades than they appear. Apple has improved the tentpole features – performance, battery, Apple Intelligence and the camera to make it a pro-level device that’s tailor-made for a high-end user and content creator.

articles.title: Votre box Wi-Fi bride votre smartphone ? Le réglage caché pour doubler le débit
articles.text:
Votre box Wi-Fi bride votre smartphone ? Le réglage caché pour doubler le débit
Votre téléphone est compatible Wi-Fi 7, votre box aussi, et pourtant le débit stagne. En cause, des réglages d'usine volontairement prudents qui gardent la connexion sur les vieilles fréquences. En ouvrant la bande 6 GHz et en activant le mode MLO, on peut faire bondir le débit réel d'un smartphone bien au-delà de 2 Gb/s. À condition d'avoir le bon matériel.
Vous venez de recevoir la fibre à 8 Gb/s et un smartphone flambant neuf. Sur le papier, de quoi télécharger un film en quelques secondes. Dans les faits, l'application de test affiche péniblement 800 Mb/s en Wi-Fi, à peine mieux qu'avec votre ancien téléphone. Frustrant, et surtout injustifié, car la puissance est bien là, tapie dans votre box. Elle attend juste qu'on la libère.
Pourquoi votre box se bride toute seule
À sa sortie d'usine, une box est réglée pour ne froisser personne, surtout pas vos plus vieux appareils. Le raisonnement des fabricants est simple : un réseau domestique accueille des dizaines d'équipements de générations différentes, du smartphone récent à l'ampoule connectée d'il y a cinq ans. Activer d'emblée les fonctions les plus avancées du Wi-Fi 7 risquerait de dérouter ces anciens matériels, provoquant déconnexions et erreurs. Par prudence, la box privilégie donc les fréquences historiques, le 2,4 et le 5 GHz, et laisse dormir le meilleur.
Asus ZenWiFi BT8
Ce meilleur porte deux noms. D'abord la bande 6 GHz, la plus rapide et la moins encombrée, souvent désactivée ou réservée en coulisses à la liaison entre la box et ses répéteurs. Ensuite le mode MLO, pour Multi-Link Operation, la vraie rupture du Wi-Fi 7. Là où les générations précédentes rattachaient un appareil à une seule fréquence, le MLO lui permet d'en utiliser plusieurs en même temps, le 5 et le 6 GHz combinés par exemple, additionnant leurs capacités tout en réduisant la latence. C'est ce cumul qui propulse un mobile compatible au-delà des 2 Gb/s réels.
Les réglages qui libèrent le débit
La manœuvre se joue dans l'interface d'administration de la box, accessible depuis un navigateur ou l'application de l'opérateur. Trois réglages font la différence. Ouvrez d'abord la bande 6 GHz aux appareils clients, et forcez si possible la largeur de canal sur 320 MHz, la plus généreuse, au lieu des 160 MHz par défaut. Activez ensuite le mode MLO, souvent via un réseau dédié qui diffuse sous un même nom sur le 5 et le 6 GHz. Vérifiez enfin que la sécurité est bien en WPA3, car le vieux WPA2 bride automatiquement les débits du Wi-Fi 7.
Un dernier maillon est à surveiller, côté matériel. Le port utilisé et le câble reliant la box doivent suivre la cadence : un port à 2,5 ou 10 Gb/s et un câble de catégorie 6A au minimum, sans quoi le filaire devient le goulot d'étranglement. Ces réglages en place, le smartphone compatible établit deux liaisons parallèles et exploite enfin toute la fibre.
Tous les téléphones et box ne se valent pas
Reste une réalité à connaître avant de se lancer, car la promesse a ses limites. Du côté des smartphones, la fracture est nette. Les Android récents, Samsung Galaxy S25 et S26, Google Pixel 8, 9 et 10, exploitent les canaux de 320 MHz et grimpent au-delà de 2,5 Gb/s. Les iPhone 16 et 17, eux, plafonnent : Apple limite la largeur de canal à 160 MHz, et le débit réel stagne autour de 1,5 à 1,8 Gb/s, MLO activé ou non.
TP-Link TP-Link Deco BE25
Côté box, le piège est plus sournois. Toutes les box estampillées Wi-Fi 7 ne se valent pas, et beaucoup, en France, sont bi-bande : elles ne diffusent que sur le 2,4 et le 5 GHz, sans la fameuse bande 6 GHz. Sur ces modèles, ouvrir le 6 GHz est tout simplement impossible, et le MLO n'offre qu'une fraction de son potentiel. Avant de plonger dans les réglages, vérifiez donc que votre box est bien tri-bande (voir encadré). Sans 6 GHz, l'astuce du doublement de débit restera hors de portée, quel que soit votre smartphone.

articles.title: Des pluies de rayons cosmiques ont été créées pour la première fois en laboratoire
articles.text:
Depuis la Terre, il peut arriver que de grandes traînées lumineuses vertes ou rouges traversent le ciel, notamment dans les latitudes les plus élevées, mais aussi parfois jusqu’à la France. Le phénomène des aurores boréales, s’il n’est pas familier à tout un chacun, reste un processus vu très régulièrement depuis le sol et qui fascine à travers le monde.
Mais dans l’espace, ce sont des phénomènes bien plus complexes, et parfois difficiles à expliquer, qui se déroulent. Pour en savoir plus, une équipe de la collaboration ATLAS, menée par le physicien Jesse Liu (université de New York), a mobilisé les capacités du Grand Collisionneur de Hadrons, cet immense accélérateur de particules installé au CERN, en Suisse. Ils publient leurs résultats dans la revue scientifique Physical Review Letters.
Voir une gerbe de particules cosmiques de plus près
Dans leur « état naturel », les gerbes de particules cosmiques se forment lorsque des rayons cosmiques – des particules très énergétiques venues de l’espace, le plus souvent des protons – entrent en collision avec l’atmosphère terrestre. Plus précisément, ces rayons heurtent des particules de gaz présents dans la haute atmosphère terrestre. L’énergie libérée par ces collisions engendre une cascade de nouvelles particules qui file vers le sol. Attention toutefois : ces gerbes ne se confondent pas avec les aurores boréales évoquées plus haut. Ces dernières, bien moins énergétiques, sont dues au vent solaire canalisé par le champ magnétique terrestre.
Mais les détails de tous ces mécanismes restent encore bien flous pour les spécialistes de la question, ce qui les a poussés à observer le phénomène de plus près, et sans se reposer sur des simulations informatiques qui, selon les paramètres, provoquent l’apparition de résultats contradictoires. D’autant plus lorsque l’on fait entrer dans l’équation des phénomènes autrement plus violents que ceux qui se déroulent à la surface du Soleil.
Dans le Grand Collisionneur de Hadrons, les scientifiques ont fait se percuter des noyaux d’oxygène et des protons, afin de recréer sur place le genre de rayons cosmiques qui apparaissent lors d’une supernova. L’idée étant de comprendre ce qui se passe lorsque les rayons cosmiques sont très différents de ceux qui sont créés par le Soleil lors de ses éruptions.
Mieux que par ordinateur
La collision entre les protons, qui jouent le rôle du rayon cosmique issu d’une supernova, et les noyaux d’oxygène, qui représentent l’atmosphère terrestre, constitue la première mesure en laboratoire d’une gerbe de particules cosmiques.
Pour observer tout cela, les auteurs de l’étude se sont servis d’une caméra à 100 millions de pixels pour capter le maximum de collisions, sachant qu’il y en a eu environ 40 millions par seconde ! Les premiers résultats ne révèlent pas les secrets des mécanismes qui se déroulent lors de ces phénomènes. En revanche, ils confirment une chose. Les simulations informatiques qui tentent d’en saisir la complexité sont à côté de la plaque.
Les premières mesures réalisées ainsi montrent que les précédents modèles ne correspondent pas à ce qui se joue en réalité lorsque les particules cosmiques entrent en collision avec les atmosphères des planètes. Des données d’autant plus utiles que le peu d’interactions réelles dont nous pouvons être témoins concerne uniquement le couple Terre-Soleil, ou, plus rarement, Mars. Mais lorsqu’il s’agit d’étoiles plus grosses, plus brillantes ou plus actives que la nôtre, les réactions peuvent être tout autres.

articles.title: London’s Unit1 Studio secures €23.3 million to scale avatar concerts beyond the one-venue ABBA Voyage model | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Unit1 Studio, the London-based end-to-end avatar concert producer, has raised €23.3 million (£20 million) in new financing.
The round combines an oversubscribed equity investment with additional production financing. The equity round was led by Balderton Capital. Existing investors Mercuri, Gilston Music, and Paul McGuinness, long-time manager of U2, also participated in the round.
“Until now, avatar concerts have been locked behind the economics of ABBA Voyage – a one-off, one-location proposition. Unit1’s innovative new technology will fundamentally change that, opening up the genre to a whole generation of legacy artists,” said Daniel Waterhouse, General Partner at Balderton.
The funding comes as Unit1 announced it has successfully moved its KT Tunstall avatar demo-concert from Brompton Technology’s testing facility in Gunnersbury, west London, to a new permanent studio at Tileyard London. The company says it completed the relocation in just four days, a process that has traditionally been costly and time-consuming for avatar production.
Unit1 Studio produces immersive avatar concerts that recreate live performances by artists, aiming to connect fans with musicians regardless of time or geography. The company is led by CEO Barney Wragg, formerly of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Really Useful Group (now LW Entertainment) and a veteran of AEG, EMI and Universal Music Group.
He is joined by Creative Director Jonathan Butterell, known for the West End musical and BAFTA-nominated film Everyone’s Talking About Jamie, and Technical Director Pavle Mihajlovic, co-founder of video game studios Electric Saint and Flavourworks.
The company has also strengthened its creative bench by bringing in hyper-real avatar creators Greg Meeres Young (known for work on Planet of the Apes and Lord of the Rings) and Sefki Ibrahim, who worked on ABBA Voyage. John Kennedy, former Chairman/CEO of Universal Music UK and the IFPI, has joined the board as a non-executive director.
“Barney is hugely respected in the industry and has managed to solve a structural problem that everyone knew existed but nobody had cracked. As a founder, Barney brings a unique blend of creative vision and commercial nous to every project that he sets his mind to, and having followed his journey for many years I couldn’t be more delighted to formally partner for the next chapter of Unit1,” added Waterhouse.
Unit1 Studio says ABBA Voyage has demonstrated audience appetite for avatar concerts of artists no longer touring. However, the cost of developing and replicating similar productions has kept the format out of reach for most artists. With its technology, Unit1 Studio argues that it will now be possible to replicate similar productions across multiple venues simultaneously.
The company aims to match how the touring theatre productions are adapted for different cities and open the door to shows that recoup development costs within twelve months.
“Unit1 is, and will always be, about expanding the connection between fan and artist regardless of time or geography. ABBA Voyage proved audiences love avatar concerts but the development and relocation costs have meant the opportunity of avatar concerts is not being realised,” said Barney Wragg, founder and CEO of Unit1 Studio.
He added, “Our ability to develop these shows at a fraction of the cost and replicate them to any location finally makes these shows a commercial reality. The combination of our technology, new financing and our growing team, means we can develop shows for artists and fans worldwide.”
The financing will fund Unit1’s expanding roster of concerts in development, though the company has not yet disclosed which artists it is working with, saying announcements will follow once tickets go on sale.

articles.title: The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics
articles.text:
The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics
- Date:
- September 15, 2026
- Source:
- Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo
- Summary:
- A mathematical shape famous for covering a surface without ever repeating has revealed an unexpected ability to twist light into unusual chiral patterns. The discovery could lead to new ways of controlling light, polarization, and advanced optical devices.
- Share:
A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to new ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.
In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.
The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem
The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.
Familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.
In 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.
"What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," says lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena."
Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure
To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.
When laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.
Chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.
"We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials."
Light Responds to Direction and Polarization
The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.
When the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This showed that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a new type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.
"These results open a new direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity."
From Abstract Mathematics to New Optical Physics
The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.
More broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover new ways to control and study light.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yuto Moritake, Masato Takiguchi, Takuma Aihara, Masaya Notomi. Chiral diffraction from aperiodic monotile structure. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75023-7

articles.title: Tesla quiere conquistar Europa con el Semi, su camión eléctrico, y acaba de anunciar un paso clave para conseguirlo
articles.text:
Tesla ya ha puesto cifras a sus planes de carga para su camión Semi en Europa. En la feria IAA Transportation de Hannover, el responsable de desarrollo del camión, Dan Priestley, confirmó que la empresa instalará más de 100 puntos de carga con capacidad de 1 megavatio en 21 ubicaciones del continente, según compartían desde InsideEVs.
El anuncio. Priestley dijo que la primera oleada de ubicaciones llegará a Alemania, Francia, el Reino Unido, Suecia y los países del Benelux, siendo éstos los países a los que llegarán primero sus cargadores de megavatio. No se dieron fechas de apertura ni ubicaciones exactas, y de hecho el propio Semi no llegará a Europa hasta 2027. Así que aún tendremos que esperar para conocer más detalles al respecto.
Camión e infraestructura. Un camión eléctrico, evidentemente, necesita de una buena infraestructura de carga para operar en óptimas condiciones. En EEUU, el negocio de Tesla con Semi ha sido más o menos anecdótico. En Europa está por ver, aunque en el continente sí tenemos una infraestructura de carga más madura.
El hardware Megacharger de Tesla tiene una capacidad nominal de 1,2 megavatios, pero la versión europea del Semi alcanza un máximo de 800 kW de potencia de carga. Esto sigue permitiendo recargas rápidas durante las pausas obligatorias del conductor, algo fundamental para la viabilidad de los camiones eléctricos en Europa.
Infraestructura compartida. Tesla afirma que la red no será exclusiva para sus propios camiones. Tanto el Semi como el cargador utilizan el conector MCS 3.2, el enchufe de megavatio de siete pines estándar de la industria, y Tesla también distribuirá adaptadores CCS para que los propietarios del Semi puedan utilizar otros cargadores en todo el continente. Así que Tesla está construyendo sobre un estándar compartido en lugar de uno propietario, algo que no siempre ha hecho con los Supercargadores de sus coches.
La competencia. Tesla no está sola en este sector y ni siquiera es el actor más grande. Milence, una empresa conjunta entre Daimler Truck, Traton y Volvo, ya opera 13 estaciones de carga en seis países europeos tras abrir su primera ubicación en el puerto de Amberes-Brujas en febrero de 2025. Con el respaldo de 111,5 millones de euros de financiación de la UE para un proyecto llamado MILES, Milence tiene como objetivo construir 284 puntos de carga de megavatio y 264 puntos CCS en 71 ubicaciones de diez estados miembros para finales de 2027, un objetivo que supera con creces las 21 ubicaciones iniciales de Tesla.
El modelo de negocio. En lugar de limitarse a construir cargadores públicos, Tesla también vende el hardware directamente a las empresas. Su programa “Semi Charging for Business” ya está activo en Alemania, los Países Bajos, Bélgica, Francia y el Reino Unido, lo que permite a los operadores logísticos comprar Megachargers o Basechargers para sus propios depósitos. Un paquete Megacharger, con un armario de potencia y dos puntos de carga, cuesta unos 163.000 euros; el Basecharger más pequeño, de 120 kW, cuesta 17.000 euros, aunque debe pedirse por parejas. Se espera que las entregas comiencen hacia mediados de 2027, el mismo año en que en principio llegará el propio camión.
Sin presión legal. A diferencia de los planes de Tesla, nada de esto viene exigido por la legislación de la UE. La normativa solo exige puntos de carga convencionales para camiones de al menos 350 kW cada 60 km en la red principal y cada 100 km en la secundaria para 2030. La infraestructura de cargadores a nivel de megavatio que están construyendo Tesla y Milence es una apuesta comercial, no una obligación legal, orientada a dar servicio a camiones eléctricos de larga distancia que necesitan una recarga rápida durante la pausa de 45 minutos que los conductores deben hacer cada cuatro horas y media.
El verdadero cuello de botella. Incluso con el hardware listo, el factor limitante puede no ser la velocidad de despliegue de Tesla, sino la propia red eléctrica. Un depósito logístico que opere una flota eléctrica necesita mucha más potencia de la que consume actualmente, y los tiempos de conexión a la red en partes de Europa pueden prolongarse varios años en lugar de meses, según recuerdan desde The Next Web.
Próximos pasos. Por ahora, Tesla no ha abierto ni un solo Megacharger público en Europa y no ha nombrado ubicaciones exactas, corredores ni fechas de lanzamiento para los 21 sitios. El despliegue se probará junto con el propio camión a partir de 2027, cuando está previsto que lleguen tanto el hardware como las primeras entregas europeas del Semi. Así que hasta esa fecha toca esperar.

articles.title: Gemini hacked three companies during security tests, and Google kept it quiet for months
articles.text:
What just happened? With OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta all hitting the headlines for their AI agents going rogue, it seems that Google might have been feeling a bit superior – but apparently not. The company has confirmed that its Gemini AI breached the systems of three other companies during cybersecurity tests. In one instance, it repeatedly guessed passwords until it found the right one, and Google wasn't very forthcoming about what happened.
The incidents, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, took place in May during an evaluation by AI security firm Irregular. Gemini was supposed to work with fictional companies in a controlled test environment. However, an unintended internet connection gave the model access to real websites, and it treated them as part of the exercise.
In one test, Gemini was asked to retrieve information from software belonging to a fake company that shared its name with a real business. The AI guessed passwords until it gained access to the real firm's protected system.
In the other cases, the model found credentials in public online repositories and used them to enter two more companies' systems.
Google says that in all three instances, Gemini stopped once it realized the targets were real. The company didn't disclose the incidents publicly when Irregular informed it in late July. It says no damage was done, the affected organizations were notified, and the testing procedures have since been changed. Google has not named the companies or identified which Gemini model was involved.
Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, said the incidents show why powerful AI models need to be trained to act responsibly. Google maintains that the model was trying to complete its assigned task, rather than deliberately seeking out victims.
This is just the latest in a series of similar incidents involving big AI companies. OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face and compromised accounts across several other services after escaping a test environment. Anthropic disclosed that Claude models accessed three organizations' production systems during evaluations; another model tried to trick a real developer into accepting malicious code.
Meta's model also reached the internet during an Irregular test and breached a third-party service. Meta blamed the breach on a testing misconfiguration. Unsurprisingly, Google and the other companies never publicly apologized for any of these breaches.
These incidents, alongside warnings from AI developers themselves, have intensified fears that the technology could threaten humanity's survival. We've also seen Anthropic boss Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and xAI owner Elon Musk support calls for a slowdown in frontier model development.
Elsewhere, Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar have announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would permanently ban the development and deployment of superintelligent AI and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator has established safety rules. Individuals who violate the proposed restrictions could face up to 20 years in prison.

articles.title: CrowdSec Confirms Source Code Stolen in Supply Chain Attack
articles.text:
French cybersecurity firm CrowdSec has confirmed that approximately 300 private and public repositories were compromised and source code was stolen from them.
The company provides open source, crowdsourced threat intelligence, including a lightweight security engine to detect and block attacks targeting servers, networks, and applications.
Last week, the French outfit learned that source code had been stolen from its GitHub repositories in May 2026.
CrowdSec has confirmed the report, noting that both private and public code was exfiltrated, and that roughly 300 repositories were affected, including approximately 170 private ones.
“The private part contains the source code for our SaaS console, some AWS Cloud routines, some connectors, and automations,” the company said.
According to CrowdSec, no credentials or other types of data related to its customers were leaked, and the impact is limited to its own organization.
“Our team quickly hunted for any token, credential, or sensitive leak that could enable lateral movement but found none so far,” it said.
Additionally, the cybersecurity firm says that, while valuable, the code stolen from its private repositories cannot be used to cause harm, as it can not replicate its network and can only be used with its data and tools; therefore, it cannot be used out of context.
“We regularly audited the SaaS source code, and its leakage shouldn’t pose an immediate threat either. Most of the leaked code has evolved significantly over those four months, but we will closely monitor for any abnormal activity,” CrowdSec says.
The data breach, it explains, was likely a direct result of the May 2026 TanStack supply chain attack, in which TeamPCP published 84 malicious artifacts across 42 TanStack packages.
Because CrowdSec used a TanStack package in May, the malware used in the campaign likely compromised an API key that allowed the attackers to read its private codebase.
The leak likely occurred in May, during the short exploitation window, and CrowdSec immediately rotated all potentially affected tokens and credentials.

articles.title: Collapse of mainstream optical drive supply kills high-end CD players — PS Audio and Naim halt production as component costs double
articles.text:
Collapse of mainstream optical drive supply kills high-end CD players — PS Audio and Naim halt production as component costs double
What would happen if the optical drive on your Hi-Fi player fails and replacements are no longer available?
Many audiophiles still prefer physical media like CDs and vinyl over streaming, especially those who want to own their music, which is why we’re seeing a resurgence in sales for these media. However, one major concern hitting some Hi-Fi brands is the lack of optical drives built for mainstream computers, which has caused the supply chain for key components to dry up. According to Headphonesty, Naim’s Uniti Star and PS Audio’s PMG Super Audio CD Transport have ended production because their suppliers no longer make the optical hardware these units need.
Unfortunately, both companies cannot easily find replacements for these out-of-production components. “The drives appropriate for a PMG are no longer available,” PS Audio CEO Paul McGowan said in the company forum. He also added that building its own optical disc reader is beyond PS Audio’s capabilities, saying that its expertise is in electronics and software. It’s also the same problem that Naim is facing, with one commenter in its own forum saying that it assembles components instead of manufacturing them from raw parts and materials.
PS Audio’s problems began in June 2024, when D&M Holdings, which owns Denon and Marantz, said that it would stop taking orders for its SACD/CD mechanism by the end of the following month. This meant that the company needed to place its final order before the deadline, with costs doubling as other brands scrambled to build their stockpiles. This was probably because D&M was the only company producing and selling that particular component to third parties. McGowan stated that Marantz has ended production of its SACD/CD drives and that PS Audio has completely bought out the company’s last remaining inventory.
While it’s unclear which supplier Naim used for its Uniti Star Streaming Amplifier, it’s been said that the company did consider an alternative supplier for its optical drives. Unfortunately, this is not an easy swap in the production line, as these optical media readers are often built as an assembly, meaning installing a different model requires new control codes and mechanical tweaks inside these units. As Naim was considering how to integrate this substitute drive into its existing Uniti Star product, the alternative ceased production as well.
You can still buy Hi-Fi CD players and transports today, but these units from Naim and PS Audio are already out of stock if you want them brand new. Thankfully, the two companies keep some components in their inventory for repairs, so existing owners don’t have to worry about getting their expensive systems bricked just because the optical readers on their devices have failed.

Jowi Morales is a tech enthusiast with years of experience working in the industry. He’s been writing with several tech publications since 2021, where he’s been interested in tech hardware and consumer electronics.
